sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what Kubernetes is and what problem it solves, how it differs from Docker and Docker Compose, the core objects to know, and whether you really need it.

Kubernetes runs containers across a group of machines and keeps them running. You describe what you want. Five copies of this image, reachable at this address, with this much memory, and it works continuously to make reality match that description.

The word people use is declarative. You do not tell Kubernetes to start a container. You tell it what should be true, and controllers inside the cluster keep checking reality against that and correcting the difference. That single idea explains most of how Kubernetes behaves, including the parts that seem strange at first.

sections.title: The problem it solves
paragraphs: Running one container is easy. docker run and you are done.

The difficulty arrives with the questions that follow. What happens when the process crashes at 3am? When the machine it is on dies? When traffic triples and you need more copies, and where do they go? How do you deploy a new version without dropping requests? How does one service find another when addresses keep changing?

Every one of those has an answer without Kubernetes. The answers tend to be scripts, a load balancer someone configures by hand, a runbook, and a person who knows how it all fits together. Kubernetes replaces that with a system that does it continuously and identically whether you have three containers or three thousand.

sections.title: A concrete example
paragraphs: An API runs three replicas. A node fails, taking one with it.
Without an orchestrator: your monitoring alerts, someone wakes up, starts a replacement somewhere, updates the load balancer, and confirms. Fifteen minutes if things go well.

With Kubernetes: a controller notices that observed state (two replicas) does not match desired state (three), schedules a replacement on a healthy node, and the Service starts routing to it once its readiness probe passes. Typically under a minute, with nobody involved.
Nothing here required intervention, and nothing behaves differently at 3am.

sections.title: Kubernetes vs Docker Compose
paragraphs: The most useful comparison, because most people arrive from Compose.

Compose is genuinely better for local development and for a single-server deployment. It is simpler, faster to write, and easier to reason about. The moment you need more than one machine, or zero-downtime deploys, or automatic scaling, Compose stops being enough, and that is precisely the boundary where Kubernetes starts being worth its complexity.

Docker and Kubernetes are not alternatives, incidentally. Docker builds the images; Kubernetes runs them across machines. Kubernetes stopped using Docker as its runtime in version 1.24, but images built with Docker work exactly as before, because they follow the OCI standard.

sections.title: The objects you need on day one
paragraphs: You can be productive knowing five things.
Cluster: the whole system: a control plane that makes decisions and worker nodes that run your containers.
Node: one machine, virtual or physical, that runs workloads.

Pod: the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules. Usually one container, occasionally a couple that must share a network namespace and lifecycle. Pods are disposable; they are created and destroyed constantly.
Deployment: declares how many identical Pods should exist and handles rolling updates and rollbacks. This is what you write for a stateless application.
Service: a stable name and address in front of a changing set of Pods. Pod IPs change constantly; Service addresses do not.
Put together: a Deployment keeps three Pods running across your Nodes, and a Service gives clients one address that reaches whichever Pods currently exist.
Delete one and watch what happens:
A replacement appears within seconds. Nobody asked for it. The Deployment simply observed that there were two Pods where three were wanted.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80

Assigns pods to nodes
Reconciles desired state
Cloud Controller Manager

The control plane decides what should happen. The API server is the only way in, and everything, kubectl, controllers, the nodes themselves, talks to it. etcd stores cluster state. The scheduler picks nodes for new Pods. Controllers watch for differences between desired and actual state and act on them.
Worker nodes do the work. The kubelet on each node starts and monitors containers and reports back. kube-proxy programs the networking rules that make Services reachable.

The split matters because it explains failure behaviour. If the control plane goes down, running Pods keep running and keep serving traffic. You just cannot change anything or replace failed Pods. It is a management outage, not necessarily a service outage.

sections.title: Do you actually need Kubernetes?
paragraphs: Worth asking honestly, because the answer is often no.

Probably not if you run a single application on one or two servers, your team is small and has no Kubernetes experience, you deploy a few times a month, or a managed platform like ECS, Cloud Run, App Runner or Fly.io covers what you need. Kubernetes is a real operational commitment. Upgrades, networking, storage, RBAC, and a steady stream of things to keep current.

Probably yes if you run many services that need to be deployed independently, you need zero-downtime deploys and autoscaling as a matter of routine, you are running across multiple environments or clouds and want one deployment model, or your team is already large enough for a platform function.

The honest failure mode is a small team adopting Kubernetes for a single application and then spending more time on the cluster than on the product. If you are unsure, start with something managed and move when you feel a specific limitation, not before.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is Kubernetes in simple terms?

Kubernetes is a system that runs containers across a group of machines and keeps them running. You give it a description of what should be true. How many copies of an application, how much memory each gets, how they are reached, and it continuously compares that against reality and fixes any difference. If a container crashes it is restarted; if a machine dies its workloads are moved elsewhere; if you change the image it rolls out the new version gradually. You describe the destination rather than the steps.
What is the difference between Docker and Kubernetes?

They do different jobs and are usually used together. Docker builds container images and runs containers on a single machine. Kubernetes takes images, which may well have been built with Docker, and runs them across many machines with scheduling, health checking, load balancing, rolling updates and scaling. Kubernetes removed Docker as its container runtime in version 1.24, but that changed nothing for users. Images follow the OCI standard, so Docker-built images run on Kubernetes exactly as before.
Should I learn Docker before Kubernetes?

Yes. Kubernetes assumes you already understand images, containers, ports, volumes and environment variables, and a great many Kubernetes problems turn out to be container problems wearing a disguise: a wrong entrypoint, a missing environment variable, a process writing to a path that is not persisted. Being comfortable with docker build, docker run and writing a Dockerfile will make the Kubernetes learning curve markedly shorter.
Is Kubernetes overkill for a small project?

Often, yes. If you run one application on one or two servers, deploy occasionally, and have no one with Kubernetes experience, the operational overhead. Upgrades, networking, storage, access control, and keeping up with a fast-moving ecosystem. Will likely cost more than it returns. Docker Compose on a single server, or a managed platform such as ECS, Cloud Run or App Runner, is a perfectly respectable choice. Move to Kubernetes when you hit a specific limitation you can name.
What is the difference between Kubernetes and Docker Compose?

Compose orchestrates containers on one machine; Kubernetes orchestrates them across a cluster. Both restart a crashed container, but only Kubernetes reschedules workloads when an entire machine fails, performs rolling updates without downtime, scales automatically on load, and uses health probes to decide which instances receive traffic. Compose is simpler and better for local development and single-server deployments. The crossover point is the second machine.
How long does it take to learn Kubernetes?

Deploying an application and understanding Pods, Deployments and Services takes a few days of hands-on work. Being genuinely comfortable. Debugging networking, understanding storage and access modes, reasoning about scheduling and resource limits, and operating upgrades. Takes months of real use. The most effective approach is a local cluster with kind or minikube and deliberately breaking things: delete Pods, set a memory limit too low, misconfigure a probe. The failure modes are what you actually need to recognise.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand Kubernetes architecture: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet and kube-proxy, and what happens when you run kubectl apply.
A Kubernetes cluster splits into two halves. The control plane decides what should happen. The nodes make it happen.
Knowing which component does what is not trivia. It is what turns "the cluster is broken" into a specific thing to check.
Entry point for all requests
Assigns pods to nodes
Reconciles desired state
Cloud Controller Manager
Integrates with cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure)

sections.title: Control plane
paragraphs: The only door into the cluster. Every component, kubectl, controllers, the scheduler, the kubelets on every node, talks exclusively to the API server, and none of them talk to each other or to etcd directly.
It authenticates the caller, authorises the request against RBAC, runs admission controllers that can mutate or reject the object, validates it, and writes it to etcd.
It is stateless, so it scales horizontally, and production clusters run several behind a load balancer.

When it fails: you lose all control. kubectl stops working, no deployments, no scaling, no self-healing. Running Pods keep running and keep serving traffic, because nodes do not need it to keep doing what they are already doing.

A distributed key-value store holding the entire cluster state. Every object, its spec and its status. Nothing else in Kubernetes is stateful. Lose etcd without a backup and you have lost the cluster, even with every node still healthy.

It uses Raft consensus, which is why you run an odd number of members. A three-member cluster tolerates one failure; five tolerates two. Four is worse than three. More nodes to fail, the same tolerance.
etcd is sensitive to disk latency in a way people underestimate. Slow disks produce leader elections, which look like random cluster-wide instability. Give it fast SSDs.
On a managed cluster, EKS, GKE, AKS, the provider runs and backs up etcd, which is a large part of what you are paying for.
Watches for Pods with no node assigned and picks one. It does not start anything; it writes the chosen node onto the Pod, and that node's kubelet does the rest.

Two phases: filtering removes nodes that cannot run the Pod (not enough free CPU or memory, a taint with no matching toleration, an unsatisfiable node selector or affinity rule, no access to the required volume), then scoring ranks the survivors and the highest wins.
When it fails: new Pods sit in Pending forever. Everything already running is unaffected.
That is also the clue when a single Pod is stuck Pending. The scheduler filtered out every node, and kubectl describe pod reports exactly why:
One binary running many controllers, each an independent loop: observe current state, compare to desired state, act on the difference.
When it fails: nothing self-heals. Deleted Pods are not replaced, failed nodes are not drained, deployments do not progress. Existing workloads keep serving.
Where present, this is the part that talks to the cloud provider: provisioning load balancers for LoadBalancer Services, attaching storage volumes, and updating node metadata such as region and zone.
When it fails: LoadBalancer Services stay <pending> and volumes do not attach.

codeBlock.code:
# Back it up. This is the one thing you cannot recreate.
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%F).db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

sections.title: Node components
paragraphs: The agent on every node. It watches the API server for Pods assigned to it, tells the container runtime to start them, mounts their volumes, runs their probes, and reports status back.

It is the component that actually runs your containers, and it is deliberately independent: a kubelet that cannot reach the API server keeps its existing containers running. That is why a control plane outage does not stop traffic.

When it fails: the node stops reporting and is marked NotReady. After roughly five minutes the node controller starts evicting its Pods so they can be rescheduled elsewhere, but the containers on the failed node may still be running, which is why a partitioned node is a genuinely awkward failure.
Implements Services. It watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs the node's iptables or IPVS rules so traffic to a Service's virtual IP is rewritten to a real Pod IP.
The key insight: there is no proxy process in the request path. kube-proxy writes kernel rules and gets out of the way. That is why Service load balancing is per-connection and cannot inspect HTTP.
When it fails: existing rules stay in place so current Services keep working, but new Services and changed endpoints are not programmed.
Actually runs the containers, containerd most commonly, or CRI-O. Kubernetes talks to it through the Container Runtime Interface.
Docker was removed as a supported runtime in Kubernetes 1.24. This changed nothing about images: Docker builds OCI images and containerd runs them.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe node <name>    # conditions: MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, Ready

sections.title: What happens when you run kubectl apply
paragraphs: Request flow: kubectl → running pod
Validates & persists to etcd
Pulls image & starts container
✓ Desired state achieved
Validates & persists to etcd
Pulls image & starts container
✓ Desired state achieved

Nothing in that chain is a direct call between components. Each one watches the API server and reacts. That is why Kubernetes is resilient to any single piece being briefly unavailable, and why "eventually consistent" describes its behaviour better than "immediate".

sections.title: Control plane vs node, side by side
paragraphs: Control plane nodes normally carry a taint preventing workloads from being scheduled there. Removing it on a single-node dev cluster is standard; doing it in production means an application can starve the control plane.

paragraphs: kube-scheduler crashes and does not restart. What is the observable effect on the cluster?
A team runs a four-member etcd cluster for extra safety. How many member failures can it tolerate while still accepting writes?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What are the main components of Kubernetes architecture?

The control plane comprises the API server (the single entry point for every request), etcd (the key-value store holding all cluster state), the scheduler (assigns Pods to nodes), the controller manager (runs the reconciliation loops that provide self-healing), and on cloud clusters the cloud controller manager (provisions load balancers and volumes). Each worker node runs the kubelet (starts and monitors containers), kube-proxy (programs Service networking rules), and a container runtime such as containerd.
What happens if the Kubernetes control plane goes down?

Running Pods keep running and keep serving traffic. Kubelets deliberately continue managing the containers they already have when they cannot reach the API server, and kube-proxy's existing kernel rules keep routing Service traffic. What stops is change: no deployments, no scaling, no rescheduling of failed Pods, and kubectl does not work. It is a control outage rather than a service outage, though it becomes a service outage if something fails during it, since nothing will replace it.
Why does etcd need an odd number of members?

etcd uses Raft consensus, which requires a strict majority of members to agree before committing a write. Three members need two healthy and tolerate one failure; five need three and tolerate two. A four-member cluster still needs three healthy, so it tolerates exactly one failure, the same as three members, while giving you an extra machine that can fail. Even numbers add cost and risk without adding fault tolerance.
What is the difference between kubelet and kube-proxy?

The kubelet manages containers: it watches for Pods assigned to its node, instructs the container runtime to start them, mounts volumes, executes liveness and readiness probes, and reports status to the API server. kube-proxy manages Service networking: it watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs iptables or IPVS rules so traffic sent to a Service's virtual IP is rewritten to a real Pod IP. One runs your workloads, the other makes them reachable.
Does Kubernetes still use Docker?

Not as a runtime. Kubernetes removed the Docker shim in version 1.24 and uses containerd or CRI-O through the Container Runtime Interface. This has no effect on images: Docker produces OCI-compliant images and containerd runs them, so anything built with docker build works unchanged. The only practical difference is on the nodes themselves, where docker ps no longer shows Kubernetes containers, crictl ps does.
Why is my Pod stuck in Pending?

The scheduler filtered out every node and found nowhere to place it. kubectl describe pod <name> reports the exact reason in its events, usually something like 0/5 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient memory, 2 node(s) had untolerated taint. The frequent causes are resource requests larger than any node's free capacity, taints without matching tolerations, node selectors or affinity rules that match nothing, and a PersistentVolumeClaim that cannot bind or is in the wrong Availability Zone.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Compare ways to install Kubernetes: kind, Minikube, Docker Desktop, k3s, kubeadm and managed clusters, and pick the right one for learning or production.
There is no single "install Kubernetes" step. There are several distributions aimed at different purposes, and picking the wrong one wastes a lot of time.
For learning, the answer is almost always kind or minikube. For production, it is almost always a managed cloud cluster.

sections.title: For learning: kind or minikube
paragraphs: Runs each Kubernetes node as a Docker container. It is the fastest to start and stop, which makes it the better choice for CI and for repeatedly throwing clusters away.
A multi-node cluster is a short config file, which matters because single-node clusters hide every scheduling and affinity problem you will eventually meet:
The main friction is that images must be loaded into the cluster explicitly, since it has no access to your local Docker images:
Older, more batteries-included. Its add-on system is the reason to prefer it. Ingress, metrics-server and a dashboard are one command each rather than a Helm install.
minikube tunnel is genuinely useful: it satisfies LoadBalancer Services, which otherwise sit at <pending> forever on any local cluster.
kind if you want speed, multi-node, or CI. minikube if you want Ingress and metrics-server working with minimal setup.
Both are fine. Do not spend long deciding.

codeBlock.code:
brew install kind          # or: go install sigs.k8s.io/kind@latest
kind create cluster --name dev
kubectl get nodes

sections.title: Docker Desktop
paragraphs: Kubernetes is a checkbox in its settings, which makes it the lowest-effort option if you already run Docker Desktop.

The limitations are real: single node only, a Kubernetes version tied to the Docker Desktop release, and it competes with your containers for the same VM resources. Fine for a quick look, limiting past that.

sections.title: k3s
paragraphs: A certified Kubernetes distribution in a single binary under 100MB, with etcd swapped for SQLite by default and legacy cloud providers stripped out.

Genuinely production-grade for edge deployments, IoT, and small servers. It is also a pleasant way to run a real cluster on a spare machine or a cheap VPS, and it includes Traefik and a load balancer implementation out of the box.

codeBlock.code:
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -
sudo k3s kubectl get nodes

sections.title: kubeadm
paragraphs: The official tool for building a cluster on real machines. You install a container runtime, run kubeadm init, install a CNI plugin, and join workers.
Worth doing once. Installing the CNI by hand and watching CoreDNS go from Pending to Running teaches more about how clusters fit together than any amount of reading.
Worth being honest about as a production choice: you own etcd backups, certificate rotation, control plane upgrades and node patching. That is a real ongoing job.

codeBlock.code:
sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/calico.yaml
kubeadm token create --print-join-command

sections.title: Managed clusters
paragraphs: For production, use EKS, GKE or AKS unless you have a specific reason not to. The provider runs the control plane, backs up etcd, and handles its upgrades.

The control plane fee is small next to the cost of someone maintaining one. Note that you still own the worker nodes, the networking, add-on upgrades and access control. Managed means the control plane, not the whole cluster.

codeBlock.code:
# AWS
eksctl create cluster --name production --region us-east-1 --nodes 3

# GCP
gcloud container clusters create-auto production --region us-central1

# Azure
az aks create --resource-group rg --name production --node-count 3

sections.title: Resources you will actually need
paragraphs: Kubernetes is not light. A local cluster wants at least 2 CPUs and 4GB of RAM free, and 4 CPUs with 8GB makes a real difference once you install an ingress controller and a monitoring stack.
If Pods sit Pending with Insufficient cpu on a fresh local cluster, the cluster is too small rather than misconfigured:

codeBlock.code: minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=8192

sections.title: After installing
paragraphs: All kube-system Pods Running means the cluster is healthy. CoreDNS stuck Pending on a kubeadm cluster means the CNI plugin has not been installed.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A          # control plane components should be Running

paragraphs: You build myapp:dev locally and deploy it to a kind cluster. The Pod reports ImagePullBackOff even though docker images lists it. Why?
A LoadBalancer Service on minikube shows EXTERNAL-IP as pending indefinitely. What is the explanation?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the easiest way to install Kubernetes for learning?

kind or minikube. kind runs each node as a Docker container and starts in well under a minute, making it ideal for throwing clusters away and recreating them. minikube is a little slower but has an add-on system that installs Ingress, metrics-server and a dashboard with one command each. Either is a good choice, and both are far more appropriate for learning than building a cluster with kubeadm.
What is the difference between kind and minikube?

kind creates nodes as Docker containers, which makes it very fast and well suited to CI pipelines, and multi-node clusters are a few lines of config. minikube typically runs in a VM or Docker and provides curated add-ons, so getting Ingress or metrics-server working takes one command rather than a Helm install. kind requires kind load docker-image to make local builds available; minikube offers minikube tunnel to make LoadBalancer Services function. Both are fine. Choose on whether you value speed or bundled add-ons.
Should I use Docker Desktop's built-in Kubernetes?

It is a reasonable low-effort option if you already run Docker Desktop, since enabling it is a checkbox. The limitations are that it is single-node, its Kubernetes version is tied to the Docker Desktop release, and it shares resources with your containers. For anything beyond a quick look. Particularly anything involving scheduling, node affinity or multi-node behaviour. Kind or minikube will serve you better.
Can I run Kubernetes in production without a cloud provider?

Yes. kubeadm builds a conformant cluster on your own machines, and k3s is a certified lightweight distribution that runs well on small servers and edge hardware. Be clear about what you take on: etcd backups, certificate rotation, control plane upgrades, node patching, and the networking and storage integrations a cloud provider supplies. For most teams the managed control plane fee is smaller than the engineering time it replaces.
How much memory and CPU does a local cluster need?

At least 2 CPUs and 4GB of RAM free, and 4 CPUs with 8GB is a much better experience once you add an ingress controller or a monitoring stack. Kubernetes control plane components alone consume a meaningful share of a small allocation. If Pods sit Pending with Insufficient cpu on a freshly created cluster, the cluster is undersized rather than misconfigured. Restart it with more resources.
Why are my CoreDNS Pods stuck in Pending after kubeadm init?

No CNI plugin is installed. kubeadm init deliberately leaves the choice of network plugin to you, and without one Pods cannot be assigned addresses, so CoreDNS cannot start. Apply a CNI such as Calico, Flannel or Cilium and CoreDNS moves to Running within a minute. If you passed --pod-network-cidr to kubeadm init, make sure the plugin's configuration uses the same range.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Install Minikube, run minikube start, enable add-ons like ingress, reach services with minikube tunnel, and build images locally without a registry.

Minikube runs a local Kubernetes cluster in a VM or a Docker container. Its distinguishing feature is the add-on system: Ingress, metrics-server and a dashboard are one command each, rather than a Helm install and a configuration file.

sections.title: Install
paragraphs: You also need a driver. Docker is the usual choice and works everywhere.

codeBlock.code:
# macOS
brew install minikube

# Linux
curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
sudo install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube

# Windows
winget install Kubernetes.minikube

sections.title: Start a cluster
paragraphs: Set --cpus and --memory explicitly. The defaults of 2 CPUs and 2GB are enough for a bare cluster and not enough once you add an ingress controller or anything else. Insufficient cpu on a fresh minikube is nearly always this.
Other options worth knowing at start time:
A multi-node cluster is worth creating. Single-node hides every scheduling, affinity and anti-affinity problem you will eventually meet in a real cluster.

codeBlock.code: minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=8192

sections.title: Add-ons
paragraphs: This is why people choose minikube.
metrics-server is the one to enable immediately, without it kubectl top fails and every HorizontalPodAutoscaler reports <unknown>.

codeBlock.code:
minikube addons list
minikube addons enable ingress
minikube addons enable metrics-server

sections.title: Reaching your services
paragraphs: A local cluster has no cloud load balancer, so there are three ways in.
NodePort, with a helper to give you the URL:
LoadBalancer, which needs minikube tunnel running in a separate terminal:

Without it, LoadBalancer Services sit at <pending> forever. The tunnel creates a route to the cluster and assigns them addresses, and it usually asks for a password because it modifies network routes.
Ingress, once the add-on is enabled:
Or skip all of it for quick checks:

codeBlock.code: minikube service payments-api --url

sections.title: Building images without a registry
paragraphs: Minikube's cluster cannot see your host's Docker images. Rather than pushing to a registry, point your shell at minikube's own Docker daemon:

The image is now built inside the cluster's daemon and immediately available. Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent, with Always, or an unpinned latest tag which defaults to Always, the kubelet tries the registry anyway and fails.
The alternative, if you prefer not to change your shell environment:

codeBlock.code:
eval $(minikube docker-env)
docker build -t myapp:dev .

sections.title: Profiles
paragraphs: Several independent clusters, useful for keeping projects apart or testing across Kubernetes versions:
Each profile is a separate VM or container with its own resources. They are not free, so delete the ones you are not using.

codeBlock.code:
minikube start -p payments --cpus=4 --memory=8192
minikube start -p legacy --kubernetes-version=v1.28.0

minikube profile list
minikube profile payments        # set the default
kubectl config use-context payments

sections.title: Housekeeping
paragraphs: stop then start is much faster than recreating, and preserves everything you deployed.
When something is genuinely wrong, minikube delete && minikube start is usually quicker than debugging the local cluster itself.

codeBlock.code:
minikube stop                  # keep the cluster, free the resources
minikube start                 # resume it
minikube delete                # remove it entirely
minikube delete --all          # every profile

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: You run eval $(minikube docker-env), build myapp:dev, and deploy it. The Pod still reports ImagePullBackOff. What is the most likely cause?
Immediately after minikube start with default settings, enabling the ingress add-on leaves Pods Pending with "Insufficient cpu". What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How much memory and CPU should I give minikube?

At least 4 CPUs and 8GB if your machine allows it, passed as minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=8192. The defaults of 2 CPUs and 2GB are enough for an empty cluster and run out as soon as you enable an ingress controller or deploy a few workloads, producing Insufficient cpu errors that look like a misconfiguration but are simply a lack of capacity. The setting only applies at creation, so changing it means deleting and recreating the cluster.
How do I access a service running in minikube?

For a NodePort Service, minikube service <name> --url prints a working URL. For a LoadBalancer Service you need minikube tunnel running in a separate terminal, otherwise the external IP stays <pending> indefinitely. With the ingress add-on enabled, minikube ip gives the address to point a hosts-file entry at. For a quick check none of that is necessary, kubectl port-forward service/<name> 8080:80 works immediately.
Why is my LoadBalancer Service stuck pending in minikube?

There is no cloud provider to create a load balancer, so nothing ever assigns the external IP. minikube tunnel fills that role by creating a network route into the cluster and assigning addresses to LoadBalancer Services. It has to keep running in its own terminal, and it usually prompts for a password because it modifies system routes.
How do I use a locally built Docker image in minikube?

Run eval $(minikube docker-env) to point your shell at minikube's own Docker daemon, then build normally. The image lands directly in the cluster with no registry involved. Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent on the container, since Always, which is also the default for an unpinned or latest tag, makes the kubelet attempt a registry pull that fails. eval $(minikube docker-env -u) switches your shell back. Alternatively, minikube image load myapp:dev copies an already-built image in.
What is the difference between minikube stop and minikube delete?

stop shuts the cluster down while preserving its state, so minikube start brings everything back including your deployments. Much faster than recreating. delete removes the cluster and all its data permanently. Use stop to reclaim memory and CPU between work sessions, and delete when you want a clean slate or when troubleshooting the local cluster itself has become slower than rebuilding it.
Can I run more than one minikube cluster?

Yes, using profiles: minikube start -p payments and minikube start -p legacy --kubernetes-version=v1.28.0 create independent clusters, each with its own kubectl context. minikube profile list shows them and minikube profile <name> sets the default for minikube commands. Each profile is a separate VM or container consuming real CPU and memory, so delete profiles you are not actively using.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Install kind and run kind create cluster to get a local Kubernetes cluster in Docker. Covers multi-node configs, pinned versions, local images, ingress and CI.
kind, Kubernetes IN Docker, runs each cluster node as a Docker container. Clusters start in well under a minute, multi-node is a few lines of config, and deleting one is instant.
That speed is why it has become the default for CI pipelines and for anyone who recreates clusters often.

sections.title: Install
paragraphs: It needs a working Docker or Podman installation, and nothing else.

codeBlock.code:
# macOS
brew install kind

# Linux
curl -Lo ./kind https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/dl/latest/kind-linux-amd64
chmod +x ./kind && sudo mv ./kind /usr/local/bin/kind

# Windows
winget install Kubernetes.kind

sections.title: A first cluster
paragraphs: Note the kubectl context is kind-dev. Kind prefixes every context name with kind-.

codeBlock.code: kind create cluster --name dev

sections.title: Multi-node, which is the point
paragraphs: Create a multi-node cluster even for simple work. Single-node clusters hide everything interesting about scheduling: pod anti-affinity does nothing, topology spread constraints do nothing, ReadWriteOnce volume conflicts never appear, and node drains are meaningless. Those are exactly the behaviours that surprise people in a real cluster.

codeBlock.code:
# kind-config.yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
  - role: worker
  - role: worker

sections.title: Pinning the Kubernetes version
paragraphs: Pin it to match the cluster you actually deploy to. Particularly useful for testing an upgrade before it happens.

codeBlock.code:
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    image: kindest/node:v1.30.6
  - role: worker
    image: kindest/node:v1.30.6

sections.title: Loading local images
paragraphs: This is the one piece of friction with kind. Each node is a Docker container with its own containerd image store, so your host's images are invisible to it. A Pod referencing a locally built image gets ImagePullBackOff.
Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent, since Always, the default when the tag is latest or absent, makes the kubelet attempt a registry pull that will fail.
Forgetting kind load is the single most common kind problem, and it is worth adding to any build script that targets kind.

codeBlock.code:
docker build -t myapp:dev .
kind load docker-image myapp:dev --name dev

sections.title: Ingress
paragraphs: Reaching an Ingress from your host needs port mappings declared at cluster creation. They cannot be added afterwards:
localhost then reaches your Ingress. The ingress-ready=true label is what the kind-specific ingress-nginx manifest uses to place the controller on the node with the port mappings.
LoadBalancer Services stay <pending> on kind unless you install MetalLB. For local work, Ingress or kubectl port-forward is simpler.

codeBlock.code:
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    kubeadmConfigPatches:
      - |
        kind: InitConfiguration
        nodeRegistration:
          kubeletExtraArgs:
            node-labels: "ingress-ready=true"
    extraPortMappings:
      - containerPort: 80
        hostPort: 80
        protocol: TCP
      - containerPort: 443
        hostPort: 443
        protocol: TCP
  - role: worker

sections.title: Mounting host directories
paragraphs: Useful for iterating on code without rebuilding images:
The path is then available to a hostPath volume inside the cluster.

codeBlock.code:
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    extraMounts:
      - hostPath: /Users/me/work/payments
        containerPath: /src

sections.title: kind in CI
paragraphs: kind is the standard way to run integration tests against a real Kubernetes API:

Cluster creation adds well under a minute, which is what makes this practical on every push. Testing against a real API server catches admission, RBAC and manifest errors that no amount of YAML linting will.

codeBlock.code:
# .github/workflows/test.yml
name: test
on: [push]
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: helm/kind-action@v1
        with:
          cluster_name: ci
          config: kind-config.yaml
      - run: docker build -t myapp:ci .
      - run: kind load docker-image myapp:ci --name ci
      - run: kubectl apply -f manifests/
      - run: kubectl wait --for=condition=available deployment/myapp --timeout=120s
      - run: ./run-integration-tests.sh

sections.title: Debugging
paragraphs: If a cluster will not create at all, it is usually Docker: not running, out of disk, or out of memory. docker system prune and raising Docker Desktop's memory allocation resolve most cases.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pods -A                          # control plane should all be Running
docker ps                                    # each node is a container
docker exec -it dev-control-plane bash        # shell onto a node
kind export logs ./kind-logs --name dev      # everything, for inspection

sections.title: kind or minikube?
paragraphs: kind for speed, multi-node and CI. minikube if you want Ingress and metrics-server without assembling them.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An ingress-nginx controller is running in a kind cluster, but curl localhost times out. The cluster was created with kind create cluster with no config file. What is wrong?
A Deployment with podAntiAffinity requiring replicas on different nodes runs three replicas happily on a single-node kind cluster. Why does the rule appear ignored?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is kind and how is it different from minikube?

kind runs each Kubernetes node as a Docker container rather than in a VM, which makes cluster creation and deletion very fast and multi-node configurations trivial. That speed is why it is the usual choice for CI. minikube is somewhat slower but ships curated add-ons, so Ingress and metrics-server are one command each rather than a manual install. The practical split is kind for speed, multi-node and pipelines; minikube for a batteries-included local environment.
Why does my locally built image give ImagePullBackOff in kind?

Because kind nodes are Docker containers with their own containerd image store, and your host's Docker images are not visible inside them. Run kind load docker-image myapp:dev --name <cluster> to copy it in. Also set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent, since Always, which is the default when the tag is latest or omitted, makes the kubelet try a registry pull that fails. Forgetting kind load is the most common kind problem by a wide margin.
How do I create a multi-node cluster with kind?

Write a config file listing the nodes you want, with one control-plane role and one or more worker roles, then pass it with kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml. It is worth doing even for simple work: on a single node, pod anti-affinity and topology spread constraints have no observable effect, ReadWriteOnce volume conflicts never occur, and node drains are meaningless. All of which then surprise you in a real cluster.
How do I use an Ingress controller with kind?

Declare extraPortMappings for ports 80 and 443 in the cluster config, and label the control-plane node with ingress-ready=true. These must be set when the cluster is created, because Docker fixes published ports at container creation. Adding them later means recreating the cluster. Then apply the kind-specific ingress-nginx manifest, which schedules the controller onto the labelled node, and localhost will reach your Ingress.
Why is my LoadBalancer Service pending in kind?

There is no cloud provider to fulfil the request, so the external IP is never assigned. Install MetalLB if you genuinely need LoadBalancer Services to work, but for local development an Ingress with extraPortMappings, or simply kubectl port-forward, is considerably less setup for the same result.
Can I use kind in CI pipelines?

Yes, and it is the standard approach for integration testing against a real Kubernetes API. helm/kind-action sets up a cluster in a GitHub Actions job in under a minute, after which you build your image, kind load it, apply your manifests, and run tests. Because it is a genuine API server, it catches admission controller rejections, RBAC problems and invalid manifests that YAML linting cannot detect.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Install kubectl, stay within the supported version skew, connect to a cluster with kubeconfig, enable shell completion and add useful krew plugins.
kubectl is the command-line client for the Kubernetes API. It is a single binary with no dependencies, and it is the tool you will spend most of your Kubernetes time in.

sections.title: Install
paragraphs: For upgrades through your package manager, the official apt and yum repositories are the better route. Note they are versioned per minor release, so moving from 1.31 to 1.32 means updating the repository URL as well.
choco install kubernetes-cli and scoop install kubectl work equally well.
--client matters here, without it, kubectl version tries to contact a cluster and errors if none is configured.

codeBlock.code: brew install kubectl

sections.title: Version skew
paragraphs: kubectl is supported one minor version either side of the cluster's API server. A v1.31 client works with 1.30, 1.31 and 1.32.
Outside that range things mostly work until they suddenly do not, usually a missing field on a newer resource, or a subcommand the older server does not recognise.

If you work across clusters on different versions, asdf or kubectl version-switching tools let you keep several binaries and select per context. In practice, keeping the client at the newest cluster version you talk to covers most cases.

codeBlock.code: kubectl version          # shows both client and server

sections.title: Connecting to a cluster
paragraphs: kubectl reads ~/.kube/config. Local cluster tools write it for you:
Cloud CLIs add a context on request:
kubectl cluster-info returning a URL means you are connected. connection refused usually means no cluster is running; Unauthorized means credentials, not connectivity.
Several config files can be merged with a colon-separated KUBECONFIG:

codeBlock.code:
kind create cluster                    # writes and selects the context
minikube start                         # same

sections.title: Set this up on day one
paragraphs: The highest-value five minutes you will spend. Completion covers resource names, not just subcommands, so you stop copying and pasting Pod names:
The second line is what most people omit, and without it completion stops working through the alias.

Nothing in kubectl's output tells you which cluster you are on, and running a destructive command against the wrong one is the most common serious mistake people make. Show the context in your prompt, kube-ps1, or the Kubernetes segment in starship, powerlevel10k or oh-my-zsh:

codeBlock.code:
# bash
echo 'source <(kubectl completion bash)' >> ~/.bashrc

# zsh
echo 'source <(kubectl completion zsh)' >> ~/.zshrc

# fish
kubectl completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/kubectl.fish

sections.title: Plugins worth having
paragraphs: krew is kubectl's plugin manager:
kubectl neat deserves particular mention: kubectl get pod x -o yaml includes managed fields, status and defaults, and neat strips it to something you can actually read or reuse as a manifest.
Outside krew, stern for multi-Pod log tailing and k9s for a terminal UI are both worth installing.

codeBlock.code: kubectl krew install ctx ns tree neat

sections.title: Commands to confirm it works
paragraphs: kubectl explain is the one to remember. It documents fields against the server you are connected to, so it always matches your version rather than whatever a search result described.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl api-resources        # every type this cluster supports, with short names
kubectl explain pod.spec     # field docs from the live API server

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: On a fresh machine with no cluster configured, kubectl version fails with a connection error. How do you check the installed version?
A developer adds alias k=kubectl and sources kubectl completion. Completion works for kubectl but not for k. What is missing?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I install kubectl?

Use your platform's package manager: brew install kubectl on macOS, winget install -e --id Kubernetes.kubectl on Windows, and either the official apt or yum repository or the release binary on Linux. It is a single static binary with no dependencies, so downloading it and placing it on your PATH works anywhere. Confirm with kubectl version --client.
Does kubectl need to match my cluster version?

Not exactly. kubectl is supported within one minor version either side of the API server, so a v1.31 client works with clusters running 1.30, 1.31 or 1.32. Beyond that, most things still work until a newer resource field or subcommand is missing, at which point failures look confusing. kubectl version shows both client and server so you can check the gap. If you manage clusters on different versions, keep the client at the newest version you talk to.
Why does kubectl version give a connection error?

Because it reports both the client and the server version by default, so it tries to reach a cluster. With no kubeconfig, or no cluster running, that fails. kubectl version --client reports only the local binary and contacts nothing. This trips up almost everyone immediately after installing, and does not indicate a problem with the installation.
How do I connect kubectl to my cluster?

Local tools handle it for you, kind create cluster and minikube start both write and select a context in ~/.kube/config. For cloud clusters, run the provider's command: aws eks update-kubeconfig, gcloud container clusters get-credentials, or az aks get-credentials. Verify with kubectl cluster-info, which prints the API server URL when connected. A connection refused means no cluster is reachable; Unauthorized means the credentials are the problem rather than the connection.
How do I enable kubectl autocompletion?

Source the completion script from your shell profile: echo 'source <(kubectl completion zsh)' >> ~/.zshrc for zsh, or the bash equivalent. It completes resource names as well as subcommands, so you stop copying and pasting Pod names. If you also alias k=kubectl, add complete -o default -F __start_kubectl k, without that line completion works for kubectl but not through the alias, which is the step most people miss.
What kubectl plugins are worth installing?

Install krew first, then ctx and ns for fast context and namespace switching, tree for viewing resource ownership hierarchies, and neat for stripping managed fields and status out of get -o yaml so the output is readable. Outside krew, stern handles multi-Pod log tailing far better than kubectl logs -l, and k9s gives you a terminal UI that makes browsing a cluster much quicker than repeated get and describe commands.

quickReference.explanation: Command: aws eks update-kubeconfig --region us-east-1 --name production

paragraphs: Learn the kubectl commands you will run daily: get, apply, describe, delete, selectors, output formats, namespaces and tips to work faster with kubeconfig.
kubectl is a REST client. Every command turns into an HTTP request to the API server, authenticated with credentials from your kubeconfig.
Internalising that explains a lot. Every kubectl verb maps to an HTTP method, anything you can do in a manifest you can do through the API, and permission errors are RBAC decisions, not client bugs.

sections.title: Where it gets its configuration
paragraphs: ~/.kube/config holds clusters, users and contexts. A context pairs a cluster with credentials and a default namespace.

Check your context before running anything destructive. Running a command against the wrong cluster is the most common serious mistake people make with Kubernetes, and nothing in the output warns you. Tools like kubectx, or a shell prompt showing the current context, are worth the five minutes to set up.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl config current-context     # which cluster am I pointed at?
kubectl config get-contexts        # all of them
kubectl config use-context prod    # switch

sections.title: Imperative and declarative
paragraphs: Two ways to work, and the distinction matters more than it first appears.
Imperative: tell the cluster to do something now:
Fast, good for learning and debugging, and untracked. Nothing records why the cluster is in this state, and nobody can reproduce it.
Declarative: write the desired state in a file, apply it:
The file is reviewable, diffable, version-controlled, and reproducible. This is how anything real should be managed.
The productive middle path is to generate manifests imperatively and then keep them:
That gives you a valid skeleton in seconds without memorising the schema. Edit it, commit it, apply it.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80

sections.title: apply vs create vs replace
paragraphs: apply performs a three-way merge between the last applied configuration, your file, and the live object. That is why it can update one field without discarding changes made by controllers, and why mixing apply with kubectl edit produces confusing results.
Preview before applying to anything that matters:
--dry-run=server validates against the real API server including admission controllers, so it catches far more than client-side validation.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl diff -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --dry-run=server

sections.title: The commands you will actually run
paragraphs: kubectl describe is the single highest-value command. The Events section at the bottom usually states the problem in plain language. Failed scheduling, image pull errors, probe failures, volume mount problems.

codeBlock.code:
# What is here?
kubectl get pods
kubectl get pods -o wide                 # + IPs and nodes
kubectl get pods -A                      # every namespace
kubectl get pods -w                      # watch changes live
kubectl get all                          # common resource types in one view

# What is wrong with it?
kubectl describe pod <name>              # spec, status and events. Start here
kubectl logs <name>
kubectl logs <name> --previous           # the run that crashed
kubectl logs <name> -f                   # follow
kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=50        # across all matching Pods

# Get inside
kubectl exec -it <name> -- sh
kubectl port-forward pod/<name> 8080:80

# Change things
kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml
kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=5
kubectl rollout restart deployment/web
kubectl delete -f manifest.yaml

sections.title: Selecting and filtering
paragraphs: Label selectors are how everything in Kubernetes finds everything else, so they are worth being fluent in. Most commands accept -l, including logs and delete.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pods -l app=web                      # by label
kubectl get pods -l 'env in (staging,prod)'      # set-based
kubectl get pods --field-selector status.phase=Running
kubectl get pods --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get pods --show-labels

sections.title: Output formats
paragraphs: Two genuinely useful one-liners:

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pod web-abc -o yaml           # the full object as stored
kubectl get pod web-abc -o json

# Extract one value
kubectl get pod web-abc -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'

# Build a custom table
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=\
NAME:.metadata.name,\
STATUS:.status.phase,\
NODE:.spec.nodeName,\
RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount

sections.title: Namespaces
paragraphs: Forgetting the namespace is the most common reason kubectl get pods returns "No resources found" when you know something is running.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl get pods -A

# Stop typing -n on every command
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=payments

sections.title: Making it fast
paragraphs: kubectl explain documents any field from the live API server, which beats searching for documentation that may describe a different version than you are running.

codeBlock.code:
# Shell completion. Do this once, it pays for itself immediately
source <(kubectl completion bash)     # or zsh
echo 'source <(kubectl completion bash)' >> ~/.bashrc

# The near-universal alias
alias k=kubectl
complete -o default -F __start_kubectl k

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: You run kubectl create -f deployment.yaml, edit the replica count in the file, and run the same command again. What happens?
kubectl get pods returns "No resources found in default namespace" but a colleague confirms the application is running. What is the most likely explanation?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between kubectl apply and kubectl create?

create maps to an HTTP POST and fails if the object already exists, so it is for one-off creation only. apply creates the object if absent and updates it if present, using a three-way merge between the last applied configuration, your file and the live object. That merge is what lets it change one field without discarding values set by controllers, and it is what makes running the same command repeatedly safe. Use apply with manifests in version control; use create mainly with --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate those manifests.
How do I see why a Pod is failing?

Start with kubectl describe pod <name> and read the Events section at the bottom, which usually states the cause directly. Failed scheduling with the reason, an image pull error with the registry's own message, or a failing probe. If the container is crash-looping, kubectl logs <name> --previous shows output from the run that actually failed; plain kubectl logs shows the instance that has only just started and typically has nothing yet. For the termination reason specifically, kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}' returns values like OOMKilled.
How do I switch between clusters and namespaces?

kubectl config get-contexts lists available contexts and kubectl config use-context <name> switches cluster. For namespaces, kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> changes the default so you stop typing -n on every command. Because nothing in the output tells you which cluster you are on, showing the current context in your shell prompt, or using kubectx and kubens, is a worthwhile safeguard against running something destructive in the wrong place.
How do I generate YAML without writing it by hand?

Use an imperative command with --dry-run=client -o yaml, for example kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deployment.yaml. Nothing is sent to the cluster and you get a valid manifest to edit and commit. The same trick works for Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets and Jobs, and it is far quicker than recalling the schema. kubectl explain <resource>.<field> documents any field against the version of Kubernetes you are actually running.
Why does kubectl get pods show nothing when my app is running?

Almost always the namespace. kubectl operates on one namespace at a time, defaulting to the one in your current context, so a workload in payments is invisible from default. Run kubectl get pods -A to search everywhere. The other possibility is that you are connected to a different cluster than you think, kubectl config current-context settles that immediately.
What does kubectl diff do?

kubectl diff -f manifest.yaml shows what applying that file would change, comparing your manifest against the live objects in the cluster and printing a unified diff. It is the closest equivalent to terraform plan and is worth running before any change to a production namespace. Pair it with kubectl apply --dry-run=server, which validates against the real API server including admission controllers and catches problems that client-side validation cannot see.

paragraphs: Inspect cluster resources with kubectl get and describe. Use -o wide, jsonpath and custom-columns, read events, and know when to choose get over describe.
get lists resources and answers "what exists". describe shows one resource in full, including the events attached to it, and answers "why is this not working".
Most Kubernetes debugging is describe followed by reading the bottom of the output.

sections.title: get
paragraphs: kubectl get all is a convenience rather than a promise. It covers Pods, Services, Deployments, ReplicaSets and StatefulSets, but not ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, Ingresses or anything custom.
Three columns carry most of the signal:
Live updates as things change. The clearest way to see a rolling update actually happen.
Label selectors are how Kubernetes objects find each other, and --show-labels is how you check why a Service selector is not matching.
Field selectors filter on object fields rather than labels:
Sorting events by timestamp is worth memorising. The default order is not chronological, which is confusing exactly when you are in a hurry.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pods
kubectl get pods,services,deployments        # several types at once
kubectl get all                              # common types in this namespace
kubectl get pods -A                          # every namespace
kubectl get pods -n payments

sections.title: Output formats
paragraphs: -o yaml shows the object as stored, including status and defaults you never wrote. It is the definitive answer to "what is actually configured".
Extracting one value, for scripts or just to avoid scrolling:
A readable table of exactly what you want:

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pod payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 -o yaml
kubectl get pod payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 -o json

sections.title: describe
paragraphs: describe assembles the object, its defaults, related objects, and, the part that matters, the events for it.
That last line is the whole diagnosis: the readiness path returns 404, so the Pod never becomes Ready and gets no traffic. No log reading required.
Events you will meet constantly:
describe works on everything, and is just as useful elsewhere:

codeBlock.code: kubectl describe pod payments-api-7d4f-m3p9

sections.title: Events on their own
paragraphs: describe only shows events for one object. Cluster-wide:

Events expire after about an hour by default. If an incident is more than an hour old, the event that explains it is already gone, which is a good argument for shipping events into your logging system.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get events --field-selector type=Warning
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=payments-api-7d4f-m3p9

sections.title: get or describe?
paragraphs: The habit worth building: get to find the broken thing, describe to find out why, logs only if describe did not say.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: kubectl get pods shows a Pod as Running with READY 0/1 and RESTARTS 0. What does this tell you?
You investigate a crash that happened three hours ago. kubectl describe pod shows no events at all, though the Pod clearly restarted. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between kubectl get and kubectl describe?

get lists resources with a short status summary and works across many objects at once, which makes it the right tool for finding things and for scripting. describe renders one object in full. Its spec, its defaults, related objects, and crucially the events attached to it. Events are where Kubernetes explains itself, so describe is what you run when something is broken and get is what you run to find out what exists.
How do I see why a Pod is failing?

kubectl describe pod <name> and read the Events section at the bottom. It usually states the cause outright: FailedScheduling with the per-node reasons, an image pull error quoting the registry's own message, Unhealthy with the probe's status code, or a FailedMount for a volume problem. Only if the events do not explain it do you need kubectl logs <pod> --previous, which shows output from the container run that actually crashed.
What does READY 0/1 mean?

Zero of one containers are passing their readiness probe. If the Pod's status is also Running, the process started fine and the probe itself is failing. A wrong path or port, an endpoint behind authentication returning 401, or an initialDelaySeconds shorter than real startup time. A Pod in this state is deliberately excluded from its Service's endpoints, so it receives no traffic, which is exactly what readiness is for.
How do I get just one field from a resource?

Use jsonpath: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'. It is particularly useful for values buried in status, such as kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}' which returns OOMKilled for a container killed on memory. For tabular output across many objects, -o custom-columns lets you build exactly the table you want rather than scrolling through YAML.
Why are my events missing?

They expire. Kubernetes keeps events for about an hour by default, set by the API server's --event-ttl, because they are high volume and treated as transient. Anything older than that is gone, which routinely means the event explaining an overnight failure has vanished before anyone looks. Exporting events into your log store, the Kubernetes Event Exporter is the usual tool, preserves them, and it is not something the common monitoring stacks do for you.
Does kubectl get all really show everything?

No, and the name is misleading. It covers the common workload and networking types. Pods, Services, Deployments, ReplicaSets, StatefulSets, DaemonSets and Jobs, but omits ConfigMaps, Secrets, PersistentVolumeClaims, Ingresses, ServiceAccounts and every custom resource. To see genuinely everything in a namespace you need to enumerate the API resources and query each, which kubectl api-resources supports but is rarely worth doing by hand.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn kubectl apply vs create vs replace, preview changes with kubectl diff, use server-side apply, delete resources safely and fix objects stuck deleting.
apply makes the cluster match a file. delete removes objects. Between them they cover most of how real workloads are managed.
The important habit is that manifests live in version control and apply is how they reach the cluster, so the repository, not the cluster, is the source of truth.

sections.title: apply
paragraphs: It creates the object if absent and updates it if present, which makes it safe to run repeatedly. The same command works on first deploy and every deploy after.
Several objects in one file, separated by ---, are applied in order:

codeBlock.code:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f ./manifests/                # every file in a directory
kubectl apply -f ./manifests/ -R             # and subdirectories
kubectl apply -k ./overlays/production        # a Kustomize overlay

sections.title: apply vs create vs replace
paragraphs: The mechanism behind apply is a three-way merge between the last applied configuration, your file, and the live object. That is why it can change one field without discarding values written by controllers, and why the annotation kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration exists on objects you have applied.

It also explains a common surprise: removing a field from your manifest removes it from the cluster, because the merge can see it was there before and is not now. A field you never declared at all is left alone.
Mixing apply with kubectl edit or console changes muddles that history and produces confusing results. Pick one.

sections.title: Preview before applying
paragraphs: This is the closest equivalent to terraform plan, and it is worth running before any change to a production namespace.

--dry-run=server sends the request to the API server, which runs validation and admission controllers without persisting anything. It catches schema errors, policy rejections and missing CRDs that client-side validation cannot see. --dry-run=client only formats locally. Useful for generating YAML, not for validating it.

codeBlock.code: kubectl diff -f deployment.yaml

sections.title: Server-side apply
paragraphs: The newer mechanism. Instead of relying on a last-applied annotation, the API server records field ownership for every manager that writes to the object. If two controllers try to own the same field, you get an explicit conflict rather than a silent overwrite:
That message is genuinely useful. Here it is telling you a HorizontalPodAutoscaler owns the replica count and your manifest should not declare it.
--force-conflicts takes ownership anyway, which is sometimes correct and should be a decision rather than a reflex.

codeBlock.code: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --server-side

sections.title: delete
paragraphs: Prefer delete -f with the same file you applied. Deleting by name is easy to get wrong, particularly when the name is similar across namespaces.
Deleting a Deployment deletes its ReplicaSets and their Pods, through owner references.
--cascade=orphan is occasionally useful, migrating Pods to a new controller, for instance, and leaves Pods that nothing manages, so use it deliberately.
Deleting a Pod managed by a Deployment does not remove it: the controller notices the shortfall and creates a replacement. That is how you restart a single Pod.

This removes everything in it. Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps and PersistentVolumeClaims. With a StorageClass whose reclaim policy is Delete, the underlying disks and their data go too. It is among the most destructive single commands available.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml        # the safest form
kubectl delete deployment payments-api
kubectl delete pods -l app=payments-api
kubectl delete pods --all -n staging

sections.title: When something will not delete
paragraphs: An object stuck in Terminating is almost always waiting on a finalizer. A marker saying "some controller must clean up before this can go".
For Pods, the usual cause is a node that has gone away, so the kubelet cannot confirm the containers stopped:

This tells the API server to forget the Pod without confirmation. On a node that is merely unreachable rather than dead, the containers may still be running, which for a StatefulSet member holding a volume can mean two instances writing to the same data. Force-delete after establishing the node is genuinely gone, not before.
For other objects, removing a finalizer by hand is a last resort:
The correct fix is nearly always to remove whatever is blocking cleanup. A Pod still using a PVC, or an operator that was uninstalled before its custom resources were deleted.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'

sections.title: Pruning
paragraphs: --prune deletes objects matching the selector that are no longer in the manifests, which is how you make apply genuinely declarative. It is powerful and easy to misuse. A wrong label selector deletes more than you intended. In practice, most teams get this behaviour from ArgoCD or Flux instead, where it is scoped and previewed properly.

codeBlock.code: kubectl apply -f ./manifests/ --prune -l app=payments-api

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Deployment manifest previously set nodeSelector. Someone removes those lines and runs kubectl apply. The live Deployment no longer has a nodeSelector. Is that expected?
A StatefulSet Pod is stuck Terminating because its node is unreachable. What is the risk of kubectl delete pod --grace-period=0 --force?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between kubectl apply and kubectl create?

create maps to an HTTP POST and fails if the object already exists, so it only handles first creation. apply creates the object when absent and updates it when present, using a three-way merge between the last applied configuration, your file, and the live object. That merge lets it update your fields without discarding values set by controllers, and makes running the same command repeatedly safe. Use apply for managed manifests and create mainly with --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate them.
What does kubectl diff do?

kubectl diff -f manifest.yaml computes what applying that file would change and prints a unified diff against the live objects, without modifying anything. It is the nearest equivalent to terraform plan and worth running before any change to a production namespace. Pair it with kubectl apply --dry-run=server, which sends the request to the API server for full validation including admission controllers but does not persist it.
What is server-side apply and should I use it?

With server-side apply the API server records which manager owns each field, so two controllers writing the same field produce an explicit conflict instead of silently overwriting each other. A message like conflict with "hpa-controller": .spec.replicas is telling you that an autoscaler owns the replica count and your manifest should not declare it. It is the more robust mechanism and is worth adopting, particularly where several controllers touch the same objects. --force-conflicts overrides ownership and should be a considered decision.
Does deleting a Deployment delete its Pods?

Yes. Owner references make deletion cascade from Deployment to ReplicaSets to Pods. --cascade=orphan keeps the children, which is occasionally useful when migrating workloads between controllers but leaves Pods that nothing manages. Note the reverse is not true: deleting a Pod that belongs to a Deployment simply causes the controller to create a replacement, which is exactly how you restart a single Pod.
Why is my Pod stuck in Terminating?

Almost always a finalizer, and for Pods the usual cause is an unreachable node. The API server will not remove the Pod until the kubelet confirms the containers stopped, and a node that is down never will. kubectl delete pod <name> --grace-period=0 --force removes it from the API. Be careful with StatefulSet Pods: if the node is merely partitioned rather than dead, the container is still running with its volume attached, and a replacement Pod writing the same data can corrupt it.
What does --prune do and is it safe?

kubectl apply -f ./manifests/ --prune -l app=myapp deletes objects matching the label selector that are no longer present in the applied manifests, which is what makes apply fully declarative rather than additive. It is genuinely useful and genuinely dangerous, because a wrong or overly broad selector deletes more than intended. Most teams get the same behaviour from ArgoCD or Flux, where pruning is scoped to an application and previewed before it runs.
