sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Debug pods with kubectl logs (including --previous), kubectl exec, port-forward and kubectl cp. Handle distroless images with kubectl debug.
Three commands for working with what is already running: read its output, get inside it, and reach it from your machine.

sections.title: logs
paragraphs: When a container is crash-looping, plain kubectl logs shows the instance that has just started, which during a backoff has produced nothing yet. --previous shows the run that actually failed, and that is where the error is.
If you learn one thing about debugging Pods, this is it. A CrashLoopBackOff with apparently empty logs is nearly always someone forgetting --previous.
With more than one container in a Pod, kubectl logs refuses to guess and errors until you pick one.
--prefix labels each line with its Pod name, which is essential when reading three replicas at once. Following many Pods is capped by --max-log-requests (default 5).
For serious multi-Pod log reading, stern remains better than anything built in.
kubectl logs reads files on the node written by the container runtime from the container's stdout and stderr. Two consequences:

codeBlock.code:
kubectl logs payments-api-7d4f-x8k2
kubectl logs payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 -f              # follow
kubectl logs payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 --tail=100
kubectl logs payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 --since=15m
kubectl logs payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 --timestamps

sections.title: exec
paragraphs: The -- separator matters. Everything after it goes to the container, so without it flags like -l are interpreted by kubectl instead.
Use sh rather than bash by default. Most slim images have no bash.
Things worth checking from inside a container:
That first one settles a great many arguments. Checking what the container actually received, rather than what the manifest says, is usually faster than reasoning about the manifest.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl exec -it payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 -- sh
kubectl exec -it payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 -c api -- bash
kubectl exec payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 -- env        # single command, no TTY
kubectl exec payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 -- ls /config

sections.title: Distroless images have no shell
paragraphs: kubectl exec needs a shell inside the container. Distroless and scratch images deliberately have none:
The answer is an ephemeral debug container. A temporary container added to the running Pod, sharing its network namespace:
--target=api shares the target container's process namespace so you can see its processes. nicolaka/netshoot carries curl, dig, tcpdump, netstat and most of what you would want.
The Pod is unchanged when you exit. Nothing is rebuilt, nothing restarts.
To debug a Pod that will not start at all, copy it with a different command:

codeBlock.code:
OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process:
exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH

sections.title: port-forward
paragraphs: Tunnels a local port through the API server to something in the cluster. This is the right way to reach an internal service from a laptop, no Ingress, no NodePort, no exposing anything.
Forwarding to a Service picks one Pod and stays with it; it is not load balanced. Forwarding to a Deployment picks one of its Pods.
Notes worth knowing: 0.0.0.0:8080:8080 as the address binds all interfaces rather than just localhost, the connection drops when the Pod is replaced, and it only handles TCP.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl port-forward pod/payments-api-7d4f-x8k2 8080:8080
kubectl port-forward service/payments-api 8080:80
kubectl port-forward deployment/payments-api 8080:8080

sections.title: Copying files
paragraphs: kubectl cp requires tar inside the container, so it fails on distroless images just as exec does.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl cp payments-api-7d4f-x8k2:/var/log/app.log ./app.log
kubectl cp ./fixture.json payments-api-7d4f-x8k2:/tmp/fixture.json
kubectl cp <pod>:/path ./local -c api          # pick a container

sections.title: A debugging order that works
paragraphs: Most problems are answered by steps 2 and 3.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl logs returns nothing at all. What is the explanation?
kubectl exec into a distroless production container fails with "exec: sh: executable file not found in $PATH". What is the right approach?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does kubectl logs show nothing for a crashing Pod?

Because it reads the container that is running now, and during a CrashLoopBackOff that instance has only just started or has not started at all. The output you need belongs to the previous, terminated instance: kubectl logs <pod> --previous. Pair it with kubectl describe pod, whose events often name the cause outright, and note that --previous only reaches back one container generation. Earlier runs are gone unless you ship logs off the node.
How do I get a shell inside a running Pod?

kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh, adding -c <container> when the Pod has more than one. Use sh rather than bash, since most slim images do not include bash. The -- separator is required so that everything after it is passed to the container instead of being interpreted by kubectl. For a Pod with several containers, kubectl will not guess and returns an error until you name one.
How do I debug a container with no shell?

Use kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container>. This attaches an ephemeral container to the running Pod that shares its network namespace, and with --target its process namespace, giving you a full toolkit against the live workload without modifying the image or restarting anything. It is the standard answer for distroless and scratch images, and the Pod returns to normal when you exit.
What does kubectl port-forward do?

It opens a tunnel from a local port, through the API server, to a port on a Pod or Service in the cluster, so kubectl port-forward service/payments-api 8080:80 makes the Service reachable at localhost:8080. This is the correct way to reach an internal service or database from a laptop without creating an Ingress or changing the Service type. Forwarding to a Service selects a single Pod and is not load balanced, and the connection drops when that Pod is replaced.
Why don't my application's logs appear in kubectl logs?

Because the application writes to a file inside the container rather than to stdout or stderr. The container runtime only captures those two streams, and that is all kubectl logs can read. The fix is to configure the application to log to stdout, ideally as structured JSON, which also makes logs collectable by a shipper such as Promtail or Fluent Bit. Writing to files inside containers means losing them entirely when the Pod is removed.
Can I view logs from all Pods in a Deployment at once?

Yes, with a label selector: kubectl logs -l app=payments-api --tail=50 --prefix. The --prefix flag labels each line with its Pod name, which is necessary to make sense of interleaved output. Following multiple Pods is capped by --max-log-requests, five by default. For sustained multi-Pod log watching, stern handles it considerably better, with colouring per Pod and automatic pickup of new Pods as they appear.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how kubeconfig works, switch clusters with kubectl config use-context, set a default namespace, merge kubeconfig files and avoid the wrong cluster.
Almost everyone ends up with several clusters, local, dev, staging, production, reachable from the same terminal, with no visual difference between them.

Running a destructive command against the wrong one is the most common serious mistake people make with Kubernetes. Nothing in kubectl's output warns you, so the safeguards have to be set up deliberately.

sections.title: How kubeconfig is structured
paragraphs: ~/.kube/config holds three lists and a pointer:
A context binds a cluster, a user and a default namespace. Switching context switches all three at once.

The exec block is how cloud clusters authenticate, kubectl shells out to aws, gcloud or az to mint a short-lived token each time. That is why an expired cloud login produces a kubectl auth error rather than a cloud CLI one.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
current-context: dev

clusters:
  - name: prod-cluster
    cluster:
      server: https://prod.k8s.example.com
      certificate-authority-data: LS0tLS1...

users:
  - name: prod-admin
    user:
      exec:
        apiVersion: client.authentication.k8s.io/v1beta1
        command: aws
        args: [eks, get-token, --cluster-name, production]

contexts:
  - name: prod
    context:
      cluster: prod-cluster
      user: prod-admin
      namespace: payments

sections.title: Everyday commands
paragraphs: kubectl config current-context before anything destructive is a cheap habit that prevents an expensive mistake.

codeBlock.code: kubectl config get-contexts

sections.title: Namespaces
paragraphs: Forgetting the namespace is the most common reason for "No resources found" when you know something is running. kubectl get pods -A settles it immediately.
The namespace is part of the context, so setting it while on staging does not affect prod. That is usually what you want.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pods -n payments
kubectl get pods -A                    # every namespace
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=payments

sections.title: Several kubeconfig files
paragraphs: The KUBECONFIG variable takes a list, and kubectl merges them in order:
Merging is useful when clusters come from different sources: a cloud CLI, a client, a local kind cluster. Keeping production in its own file that you source only when needed is itself a safeguard.
To write a genuine merged file:
--flatten inlines the certificate data, which a plain config view leaves as file references that then break.
Cloud CLIs add contexts for you:
These generate long context names like arn:aws:eks:us-east-1:111122223333:cluster/production. Rename them:

codeBlock.code:
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/.kube/prod-config:~/.kube/client-a.yaml
kubectl config get-contexts

sections.title: Not losing track of where you are
paragraphs: Put the context in your shell prompt. This is the single most effective safeguard. kube-ps1 does it, and most prompt frameworks, starship, powerlevel10k, oh-my-zsh, have a Kubernetes segment built in:
Use kubectx and kubens. Interactive switching with fuzzy matching, far less typing than the kubectl config commands, and kubectx - jumps back to the previous context:
Scope a single command instead of switching. If you only need one command elsewhere, do not change the global context at all:
This is much safer in scripts, and it is what CI should do, never rely on ambient context in automation.

Keep a read-only context for production. A second user entry bound to a read-only ClusterRole, used by default, with the admin context reserved for when you genuinely intend to change something. RBAC refusing a destructive command is a far better guard than remembering not to type it.

codeBlock.code: [prod:payments] ~/work/infra $

sections.title: Contexts in CI
paragraphs: Never depend on current-context in automation. Pass an explicit kubeconfig and context:
A pipeline that inherits whatever context happened to be set is one refactor away from deploying to the wrong cluster.

codeBlock.code:
export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/kubeconfig
aws eks update-kubeconfig --region us-east-1 --name production --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG
kubectl --context=arn:aws:eks:... apply -f ./manifests/

sections.title: Checking what you can actually do
paragraphs: kubectl auth can-i is worth knowing for two reasons: it tells you whether a permission error is RBAC or something else, and --as lets you check a service account's permissions without impersonating it in anger.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n payments
kubectl auth can-i '*' '*'                     # am I cluster admin here?
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:api

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: kubectl get pods returns "No resources found in default namespace" on a cluster where you know workloads are running. What are the two things to check?
A CI job runs kubectl apply with no --context and no explicit KUBECONFIG, relying on whatever context the runner has set. What is the problem?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a kubectl context?

A named combination of a cluster, a user credential and a default namespace, stored in your kubeconfig. Switching context with kubectl config use-context <name> changes all three at once, which is how you move between clusters without editing configuration. kubectl config get-contexts lists them with the current one marked, and kubectl config current-context prints just the active name.
How do I switch between Kubernetes clusters?

kubectl config use-context <name> changes the active context. For a single command elsewhere, kubectl --context=prod get pods avoids changing global state at all, which is safer and is what scripts should do. kubectx makes interactive switching much quicker, with fuzzy matching and kubectx - to jump back to the previous context.
How do I change the default namespace?

kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=payments sets it for the current context, so you stop passing -n on every command. Because the namespace is part of the context, changing it on staging leaves prod untouched. kubens does the same thing interactively if you have kubectx installed.
How do I use multiple kubeconfig files?

Set KUBECONFIG to a colon-separated list, export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/.kube/client-a.yaml, and kubectl merges them, exposing every context. To produce a single merged file, run KUBECONFIG=a:b kubectl config view --flatten > merged; the --flatten flag inlines certificate data, which a plain config view leaves as file paths that then break when the file moves. Keeping production credentials in a separate file you source deliberately is itself a useful safeguard.
How do I avoid running commands against the wrong cluster?

Show the current context in your shell prompt, kube-ps1, or the Kubernetes segment in starship, powerlevel10k or oh-my-zsh, so it is always visible. Prefer kubectl --context=<name> for one-off commands rather than switching globally. Most importantly, make production read-only by default with a separate admin context used only when you intend to change something, so RBAC refuses destructive commands rather than relying on you remembering which cluster you are on.
Why does kubectl ask me to log in again on a cloud cluster?

Cloud kubeconfigs use an exec credential plugin that shells out to aws, gcloud or az to obtain a short-lived token on each call. When that CLI's own session expires, kubectl surfaces it as an authentication failure even though the kubeconfig itself is fine. Re-authenticating with the cloud CLI, aws sso login, gcloud auth login, restores access without touching your Kubernetes configuration.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what a Kubernetes Pod is, what its containers share, why pod IPs change, how to write one, and how to read the statuses you see when debugging.

A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes will schedule. You can't ask Kubernetes to run a container. You ask it to run a Pod, and the Pod contains one or more containers that are guaranteed to land on the same node and share an network identity.

Almost every Pod in production has exactly one application container. The ability to hold several exists for the cases where two processes are genuinely inseparable, not as a general packaging mechanism.

sections.title: Why a wrapper around containers at all?
paragraphs: Because some things must run together, and "together" has to mean something precise. A log shipper that reads files the application writes needs the same filesystem. A proxy that intercepts the application's traffic needs the same network interface. Scheduling them independently would mean they might land on different machines, and the arrangement would fall apart.
A Pod makes co-location a guarantee rather than a hope.

sections.title: What containers in a Pod actually share
paragraphs: The shared network namespace has one consequence worth internalising: two containers in the same Pod cannot listen on the same port. They share a port space, so a second container binding :8080 fails exactly as it would on a single host.
Runs to completion before main containers start
Container 1. Main app
Your application process
e.g. log forwarder, proxy
Behind the scenes a small "pause" container holds the network namespace open so application containers can restart without the Pod losing its IP.

sections.title: Pods are disposable, and the IP goes with them
paragraphs: Every Pod gets its own cluster-routable IP. That IP belongs to the Pod, not to your application, and it is gone the moment the Pod is replaced. During a deploy, a node drain, an eviction, or a crash past the restart limit.
Nothing should ever hardcode 10.244.1.17. That is what a Service is for. It provides a stable name and virtual IP in front of whatever Pods currently exist.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get pods -o wide

sections.title: Writing a Pod
paragraphs: Three details in that manifest are worth defending in review:
Pin the image tag. :1.4.2, never :latest. A mutable tag means two Pods from the same manifest can run different code, and a restart can silently change your application version.

Always set a requests value. Without it the scheduler assumes the Pod needs nothing and will happily pack it onto a node with no room, where it competes for CPU and gets evicted first under memory pressure.

Set a memory limit but think twice about a CPU limit. Exceeding a memory limit gets the container killed (OOMKilled), which is what you want. An untethered memory leak takes down the node otherwise. CPU limits work differently: they throttle rather than kill, and an aggressive CPU limit adds latency to an application that would otherwise be fine.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  labels:
    app: payments-api
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 128Mi
        limits:
          memory: 512Mi
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
      env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          value: info

sections.title: Multi-container patterns
paragraphs: Three patterns justify a second container:
Init containers run to completion, in order, before any application container starts. Use them for migrations, waiting on a dependency, or fetching configuration.

If an init container fails, the Pod retries it and the application never starts, which is usually correct. A Pod stuck in Init:0/1 means the init container is failing or waiting; kubectl logs <pod> -c run-migrations tells you which.

Sidecars run alongside the application for its whole life: a log shipper, a metrics exporter, a service mesh proxy. Modern Kubernetes models these as init containers with restartPolicy: Always, which fixes a long-standing problem where a Job's sidecar kept running after the main container finished, so the Job never completed.
Adapters reshape output. For example, translating an application's custom metrics format into something Prometheus can scrape.
If you're reaching for a second container and it isn't one of these, you probably want a second Pod.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: run-migrations
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
      command: ["./migrate", "up"]
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2

sections.title: Lifecycle
paragraphs: A Pod's phase is a coarse summary:

restartPolicy controls what happens when a container exits: Always (the default, and what Deployments use), OnFailure, or Never. It applies to containers within the Pod. A Pod is never "restarted", it is replaced.

sections.title: Debugging: the three statuses you will actually see
paragraphs: kubectl describe pod is the right first command for all of them, because the Events section at the bottom usually states the cause outright.
Pending: nothing will schedule it. Read the events:
Common causes: requests larger than any node can satisfy, no node matching a nodeSelector or affinity rule, a taint with no matching toleration, or an unbound PersistentVolumeClaim.

ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull: the kubelet cannot fetch the image. Almost always a typo in the image name, a tag that does not exist, or a private registry with no imagePullSecret. The events name the registry error verbatim.

CrashLoopBackOff: the container starts, exits, and Kubernetes restarts it with growing backoff (10s, 20s, 40s, up to five minutes). This is a symptom, never a cause. The cause is in the logs of the run that failed:
That --previous flag is the single most useful thing to know about debugging Pods. Without it you get the logs of a container that has only just started and has nothing to say yet.

Typical causes, in rough order of frequency: a missing environment variable or config file, a failing dependency at startup, an OOMKilled container whose memory limit is too low, or a liveness probe that starts before the application finishes booting and kills it repeatedly.

codeBlock.code: kubectl describe pod payments-api-7d4f-x8k2

sections.title: Don't create bare Pods
paragraphs: A Pod you create directly is not managed by anything. If the node fails, the Pod is gone and nothing recreates it. There is no self-healing, no scaling, no rolling update.

Use a Deployment for stateless applications, a StatefulSet for anything needing stable identity or storage, a DaemonSet for one-per-node agents, and a Job or CronJob for work that finishes. Each of these creates Pods for you.
Bare Pods are for debugging:

codeBlock.code: kubectl run tmp-shell --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Pod defines two containers, both configured to listen on port 8080. What happens?
A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. You run kubectl logs and get no output at all. What is the most useful next command?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a Pod and a container?

A container is a running image with its own filesystem and process. A Pod is the Kubernetes object that wraps one or more containers and gives them a shared network namespace, a shared IP, and a shared lifecycle on a single node. Kubernetes schedules Pods, not containers. You cannot ask it to place a container directly. In practice most Pods hold exactly one container, and the multi-container capability exists for processes that genuinely cannot be separated, such as an application and its log shipper.
Why is my Pod stuck in Pending?

Nothing has been able to schedule it. Run kubectl describe pod <name> and read the Events section, which states the reason explicitly. The frequent causes are resource requests larger than any node can satisfy, no node matching a nodeSelector or affinity rule, a node taint with no matching toleration on the Pod, and a PersistentVolumeClaim that has not bound. A message like 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu means exactly what it says. Either lower the requests or add capacity.
What does CrashLoopBackOff mean and how do I fix it?

It means the container starts, exits, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with an increasing delay between attempts, up to five minutes. It is a symptom rather than a diagnosis. Read the logs of the run that failed with kubectl logs <pod> --previous, since plain kubectl logs shows the instance that has only just started. The usual causes are a missing environment variable or config file, a dependency unavailable at startup, an OOMKilled container whose memory limit is too low, and a liveness probe firing before the application has finished booting.
Can two containers in the same Pod use the same port?

No. They share one network namespace and therefore one port space, so the second process to bind fails with "address already in use", exactly as it would on a single machine. Give each container a distinct port. This same shared namespace is what lets containers in a Pod reach each other on localhost with no service discovery.
Should I ever create a Pod directly?

Only for debugging. A bare Pod has no controller behind it, so if its node fails or it is evicted, nothing recreates it. There is no self-healing, no scaling, and no rolling update. For real workloads use a Deployment for stateless services, a StatefulSet where stable identity or storage matters, a DaemonSet for per-node agents, and a Job or CronJob for work that completes. A throwaway debugging Pod via kubectl run --rm -it is the legitimate exception.
Why does my Pod keep getting OOMKilled?

The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it. Confirm it with kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}', which returns OOMKilled. Either the limit is genuinely too low for the workload, or the application has a memory leak that a higher limit will only postpone. Check actual usage with kubectl top pod before raising the number, and be aware that runtimes with their own heap settings, the JVM especially, need to be told about the container limit or they will size their heap against the node's total memory instead.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Write a Kubernetes Pod manifest with confidence. Walks through apiVersion, metadata, the container spec, ports and securityContext with a full example.
Every Kubernetes object shares the same four top-level fields, and a Pod is the clearest place to learn them because everything else embeds a Pod spec inside it.
A Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job and CronJob all contain spec.template.spec, which is a Pod spec. Learn it once.

sections.title: The four top-level fields
paragraphs: apiVersion differs by object: v1 for core types like Pod, Service and ConfigMap, apps/v1 for Deployment and StatefulSet, batch/v1 for Job. Getting it wrong gives no matches for kind.
There is a fifth field, status, which the control plane writes and you never set.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1          # which API group and version
kind: Pod               # what kind of object
metadata:               # name, namespace, labels, annotations
  name: payments-api
spec:                   # the desired state. This is the interesting part
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2

sections.title: Metadata
paragraphs: Labels are for selection; annotations are for information. Services, Deployments and NetworkPolicies all find Pods by label, so labels must be structured and consistent. Annotations hold anything else, build metadata, controller configuration, tool-specific settings, and cannot be selected on.
Name rules catch people: lowercase alphanumerics and hyphens only, at most 253 characters, and no underscores. A name that works fine as a Docker container name may be rejected here.

codeBlock.code:
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: payments
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
    app.kubernetes.io/version: "1.4.2"
    app.kubernetes.io/component: api
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "Deploy 1.4.2 (PR #455)"

sections.title: The container spec
paragraphs: containerPort does not publish or open anything. The container listens on whatever port its process binds; this field records that for humans and lets a Service reference the port by name.
Naming ports is worth doing. A Service or probe can then use targetPort: http, which survives a port number change.
The defaulting behaviour around latest catches people. Pin your tags and this stops mattering.
fieldRef exposes Pod metadata to the container without hardcoding it. Useful for logging and telemetry:

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
      imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

      ports:
        - name: http
          containerPort: 8080
          protocol: TCP

      env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          value: info
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: payments-db
              key: password
        - name: POD_IP
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: status.podIP

      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 128Mi
        limits:
          memory: 512Mi

      volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/app
          readOnly: true

  volumes:
    - name: config
      configMap:
        name: payments-config

sections.title: securityContext
paragraphs: Worth setting deliberately, because the defaults are permissive:

runAsNonRoot: true makes Kubernetes refuse to start a container whose image runs as root, which turns a silent security weakness into a visible startup failure. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true means anything needing to write requires an explicit emptyDir mount. More work initially, and it removes a large category of runtime tampering.
fsGroup sets group ownership on mounted volumes, which is how a non-root process gets write access to a PersistentVolume.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  securityContext:              # Pod level. Applies to all containers
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    fsGroup: 10001
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
    - name: api
      securityContext:          # container level. Overrides the Pod level
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]

sections.title: Full example
paragraphs: Note port: http in the probe, referencing the named port, and the /tmp emptyDir that a read-only root filesystem makes necessary.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  labels:
    app: payments-api
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    fsGroup: 10001
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
      ports:
        - name: http
          containerPort: 8080
      env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          value: info
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 128Mi
        limits:
          memory: 512Mi
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: http
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: {}
  restartPolicy: Always

sections.title: Pods are largely immutable
paragraphs: Once created, almost nothing in a Pod spec can change. You may update the image, and little else. Changing environment variables, resources or volumes requires deleting and recreating the Pod.
This is why you use a Deployment. Change its template and the Deployment creates new Pods for you, gradually, with a rollback available.

codeBlock.code:
The Pod "payments-api" is invalid: spec: Forbidden:
pod updates may not change fields other than `spec.containers[*].image` ...

sections.title: Finding fields without searching
paragraphs: kubectl explain documents fields against the API server you are actually connected to, so it matches your Kubernetes version rather than whatever version a search result described.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl explain pod.spec
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources
kubectl explain pod.spec.securityContext --recursive

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Pod declares containerPort: 8080 but the application actually listens on 3000. What happens?
You edit a standalone Pod to change an environment variable and apply it. The API server rejects the change. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What are the required fields in a Pod manifest?

apiVersion: v1, kind: Pod, a metadata.name, and a spec.containers list where each container has a name and an image. Everything else is optional, though a manifest with only those is unfit for production. Resource requests, a readiness probe and a securityContext should all be considered part of the minimum in practice. kubectl explain pod.spec documents every available field against your cluster's own API version.
What is the difference between labels and annotations?

Labels are indexed key-value pairs used for selection: Services find Pods by label, Deployments identify the Pods they own by label, and NetworkPolicies choose targets by label. Annotations hold arbitrary metadata that nothing selects on, build information, tool configuration, controller hints, and can be far larger. If something needs to find the object, it must be a label; if it only needs to know something, it belongs in an annotation.
Does containerPort actually expose the port?

No. It is informational. The container listens on whatever port its process binds, and Kubernetes neither enforces nor alters that. Declaring containerPort documents intent and, when named, lets a Service's targetPort or a probe's port reference it by name rather than number, which is more readable and survives a port change. A mismatch between the declaration and reality produces no error, only a Service or probe that cannot connect.
Why can't I edit a running Pod?

Pods are almost entirely immutable once created, because the scheduler has already placed them and reserved resources on a specific node based on their spec. Only spec.containers[*].image may be changed. To alter anything else you delete and recreate the Pod, which is precisely why real workloads use a Deployment, where changing the template creates replacement Pods gradually and keeps the previous version available for rollback.
What should I put in securityContext?

At Pod level, runAsNonRoot: true with an explicit runAsUser, an fsGroup so mounted volumes are writable by that user, and seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault. At container level, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, and capabilities: drop: ["ALL"]. runAsNonRoot is the highest-value single setting because it converts an image that silently runs as root into a visible startup failure. A read-only root filesystem usually requires adding an emptyDir at /tmp.
How do I find out what fields are available?

kubectl explain pod.spec and kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources document fields directly from the API server you are connected to, so the output always matches your cluster's version rather than whatever a search result describes. Add --recursive to see a whole subtree at once. To get a working starting point, kubectl run name --image=x --dry-run=client -o yaml generates a valid manifest without contacting the cluster.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand Kubernetes pod phases and container states, restartPolicy, termination and eviction, and why CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom rather than the cause.
A Pod has a coarse phase and each of its containers has a finer state. Reading both is how you turn "it is broken" into a specific thing to fix.

sections.title: Phases
paragraphs: Phases only move forward. A Pod never returns from Failed to Running. It is replaced by a new Pod, with a new name.
Running does not mean healthy. A Pod showing Running with READY 0/1 is failing its readiness probe and receiving no traffic. The READY column, not the phase, is what tells you it is serving.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'

sections.title: Container states
paragraphs: Each container is in one of three states, and this is where the detail lives:
The lastState field holds the previous container instance, which is where you find out why something crashed:
That one command distinguishes a memory limit problem from an application bug, and it is much faster than reading logs.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].state}' | jq

sections.title: Startup order
paragraphs: A Pod stuck at Init:0/1 means an init container is failing or waiting:

codeBlock.code: kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-container-name>

sections.title: restartPolicy
paragraphs: It applies to containers within a Pod, not to the Pod itself. A Pod is never restarted. It is replaced.

An important consequence: with restartPolicy: Always, a container that exits successfully is still restarted. A Pod meant to run a task to completion needs OnFailure or Never, which is why you use a Job rather than a Deployment for batch work.

sections.title: CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom
paragraphs: The container starts, exits, and the kubelet restarts it with an increasing delay: 10s, 20s, 40s, doubling up to a five-minute cap. The backoff resets after the container runs successfully for 10 minutes.
It tells you the container keeps dying. It does not tell you why. The cause is in the logs of the run that failed:
Typical causes, roughly in order:
Exit codes carry information: 137 is SIGKILL, usually OOM or a liveness kill; 143 is SIGTERM, a normal shutdown; 1 is a generic application error; 127 means the command was not found.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl describe pod <pod>

sections.title: Termination
paragraphs: When a Pod is deleted, two things happen at the same time, and the race between them causes dropped requests:
After terminationGracePeriodSeconds, 30 by default, anything still running gets SIGKILL.

The preStop sleep delays SIGTERM long enough for endpoint removal to reach every node, so no new requests arrive at a container that is about to stop. Meanwhile the application should handle SIGTERM by refusing new connections and finishing in-flight work.

The grace period must exceed your longest normal request, or in-flight work is killed. A container that ignores SIGTERM entirely takes the full grace period on every single deploy, which is a common reason rollouts feel slow.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
    - name: api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["sleep", "5"]

sections.title: Eviction
paragraphs: The kubelet evicts Pods when a node runs low on memory or disk, in QoS order: BestEffort first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed.
A Pod with no resource requests is BestEffort and first to go, which is a reason to set requests quite apart from any performance tuning.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pods --field-selector status.phase=Failed
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A5 Conditions

sections.title: Reading status quickly
paragraphs: A compact view of restart reasons across a namespace:

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod <name>                     # events explain most of it
kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml | yq '.status'   # the full picture

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Pod runs a migration script that completes successfully and exits 0, but Kubernetes keeps restarting it. The Pod was created directly with default settings. Why?
A container terminated with exit code 137 and its own logs end mid-request with no error. What most likely happened?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What are the Kubernetes Pod phases?

Pending means the Pod is accepted but not yet running. Being scheduled, or pulling images. Running means it is bound to a node with at least one container running. Succeeded means all containers exited 0 and will not restart, and Failed means all terminated with at least one failure. Unknown means the node stopped reporting. Phases only move forward; a failed Pod is replaced rather than recovered. Note that Running says nothing about health. The READY column does that.
What does CrashLoopBackOff actually mean?

The container starts, exits, and the kubelet restarts it with a growing delay: 10 seconds, then 20, then 40, doubling to a five-minute cap, resetting after ten minutes of stable running. It is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Find the cause with kubectl logs <pod> --previous, which shows the run that failed rather than the one just starting, and kubectl describe pod for the events. The usual culprits are missing configuration, an unreachable startup dependency, an OOM kill, or a liveness probe firing before the application is ready.
What is the difference between restartPolicy values?

Always restarts the container on any exit, including a successful one, and is the default used by Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets. OnFailure restarts only on a non-zero exit and suits Jobs. Never does not restart at all. The policy applies to containers within a Pod. A Pod itself is never restarted, only replaced. This is why a task that completes should run as a Job: under Always a successful exit is treated as something to correct.
What do exit codes 137 and 143 mean?

Codes above 128 encode the signal that terminated the process: 137 is 128 plus 9 for SIGKILL, and 143 is 128 plus 15 for SIGTERM. 143 usually indicates a normal shutdown during a deploy or scale-down. 137 means the process was killed outright, most often OOMKilled at its memory limit or terminated after failing a liveness probe. Check lastState.terminated.reason to tell those apart. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so the container never logs anything about it.
How do I make my application shut down gracefully?

Three things together. Handle SIGTERM in the application by refusing new connections and finishing in-flight requests rather than exiting immediately. Add a preStop hook that sleeps a few seconds, so removal from Service endpoints propagates to every node before the signal arrives. And set terminationGracePeriodSeconds above your longest normal request, because anything still running when it expires is SIGKILLed. Skipping the preStop delay is the usual reason a correctly-configured rolling update still drops a few connections.
Why is my Pod stuck in Init:0/1?

An init container is failing or still waiting. Init containers run to completion in order before any application container starts, so a failing one blocks the Pod indefinitely while being retried. Read its logs with kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-container-name>. The container name is required, since the main container has not started. Common causes are an init container waiting on a dependency that never becomes available, or a migration step failing against the database.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn when and how to run multiple containers in one Kubernetes Pod: init containers, native sidecars, shared emptyDir volumes, and when to avoid the pattern.
A Pod can hold several containers, and they get two things no separate Pods can have: a shared network namespace and the ability to share volumes.
That is the entire justification. If two containers do not need either, they belong in separate Pods.

sections.title: What is shared and what is not
paragraphs: The shared port space has a consequence people hit immediately: two containers in a Pod cannot listen on the same port. The second bind fails exactly as it would on a single host.

sections.title: Init containers
paragraphs: Run to completion, in order, before any application container starts.
Each must succeed before the next starts. A failure is retried per the Pod's restart policy and the application containers never run, which is usually exactly right for a migration.

Init containers are also a neat security trick: a tool needed only at startup (a secret fetcher, a git clone) lives in the init container's image, so it is absent from the long-running container's attack surface.
A Pod stuck at Init:0/2 means the first init container is failing or waiting:

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ['sh', '-c', 'until nc -z payments-db 5432; do echo waiting; sleep 2; done']
    - name: run-migrations
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
      command: ['./migrate', 'up']
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2

sections.title: Sidecars
paragraphs: A sidecar runs alongside the application for its whole life: a log shipper, a metrics exporter, a service mesh proxy.
Modern Kubernetes models these as init containers with restartPolicy: Always, which is the native sidecar mechanism:
The odd-looking placement solves real problems that plain sidecars had:
If you are on an older cluster, sidecars still work as ordinary entries in containers. You just have to handle ordering yourself, typically with a preStop hook.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: log-shipper
      image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
      restartPolicy: Always          # makes this a sidecar, not a run-once init
      volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/app
          readOnly: true
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
      volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/app
  volumes:
    - name: logs
      emptyDir: {}

sections.title: The other two patterns
paragraphs: Adapter: reshapes output the application already produces. Translating a bespoke metrics format into something Prometheus can scrape, without modifying the application.

Ambassador: proxies the application's outbound connections. The application connects to localhost:5432 and the ambassador handles TLS, connection pooling, or failover to a real database elsewhere. Simplifies the application at the cost of another process.

sections.title: Sharing data between containers
paragraphs: The shared network namespace means localhost:
And emptyDir for files:
Set a sizeLimit on any emptyDir you share. Without one, a log file that grows unchecked fills the node's disk and gets every Pod on that node evicted.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
      env:
        - name: CACHE_URL
          value: "http://localhost:6379"    # the sidecar, no service discovery
    - name: cache
      image: redis:7-alpine

sections.title: When not to use a multi-container Pod
paragraphs: The temptation is to bundle an application with its database, or a frontend with its backend. Do not.

Containers in a Pod scale together, deploy together and are scheduled together. You cannot run three API replicas and one database from the same Pod definition. You get three databases. And every application deploy restarts the database with it.
The test: would they ever need to be on different machines? If yes, separate Pods.

sections.title: Working with them
paragraphs: With more than one container, kubectl logs refuses to guess and errors until you pass -c.

Resource requests and limits are per container, and the Pod's total is their sum, so a Pod with a 512Mi application and a 256Mi sidecar requests 768Mi. Sidecars replicated across hundreds of Pods add up to real money; size them deliberately rather than copying a default.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl logs <pod> -c api
kubectl logs <pod> --all-containers --prefix
kubectl exec -it <pod> -c api -- sh
kubectl describe pod <pod>        # per-container state and events

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Job runs a batch task plus a log-shipping sidecar listed under containers. The task completes, but the Job stays active indefinitely. Why?
A team puts their API and its PostgreSQL database in one Pod "so they can talk over localhost", then scales the Deployment to three replicas. What happens?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: When should a Pod contain more than one container?

Only when the containers need a shared network namespace or a shared volume. A log shipper reading files the application writes needs the volume; a service mesh proxy intercepting the application's traffic needs the network namespace. Those are genuine reasons. If two containers merely communicate over the network, they belong in separate Pods with a Service between them, because containers in a Pod are scheduled, scaled and deployed as a single unit.
What is the difference between an init container and a sidecar?

An init container runs to completion before the application containers start, and is used for migrations, waiting on dependencies, or fetching configuration. A sidecar runs for the whole life of the Pod alongside the application. Modern Kubernetes expresses sidecars as init containers with restartPolicy: Always, which makes them start before the app containers and terminate after them. Solving startup ordering for service mesh proxies and, importantly, letting Jobs with sidecars actually complete.
Why does my Job with a sidecar never complete?

Because a Job is only complete when every container in its Pod has terminated, and a sidecar such as a log shipper has no reason to exit. The Pod stays active forever. The fix is to declare the sidecar as an init container with restartPolicy: Always rather than as an ordinary entry in containers; Kubernetes then recognises it as a sidecar and shuts it down once the main containers finish. On older clusters the workaround was for the main container to signal the sidecar to exit.
Can containers in a Pod use the same port?

No. They share a single network namespace, and therefore one IP address and one port space, exactly as two processes on the same host would. The second container to bind the port fails with "address already in use" and typically ends up in CrashLoopBackOff. Give each container a distinct port. This same shared namespace is what lets them reach each other over localhost with no service discovery at all.
How do containers in a Pod share files?

Through a volume mounted into both, usually an emptyDir. It is created when the Pod is scheduled and deleted when the Pod is removed, which matches the shared lifecycle. Mount it at whatever path each container expects; they can be different paths. Always set a sizeLimit, because an emptyDir consumes node disk and a log file growing unchecked can fill the node and cause every Pod on it to be evicted.
Should I put my application and database in the same Pod?

No. Containers in a Pod scale together, so three replicas means three databases with three separate datasets. They also deploy together, so every application release restarts the database. And they are scheduled together, so both compete for one node's resources. Run the database as a StatefulSet with its own storage and put a Service in front of it. The convenience of localhost is not worth losing independent scaling, independent deployment, and the ability to give each workload the resources it actually needs.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Configure Kubernetes liveness, readiness and startup probes. Learn when to use each, the HTTP, TCP and exec methods, timing fields and common failure modes.

Probes are how the kubelet learns whether your container is alive and whether it should receive traffic. Without them, Kubernetes assumes a running process is a working process, which is very often wrong.
They are also one of the easiest things to misconfigure into an outage, so the defaults and the timing deserve real attention.

sections.title: Three probes, three different questions
paragraphs: The distinction people most often blur is liveness versus readiness. Liveness restarts. Readiness redirects. Failing readiness is a normal, recoverable state. A Pod warming a cache or briefly overloaded should fail readiness and get no traffic, then come back. Failing liveness is a declaration that the process is unrecoverable and must be killed.

sections.title: Readiness: the one you should always set
paragraphs: Readiness gates Service endpoints. A Pod that is not ready receives no traffic.

This is also what makes a rolling update safe. During a Deployment rollout, Kubernetes waits for a new Pod to become Ready before terminating an old one. Without a readiness probe, "running" is taken to mean "ready", so traffic is routed to a process still loading configuration, and the next old Pod is terminated. The rollout reports success while users see errors.
If you set only one probe, set this one.

codeBlock.code:
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3

sections.title: Liveness: use it sparingly
paragraphs: Liveness exists for the case a process is running but permanently stuck: a deadlock, an exhausted thread pool, an event loop that will never recover.
Ask honestly whether a restart would fix the condition you are detecting. If the answer is no, a liveness probe makes things worse. It adds restarts to a system that is already struggling.

Never check dependencies in a liveness probe. A /healthz that queries the database will fail on every replica the moment the database slows, and Kubernetes will restart your entire fleet in a loop. A slow database becomes a total outage, caused by the health check.
The safe shape: liveness checks only that this process can still respond. Readiness may check whether it can usefully serve.

codeBlock.code:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 20
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  failureThreshold: 3

sections.title: Startup: for slow boots
paragraphs: Applications that take a long time to start create a dilemma: initialDelaySeconds large enough for a cold JVM makes liveness slow to detect real failures afterwards.
A startup probe resolves it. While it runs, liveness and readiness are suspended entirely:

That gives five minutes to boot and a thirty-second detection window afterwards. Without it you would need initialDelaySeconds: 300 on liveness, and a container that hung after minute six would go unnoticed for five minutes.

codeBlock.code:
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 30      # allows up to 300s to start
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3       # then react in ~30s

sections.title: Probe methods
paragraphs: exec probes are the expensive option. Every probe forks a process inside the container, and an aggressive exec probe across many Pods is a measurable CPU cost. Prefer httpGet where you can.
tcpSocket only proves the port is open, not that the application behind it works. It is a weak check, and for an HTTP service it is usually the wrong one.

codeBlock.code:
# HTTP, with a header if needed
httpGet:
  path: /healthz
  port: 8080
  httpHeaders:
    - name: X-Probe
      value: kubelet

# TCP, only proves something is listening
tcpSocket:
  port: 5432

# exec. Note this runs a process every period
exec:
  command: ["sh", "-c", "pg_isready -U postgres"]

sections.title: The timing fields
paragraphs: Time to detection is periodSeconds × failureThreshold, plus up to one timeoutSeconds. The defaults above mean roughly 30 seconds.

timeoutSeconds: 1 is the default and it is aggressive. An endpoint that occasionally takes 1.2 seconds under load will fail intermittently, and because probes get slower exactly when the system is loaded, the probe pushes a busy service over the edge. Setting it to 3 to 5 seconds costs nothing.

sections.title: A complete example
paragraphs: Two endpoints, deliberately different. /healthz answers "this process is alive" and touches nothing external. /ready answers "I can serve a request right now" and may check that a connection pool is initialised, but still not that the whole database is healthy.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: payments-api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: payments-api }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080

          # Allow up to 150s to boot
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 30

          # Then detect a wedged process in ~30s
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 3
            failureThreshold: 3

          # Gate traffic; react faster, and allow recovery
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 3
            failureThreshold: 2

sections.title: Failure modes to recognise
paragraphs: Liveness too aggressive. A slow startup plus a short initialDelaySeconds means the probe fails before the app is up, the container is killed, and it restarts into the same trap. Symptom: CrashLoopBackOff with clean application logs and Liveness probe failed in the events. Use a startup probe.
No readiness probe. Every deploy produces a short burst of errors while Kubernetes routes to Pods that are not serving yet.
Liveness that checks dependencies. A shared dependency degrades and every replica restarts simultaneously. A partial problem becomes a complete outage.
Readiness that never recovers. successThreshold must be 1 for liveness and startup probes, but for readiness a higher value adds hysteresis to a flapping service.
That last command resolves most probe arguments immediately. Wrong port, wrong path, or an endpoint that requires authentication and returns 401.

codeBlock.code:
# What the kubelet actually saw
kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A5 Events

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A liveness probe hits /healthz, which verifies the database is reachable. The database slows down for two minutes. What happens to the application?
A Java service takes about 90 seconds to become responsive. It crash-loops with "Liveness probe failed" despite the application logging no errors. What is the correct fix?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a liveness and a readiness probe?

A liveness probe answers "is this container stuck?" and a failure causes the kubelet to kill and restart it. A readiness probe answers "should this container receive traffic right now?" and a failure removes the Pod from its Service endpoints without restarting anything. Failing readiness is a normal, temporary state. A Pod warming up or briefly overloaded. Failing liveness is a statement that the process is unrecoverable. Use readiness liberally and liveness sparingly.
Why is my Pod in CrashLoopBackOff with "Liveness probe failed"?

The probe is failing before the application is ready to answer it. Check kubectl describe pod for the exact message. A timeout usually means the app has not started or the endpoint is slow, while a 404 or connection refused usually means the wrong path or port. If the application genuinely takes a long time to boot, the fix is a startup probe rather than a larger initialDelaySeconds, because a startup probe protects the boot window without weakening detection afterwards. Test the endpoint from inside the Pod with kubectl exec -it <pod> -- wget -qO- localhost:8080/healthz.
Do I need all three probes?

Readiness, essentially always. It is what makes rolling updates safe and keeps traffic off Pods that cannot serve. Liveness only when a restart would genuinely fix a condition you can detect, such as a deadlock; otherwise it adds restarts to a struggling system without helping. Startup only when the application takes long enough to boot that liveness would kill it first. A common and reasonable configuration is readiness alone, with a startup probe added for slow-starting services.
Should my health check verify the database connection?

Not in a liveness probe. A shared dependency fails for every replica at once, so the entire fleet gets restarted simultaneously and a slow database becomes a complete outage caused by the health check itself. A readiness probe may check that the application is able to serve, including that its connection pool is initialised, since removing Pods from the Service is recoverable and does not restart anything. The safest pattern is a /healthz that checks only the process and a /ready that checks whether this instance can serve a request.
What do initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold actually control?

initialDelaySeconds is how long the kubelet waits before the first probe, periodSeconds how often it repeats, timeoutSeconds how long it waits for a response, and failureThreshold how many consecutive failures trigger the action. Time to detection is roughly periodSeconds × failureThreshold. The default timeoutSeconds of 1 is worth changing. An endpoint that occasionally takes just over a second under load will fail intermittently, and probes get slower precisely when the system is busiest.
Why do my Pods get no traffic even though they are Running?

They are Running but not Ready, so they have been excluded from the Service's endpoints. kubectl get pods shows this in the READY column as 0/1, and kubectl describe pod gives the probe's failure message. Common causes are a readiness path that requires authentication and returns 401, a wrong port, or an initialDelaySeconds shorter than the application's real startup time. Confirm with kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>. An empty list means no Pod is currently ready.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how a Kubernetes Deployment manages ReplicaSets and pods, how to write one, run rolling updates and rollbacks, and when to choose a StatefulSet instead.

A Deployment is how you run a stateless application on Kubernetes. You declare what you want, this image, this many replicas, and a controller works continuously to make reality match, replacing failed pods, rolling out new versions gradually, and keeping enough history to undo a bad release.
It is the resource you will use for the overwhelming majority of workloads.

sections.title: Why not manage pods yourself?
paragraphs: A bare pod has no controller watching it. When its node reboots, the pod is gone and stays gone. Nothing scales it, nothing replaces it, and updating it means deleting and recreating it by hand with an outage in between.
A Deployment gives you self-healing, scaling, gradual rollouts, and a documented way back.

sections.title: The chain: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods
paragraphs: This indirection confuses people until they see why it exists.

A Deployment does not create pods. It creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet creates pods. Each time you change the pod template, a new image, a changed environment variable, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually scales the old one down while scaling the new one up.
Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods
replicas: 3 · strategy: RollingUpdate
desired: 3 · ready: 3

The old ReplicaSet is kept at zero replicas deliberately. That retained object is your rollback. Undoing a release scales it back up. revisionHistoryLimit controls how many are kept, defaulting to 10.
One consequence worth knowing: scaling does not create a revision. Only pod template changes do. Changing replicas from 3 to 5 adjusts the current ReplicaSet in place.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get replicasets

sections.title: Writing a Deployment
paragraphs: selector.matchLabels must match template.metadata.labels. The API server rejects a Deployment where they disagree, which is a good thing. The selector is how the Deployment finds the pods it owns.
The selector is also immutable after creation. If you need to change it, you delete and recreate the Deployment. Choose labels you can live with.

A readinessProbe is what makes a rolling update safe. Without one, Kubernetes considers a pod ready the instant its container process starts, so it will send traffic to an application still loading configuration or warming a connection pool, and, worse, will proceed to terminate the next old pod. The rollout looks clean and users see errors.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: payments-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10

sections.title: Rolling updates
paragraphs: Two settings control the shape of the rollout:

maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 is the safe default: never fewer healthy pods than you asked for, at the cost of one extra pod's resources during the rollout. The opposite, maxUnavailable: 1, maxSurge: 0, updates in place with no extra capacity but runs degraded, which only makes sense on a tightly constrained cluster.

The alternative strategy is Recreate: terminate everything, then start the new version. It causes downtime by design and exists for applications that genuinely cannot run two versions at once, such as one holding an exclusive lock or applying incompatible schema migrations.

codeBlock.code:
# Update the image
kubectl set image deployment/payments-api api=ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.5.0

# Watch it happen
kubectl rollout status deployment/payments-api

sections.title: Rollbacks
paragraphs: That CHANGE-CAUSE column comes from a kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation, and it is empty unless you set it. Do set it. During an incident, a history of revision numbers with no descriptions is nearly useless:
If a rollout is going badly and you want it to stop without reverting, pause it:
Pausing is also how you batch several changes into one rollout instead of triggering a separate one per edit.

codeBlock.code:
# What has happened to this Deployment?
kubectl rollout history deployment/payments-api

sections.title: When a rollout will not finish
paragraphs: This is the most common Deployment problem, and the diagnosis is nearly always the same shape.

progressDeadlineSeconds defaults to 600, so a stuck rollout reports failure after ten minutes. Critically, it does not roll back. It simply stops and tells you. The old pods keep serving, which is why a failed deploy usually is not an outage.
Look at the new pods, not the Deployment:
The realistic causes:
A rollout blocked because new pods will not schedule is the reason maxSurge/maxUnavailable matters on a full cluster.

codeBlock.code: kubectl rollout status deployment/payments-api

sections.title: Deployment or StatefulSet?
paragraphs: If your application is happy having any replica handle any request and keeps no local state, use a Deployment. Databases and quorum-based systems need the stable identity a StatefulSet provides.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Deployment with maxUnavailable: 0 has no readiness probe. During every rollout users see brief 502 errors, yet kubectl rollout status reports success. Why?
kubectl rollout status returns "exceeded its progress deadline" after ten minutes. What is the state of the application right now?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a Deployment and a ReplicaSet?

A ReplicaSet keeps a specified number of identical pods running, that is all it does. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and adds everything around versioning: when you change the pod template it creates a new ReplicaSet, shifts replicas from old to new gradually, and keeps the previous ReplicaSets so you can roll back. You almost never create a ReplicaSet directly; you create a Deployment and it manages them for you.
Why is my deployment stuck and not rolling out?

The rollout is waiting for new pods to become Ready and they never do. Ignore the Deployment and look at the pods: kubectl get pods -l app=<label> then kubectl describe pod <new-pod>. The usual causes are a readiness probe pointed at the wrong path or port, an initialDelaySeconds shorter than the application's real startup time, an image tag that does not exist, a crash at startup visible via kubectl logs <pod> --previous, or, with maxUnavailable: 0, no room in the cluster for the one extra surge pod.
How do I roll back a bad deployment?

kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> reverts to the previous revision, and --to-revision=N targets a specific one from kubectl rollout history. This works because old ReplicaSets are retained at zero replicas, so a rollback is really just scaling one of them back up. It is fast, but note that revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) bounds how far back you can go, and a rollback does not undo anything outside Kubernetes. A database migration applied by the bad release still needs handling separately.
What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable actually do?

They bound the rollout. maxSurge is how many pods above your replica count may exist temporarily, and maxUnavailable is how many of your desired pods may be down at once. maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 never dips below full capacity but needs room for one extra pod. maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 uses no extra capacity but runs one pod short during the update. Both accept percentages, which is more useful at larger replica counts.
How do I restart all pods in a deployment without changing the image?

kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>. It sets a timestamp annotation on the pod template, which counts as a template change and triggers a normal rolling update, so it respects your surge and unavailability settings and causes no downtime. This is the correct way to pick up a changed ConfigMap or Secret mounted as environment variables, since those do not restart pods on their own.
When should I use a StatefulSet instead?

When pod identity matters. StatefulSets give each pod a stable name and DNS entry that survives rescheduling, create a PersistentVolumeClaim per pod, and start and stop pods in order. That is what databases, message brokers and quorum-based systems need. A replica has to come back as the same member with the same data. If any replica can serve any request and keeps nothing on local disk, a Deployment is simpler and is the right choice.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create a Kubernetes Deployment with kubectl create deployment or a YAML manifest. Learn matchLabels, kubectl scale, inspecting objects and common errors.
A Deployment declares how many identical Pods should exist and what they should look like. A controller then makes that true and keeps it true.

sections.title: The quickest version
paragraphs: That is fine for experimenting and wrong for anything you intend to keep. Nothing records why the cluster is in this state, and nobody can reproduce it.
Use the imperative command to generate a manifest instead:
Nothing is sent to the cluster; you get a valid skeleton to edit and commit.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl get deployments

sections.title: The manifest
paragraphs: Four things in that file deserve a moment.
selector.matchLabels must equal template.metadata.labels. The API server rejects a mismatch, which is helpful. The selector is how the Deployment identifies the Pods it owns.

The selector is immutable. Changing it after creation requires deleting and recreating the Deployment, so pick labels you can live with. app.kubernetes.io/name and app.kubernetes.io/instance are the recommended conventions if you want something more structured than app.
Pin the image tag. :1.4.2, never :latest. A mutable tag means two Pods from one manifest can run different code, and a rollback has nothing to roll back to.
Set resource requests. Without them the scheduler assumes the Pod needs nothing, places it badly, and marks it BestEffort so it is evicted first under pressure.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  labels:
    app: payments-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api          # must match template labels below
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: payments-api        # must match selector above
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5

sections.title: What it actually created
paragraphs: Three objects, one command. The Deployment created a ReplicaSet, the ReplicaSet created the Pods, and the Pod names carry both the ReplicaSet hash and a random suffix.
That hash is derived from the pod template. Change the template and you get a new ReplicaSet with a new hash, which is the mechanism behind rolling updates and rollbacks.
The columns are worth reading precisely:
A Deployment showing 3/3 ready but 1 up-to-date is mid-rollout.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get deployment,replicaset,pods -l app=payments-api

sections.title: Scaling
paragraphs: This changes the ReplicaSet in place, scaling does not create a new revision, because the pod template has not changed.

If you scale imperatively, remember the manifest still says 3, so the next kubectl apply reverts it. Either change the file or, if load varies, use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and remove replicas from the manifest altogether so the two do not fight.

codeBlock.code: kubectl scale deployment/payments-api --replicas=5

sections.title: Inspecting
paragraphs: kubectl describe shows conditions that answer most questions directly:
Available: False means not enough Pods are ready. Progressing: False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded means a rollout gave up.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl describe deployment payments-api     # spec, conditions, events
kubectl get deployment payments-api -o yaml  # full object as stored
kubectl rollout status deployment/payments-api

sections.title: The errors you will hit
paragraphs: selector does not match template labels: the two label sets disagree. Make them identical.
field is immutable on spec.selector. You changed the selector on an existing Deployment. Delete and recreate it.
Pods Pending: nothing can schedule them. kubectl describe pod names the reason: insufficient CPU or memory, an untolerated taint, or an unbound volume claim.
Pods ImagePullBackOff: wrong image name or tag, or a private registry with no imagePullSecrets in this namespace.
0/3 ready and staying that way: the containers start but fail readiness. Check the probe path and port, and give slow-starting applications a startup probe rather than a longer initialDelaySeconds.

sections.title: Deleting
paragraphs: Deleting a Deployment cascades to its ReplicaSets and Pods through owner references. Deleting the ReplicaSet directly is a mistake. The Deployment simply recreates it.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl delete deployment payments-api
# or, preferably
kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: You edit an existing Deployment to change selector.matchLabels from app: api to app.kubernetes.io/name: api, and update the template labels to match. kubectl apply fails. Why?
You run kubectl scale deployment/api --replicas=10 during a traffic spike. The next CI deploy runs kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml and the count drops to 3. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I create a Kubernetes Deployment?

Write a manifest with apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, a replica count, a selector, and a pod template, then run kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml. The fastest way to get a correct starting point is kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deployment.yaml, which generates valid YAML without contacting the cluster. Edit that, commit it, and apply it. Managing real workloads through imperative commands leaves no record of why the cluster looks the way it does.
Why does my Deployment fail with "selector does not match template labels"?

spec.selector.matchLabels and spec.template.metadata.labels must contain the same key-value pairs. The selector is how the Deployment recognises the Pods it owns, so a mismatch would mean it creates Pods it cannot then manage, and the API server rejects it. Make the two blocks identical. Note that the selector is immutable after creation, so if you need a different label scheme later you must delete and recreate the Deployment.
What is the difference between a Deployment and a ReplicaSet?

A ReplicaSet keeps a fixed number of identical Pods running and does nothing else. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and adds version handling: changing the pod template creates a new ReplicaSet, shifts replicas from the old one to the new gradually, and retains previous ReplicaSets at zero replicas so you can roll back. You create Deployments; the ReplicaSets are an implementation detail you mostly read rather than write.
Why are my Deployment's Pods stuck at 0/3 ready?

The containers are running but failing their readiness probe, so they never become Ready. Run kubectl describe pod <name> and look at the events for the probe's failure message. The usual causes are a wrong path or port, an endpoint behind authentication returning 401, or an initialDelaySeconds shorter than the application's genuine startup time. For slow-starting applications, add a startup probe rather than inflating initialDelaySeconds, which would otherwise delay detection of real failures later.
How do I scale a Deployment?

kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=5 changes it immediately, and editing replicas in the manifest and reapplying does the same declaratively. Remember that imperative scaling is undone by the next kubectl apply if the file still specifies a different number. Where load varies, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler is the better answer, and when you adopt one, remove replicas from the manifest entirely so the autoscaler and your deployment tooling are not writing the same field.
What do READY, UP-TO-DATE and AVAILABLE mean?

READY shows how many Pods are passing readiness checks against how many are desired. UP-TO-DATE counts Pods running the current pod template, which is how you see rollout progress. AVAILABLE counts Pods that have been ready for at least minReadySeconds, so it lags READY slightly when that is configured. During a rollout these diverge, 3/3 ready with only 1 up-to-date means the new version is still being rolled out.
