sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Run zero-downtime rolling updates in Kubernetes. Tune maxSurge and maxUnavailable, use readiness probes and graceful shutdown, and fix stalled rollouts.

Change a Deployment's pod template and Kubernetes replaces its Pods gradually. Starting new ones, waiting for them to become Ready, then removing old ones, so the application stays available throughout.
That is the theory. Whether it is actually zero-downtime depends on two things people routinely skip: a readiness probe and graceful shutdown.

sections.title: What triggers one
paragraphs: Any change to spec.template creates a new ReplicaSet and starts a rollout:
Changes outside the template do not. Scaling replicas adjusts the current ReplicaSet in place and creates no revision.

kubectl rollout restart is worth knowing: it stamps an annotation on the template, which counts as a change and cycles every Pod through a normal rolling update. That is the correct way to pick up a modified ConfigMap or Secret consumed as environment variables, since those never refresh in a running process.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl set image deployment/payments-api api=ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.5.0
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml            # if the template changed
kubectl rollout restart deployment/payments-api

sections.title: Watching it
paragraphs: The old ReplicaSet is kept at zero. That retained object is your rollback.

codeBlock.code: kubectl rollout status deployment/payments-api

sections.title: maxSurge and maxUnavailable
paragraphs: Both accept an integer or a percentage, and both default to 25%.

maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 is the safe default: never fewer healthy Pods than you asked for, at the cost of one extra Pod's resources during the rollout. The trade is that the cluster must have room for that extra Pod, on a full cluster the rollout stalls with a Pending Pod and cannot progress.

The reverse, maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1, uses no extra capacity but runs one Pod short throughout. Reasonable on a tightly constrained cluster, and only if your remaining replicas can absorb the load.
At larger replica counts, percentages are more useful: maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 10% on 40 replicas rolls in sensible batches rather than one at a time.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0

sections.title: The readiness probe is what makes it safe
paragraphs: During a rollout Kubernetes waits for each new Pod to become Ready before terminating an old one. Readiness is also what gates Service endpoints.

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes treats a started process as ready. So it adds a Pod still loading configuration to the Service, and simultaneously terminates the next old Pod. The rollout reports success; users see 502s.
If you set one thing on a Deployment, set this. maxUnavailable: 0 without a readiness probe gives you the illusion of safety, not safety.
minReadySeconds adds a further hold, a Pod must stay ready for that long before counting as available, which catches applications that pass their first probe and then fall over.

codeBlock.code:
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5

sections.title: Graceful shutdown is the other half
paragraphs: When a Pod is terminated, two things happen concurrently, and the race between them is where dropped requests come from:
Endpoint propagation is not instant. A container that exits immediately on SIGTERM will still be receiving traffic when it dies.
Two fixes, used together:

The preStop sleep delays SIGTERM long enough for endpoint removal to propagate. Meanwhile the application should handle SIGTERM by refusing new connections and finishing in-flight requests. After terminationGracePeriodSeconds, 30 by default, the container is SIGKILLed regardless, so the grace period must exceed your longest normal request.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
    - name: api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["sleep", "5"]

sections.title: Recreate, when you cannot run two versions
paragraphs: Terminates everything, then starts the new version. Downtime by design.

It exists for applications that genuinely cannot run two versions simultaneously: something holding an exclusive lock, a singleton worker, or a release with an incompatible schema migration. Do not choose it to make deploys simpler.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  strategy:
    type: Recreate

sections.title: When a rollout stalls
paragraphs: progressDeadlineSeconds defaults to 600, so a stuck rollout reports failure after ten minutes. Critically it does not roll back. It stops, and the old Pods keep serving. A failed deploy is usually not an outage.
Diagnose the new Pods, not the Deployment:
To stop a bad rollout without reverting:
Pausing also lets you batch several edits into one rollout rather than triggering one per change.

codeBlock.code: error: deployment "payments-api" exceeded its progress deadline

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Deployment has maxUnavailable: 0 and a working readiness probe, yet clients see a handful of connection resets during every rollout. What is the most likely cause?
A Deployment with maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0 stalls immediately on a busy cluster. The single new Pod is Pending with "Insufficient cpu". Why can the rollout not proceed?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do rolling updates work in Kubernetes?

Changing a Deployment's pod template creates a new ReplicaSet. The Deployment controller then scales the new ReplicaSet up and the old one down in steps, bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable, waiting for each new Pod to become Ready before removing an old one. The old ReplicaSet is retained at zero replicas so a rollback is just a matter of scaling it back up. Only template changes trigger this. Adjusting the replica count alone does not.
What is the difference between maxSurge and maxUnavailable?

maxSurge is how many Pods may exist above the desired replica count during the update, and maxUnavailable is how many of the desired Pods may be unavailable at once. Both default to 25% and accept integers or percentages. maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 never drops below full capacity but requires room for one extra Pod; maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 needs no extra capacity but runs one Pod short throughout.
How do I achieve genuinely zero-downtime deployments?

Four things together. Set maxUnavailable: 0 so capacity never dips. Define a readiness probe, without which Kubernetes treats a started process as ready and shifts traffic too early. Add a preStop hook that sleeps a few seconds, so endpoint removal propagates before the container gets SIGTERM. And handle SIGTERM in the application by refusing new connections while finishing in-flight ones, with terminationGracePeriodSeconds set above your longest normal request.
Why did my rollout stop with "exceeded its progress deadline"?

The new Pods failed to become Ready within progressDeadlineSeconds, which defaults to 600. Kubernetes marks the Deployment failed and stops. It does not roll back automatically, so with maxUnavailable: 0 the old Pods are still serving and the application is up. Inspect the new Pods with kubectl describe pod: the usual causes are a failing readiness probe, an image that cannot be pulled, a crash at startup, or no cluster capacity for the surge Pod.
When should I use the Recreate strategy?

Only when the application genuinely cannot tolerate two versions running simultaneously. Something holding an exclusive lock, a singleton background worker, or a release with a schema migration that the old version cannot work against. Recreate terminates every Pod before starting any new ones, so it causes downtime by design. It should be a deliberate decision about the application's constraints, never a way to simplify a deployment.
How do I make Pods pick up a changed ConfigMap?

kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>. It sets a timestamp annotation on the pod template, which counts as a template change and triggers a normal rolling update honouring your surge and unavailability settings, so there is no downtime. This is necessary because ConfigMap values consumed as environment variables are fixed when the process starts and can never update in place. Values mounted as volumes do refresh automatically, within about a minute, unless mounted with subPath, which never updates.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Roll back a bad release with kubectl rollout undo. Learn revision history, change-cause annotations, revisionHistoryLimit and what a rollback cannot fix.
A rollback returns a Deployment to an earlier pod template. It is fast, it is one command, and it works because Kubernetes keeps the old ReplicaSets around at zero replicas.
It is also more limited than people assume during an incident, so it is worth knowing precisely what it does and does not restore.

sections.title: Revision history
paragraphs: Every pod template change creates a revision, each backed by a retained ReplicaSet:
Those zero-replica ReplicaSets are the rollback mechanism. Rolling back scales one of them back up.
Inspect a revision before choosing it:

codeBlock.code: kubectl rollout history deployment/payments-api

sections.title: Record why, not just what
paragraphs: That <none> column is the single most common regret during an incident. A list of revision numbers with no descriptions tells you nothing about which one is safe.
CHANGE-CAUSE comes from an annotation you have to set:
Better, put it in the manifest so it ships with the change:
Have CI set it automatically from the commit message or tag. It costs one line and it is what makes the history usable at 3am.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl annotate deployment/payments-api \
  kubernetes.io/change-cause="Deploy 1.5.0 - new pricing engine" --overwrite

sections.title: Rolling back
paragraphs: A rollback is itself a rolling update, so it honours maxSurge and maxUnavailable and waits on readiness probes. It is not instantaneous and it is not a hard cutover.
It also creates a new revision rather than deleting history. Rolling back from 3 to 2 produces revision 4 containing revision 2's template:
Revision 2 is renumbered as 4; the history stays complete and auditable, which matters for a post-incident review.

codeBlock.code:
# To the immediately previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/payments-api

# To a specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/payments-api --to-revision=2

# Watch it complete
kubectl rollout status deployment/payments-api

sections.title: How far back you can go
paragraphs: Only this many old ReplicaSets are kept. Beyond that the oldest are deleted and those revisions become unrollbackable.

The default of 10 is reasonable. Setting it to 0 disables rollback entirely, which occasionally appears in manifests written to reduce clutter and removes your fastest recovery option. A few extra zero-replica ReplicaSets cost nothing but an API object.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10      # the default

sections.title: What a rollback does not fix
paragraphs: This is the part worth internalising before you need it.

Database migrations. If release 1.5.0 ran a migration, rolling back the Deployment leaves it applied. If that migration dropped a column 1.4.2 depends on, the rollback makes things worse. This is why expand-and-contract migrations exist: deploy schema changes that both versions tolerate, and only remove the old shape once the new version is proven.
Deleted data. A rollback restores objects, not contents. A removed PersistentVolumeClaim comes back as an empty claim.

Anything outside this Deployment. ConfigMaps, Secrets, CRDs, other services. A rollback reverts one Deployment's pod template and nothing else, which is a strong argument for versioning ConfigMap names so config changes ride the same rollout.
In-flight side effects. Messages published, emails sent, webhooks fired. Already gone.

sections.title: Rollback or roll forward?
paragraphs: Rolling back is the right instinct when the previous version is known good and the failure is clear. It is fast and it reduces the blast radius while you investigate.

Roll forward instead when the new version has already changed persistent state in a way the old one cannot handle, when the previous version has a known problem of its own, or when the fix is genuinely small and well understood. A rollback that reintroduces a different bug is a bad trade.
If you are unsure, roll back. Restoring a known state is almost always better than debugging under pressure.

sections.title: Preventing the need
paragraphs: A correct readiness probe is the real protection: with maxUnavailable: 0, a version that never becomes Ready never displaces the old Pods, so the bad release stalls instead of taking traffic. The rollout fails and the application stays up, which is a much better outcome than a successful rollout of broken code.

codeBlock.code:
# Fail fast rather than waiting ten minutes
kubectl patch deployment payments-api -p '{"spec":{"progressDeadlineSeconds":300}}'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Release 1.5.0 ran a migration dropping an unused column, then proved buggy. After kubectl rollout undo, the old version crashes on startup. Why?
A Deployment is at revision 3. You run kubectl rollout undo to return to revision 2. What does kubectl rollout history show afterwards?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I roll back a Kubernetes deployment?

kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> reverts to the previous revision, and --to-revision=N targets a specific one listed by kubectl rollout history. Check what a revision contains first with kubectl rollout history deployment/<name> --revision=N. The rollback runs as a normal rolling update, so it honours maxSurge, maxUnavailable and readiness probes. Watch it complete with kubectl rollout status.
Why is the CHANGE-CAUSE column empty?

Because nothing set it. It reads from the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation, which Kubernetes does not populate automatically. Add it to the manifest's metadata, or run kubectl annotate deployment/<name> kubernetes.io/change-cause="..." --overwrite as part of your deploy. Having CI fill it from the commit message or release tag costs one line and turns an unusable list of revision numbers into something you can act on during an incident.
How many revisions does Kubernetes keep?

Ten by default, controlled by revisionHistoryLimit. Older ReplicaSets beyond that are deleted and their revisions can no longer be rolled back to. The default is sensible for most teams; setting it to 0 disables rollback entirely, which sometimes appears in manifests intended to reduce clutter and quietly removes the fastest recovery path available. Retained ReplicaSets sit at zero replicas and consume no compute.
Does rolling back undo database migrations?

No. A rollback changes which pod template is running and touches nothing else, no databases, no ConfigMaps, no Secrets, no external state. If the bad release applied a destructive migration, the older code will meet a schema it does not understand and may fail worse than before. The standard mitigation is expand-and-contract: ship schema changes that both the old and new versions tolerate, and only remove the old shape after the new version has proven itself.
Should I roll back or roll forward?

Roll back when the previous version is known good and the failure is clear. It restores a known state quickly and buys time to investigate properly. Roll forward when the new release has already changed persistent state in a way the old version cannot handle, when the previous version has its own known problem, or when the fix is genuinely small and well understood. When genuinely unsure, roll back; debugging under production pressure is worse than the delay.
Can I prevent bad deployments from reaching users at all?

Largely, yes. With a correct readiness probe and maxUnavailable: 0, a version that never becomes Ready never displaces the old Pods. The rollout stalls and fails after progressDeadlineSeconds while the application stays up. That converts a bad release into a failed deploy rather than an incident. Lowering progressDeadlineSeconds from its 600-second default makes the failure visible sooner, and kubectl diff -f before applying catches unintended changes.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how a Kubernetes Service finds pods with selectors, how port, targetPort and nodePort differ, how service DNS works, and which of the four types to pick.

Pods come and go, and their IP addresses go with them. A Service is the stable thing in front of them: one name, one virtual IP, and automatic load balancing across whichever pods currently match its selector.
Without Services, every deploy would break every caller.

sections.title: How a Service finds its pods
paragraphs: A Service does not reference pods by name. It carries a label selector, and Kubernetes continuously maintains a list of the pod IPs matching it.
Service → Endpoints → Pods
That matching list is stored in EndpointSlice objects, and it is the first thing to check when a Service does not work:
If that list is empty, the Service is a dead end: it will accept connections and then have nowhere to send them. Two things cause it, and they account for most Service problems people hit:

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  selector:
    app: payments-api      # matches pod labels, not pod names
  ports:
    - port: 80             # the port the Service listens on
      targetPort: 8080     # the port on the pod

sections.title: port, targetPort, nodePort
paragraphs: These three are the most commonly confused fields in Kubernetes.

So port: 80, targetPort: 8080 means callers connect to payments-api:80 and traffic arrives at the container on 8080. They are frequently the same number, which hides the distinction until the day they are not.
targetPort can also name a port declared in the pod spec, which is more readable and survives a port change:

codeBlock.code:
# in the pod
ports:
  - name: http
    containerPort: 8080

# in the Service
targetPort: http

sections.title: DNS
paragraphs: Every Service gets a DNS record. Inside the same namespace, the short name works:
Across namespaces you need the fully qualified form:
payments-api.production also resolves. A call that works from one namespace and fails from another is nearly always a missing namespace segment.
To test resolution from inside the cluster:

codeBlock.code: payments-api

sections.title: The four types
paragraphs: Reachable only from inside the cluster. This is what almost every Service should be; internal services have no business being exposed.
Opens the same port on every node, in the range 30000 to 32767, forwarding to the Service.

Useful for local clusters and quick tests. It is a poor production choice: the port range is unmemorable, you need something in front to spread traffic across nodes anyway, and every node ends up listening on a port for a service it may not run.
Asks the cloud provider for a real load balancer pointing at the Service.

The catch is cost and scale: this is one cloud load balancer per Service, each with its own hourly charge and its own IP. Ten public services means ten load balancers. That is the problem Ingress solves. One load balancer routing to many services by host and path.

An EXTERNAL-IP stuck at <pending> means no controller is fulfilling the request. On a managed cloud cluster, check subnet tagging and controller logs; on a bare-metal or local cluster, there is no cloud provider to answer, and you need something like MetalLB.
No proxying at all, just a CNAME to an external hostname. Handy for pointing an in-cluster name at a managed database while you migrate.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  type: ClusterIP

sections.title: Headless Services
paragraphs: Set clusterIP: None and Kubernetes allocates no virtual IP. DNS then returns all pod IPs instead of one Service address.

This is what StatefulSets use. Clients that need to address individual replicas. Database drivers doing their own topology discovery, quorum members talking to named peers. Need the real addresses, not a load-balanced abstraction over them.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: cassandra

sections.title: A Service is not a proxy server
paragraphs: There is no process sitting behind a ClusterIP. kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS rules on every node, and the "load balancing" is packet rewriting in the kernel. Nothing terminates TLS, nothing inspects HTTP, and there is no retry logic.
Two practical consequences:
For stickiness there is sessionAffinity: ClientIP, but as with load balancer stickiness generally, externalising session state is the better fix.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Requests to a ClusterIP Service time out. The pods are Running and serving correctly when reached by pod IP. kubectl get endpointslices shows no endpoints. What should you check first?
A gRPC service has 5 replicas behind a ClusterIP Service, but one pod receives nearly all the traffic. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer?

They are layers on top of one another. ClusterIP gives a stable internal-only virtual IP and is the default. NodePort does everything ClusterIP does and additionally opens the same port, between 30000 and 32767, on every node so external traffic can reach it. LoadBalancer does everything NodePort does and additionally asks the cloud provider to create a real load balancer pointing at those node ports. Use ClusterIP for internal services, and prefer an Ingress over many LoadBalancer Services when exposing several applications publicly.
Why does my Service have no endpoints?

Either no pod's labels match the Service selector, or matching pods are not passing their readiness probe. Compare them directly with kubectl get pods --show-labels and kubectl get svc <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'. A mismatch as small as app: payments versus app: payments-api is enough. If the labels do match, check pod readiness, because only Ready pods are added to a Service. This is intentional, but it means a misconfigured readiness probe empties the Service without any obvious error.
What is the difference between port and targetPort?

port is the port the Service itself listens on, so it is what clients inside the cluster connect to. targetPort is the port on the pod that traffic is forwarded to. With port: 80, targetPort: 8080, a client connects to my-service:80 and the container receives the request on 8080. They are often the same value, which is why the distinction only becomes visible when they differ. targetPort can also reference a named port from the pod spec, which is more readable and does not break if the number changes.
How do I call a Service in another namespace?

Use the namespace in the DNS name: service-name.namespace or the fully qualified service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. The bare short name only resolves within the same namespace, because the cluster's DNS search path appends the caller's own namespace first. A request that works from one namespace and fails from another is almost always this.
Why is my LoadBalancer Service stuck with EXTERNAL-IP pending?

Nothing is fulfilling the request. On a managed cloud cluster the cloud controller creates the load balancer, so check its logs and, on AWS, confirm your subnets carry the required role tags, since the controller discovers placement from them. On a local cluster such as kind or minikube, or on bare metal, there is no cloud provider at all and the field stays pending forever; install something like MetalLB, or use kubectl port-forward for local access.
When should I use a headless Service?

When clients need the individual pod addresses rather than a single balanced endpoint. Setting clusterIP: None makes DNS return every ready pod IP instead of one virtual IP. StatefulSets use this so each replica is individually addressable, which database clients and quorum-based systems require. It is also the foundation for client-side load balancing, which is how you get even distribution for gRPC traffic that would otherwise pin to one pod.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service works: virtual IPs, service DNS names, endpoints, testing with port-forward and headless Services.

ClusterIP is the default Service type and the one you should reach for unless you have a specific reason not to. It allocates a stable virtual IP reachable only from inside the cluster, and load balances across the Pods matching its selector.
Internal services, a database, an internal API, a cache, have no business being exposed externally, and ClusterIP is how you keep them internal.

sections.title: Creating one
paragraphs: That CLUSTER-IP comes from the cluster's service CIDR, is stable for the Service's lifetime, and is not routable from outside. EXTERNAL-IP showing <none> is correct, not a problem.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: payments
spec:
  type: ClusterIP        # the default; can be omitted
  selector:
    app: payments-api
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80           # what callers connect to
      targetPort: 8080   # the port on the Pod

sections.title: The virtual IP is not a real interface
paragraphs: Nothing is listening on 10.96.41.203. No process binds it, and you will not find it on any network interface.

kube-proxy watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs iptables or IPVS rules on every node. When a packet is sent to the Service IP, the kernel rewrites the destination to one of the backing Pod IPs and forwards it. The Service IP exists only as a set of rules.
You also cannot ping a Service IP. ICMP has no port to rewrite, so the rules do not match it. A failed ping proves nothing.

sections.title: DNS
paragraphs: Every Service gets a DNS record from CoreDNS:
Applications should use the name, never the IP. The IP is stable but it is not guaranteed, and hardcoding it means the Service cannot be recreated.
Named ports let a caller discover the port too, via an SRV record. Useful, though most applications just use the well-known port number.

codeBlock.code:
payments-api                                    # within the same namespace
payments-api.payments                           # from elsewhere
payments-api.payments.svc.cluster.local         # fully qualified

sections.title: Endpoints are the whole debugging story
paragraphs: A Service is a selector plus a list of matching Pod IPs. That list lives in EndpointSlices:
An empty list means the Service goes nowhere. Connections are accepted and then fail, which is why the symptom is usually a timeout or connection refused rather than a clear error.
There are exactly two causes:
1. The selector matches nothing.
A mismatch as small as app: payments against app: payments-api is enough. The Service is created happily either way. Kubernetes does not validate that a selector matches anything.
2. The Pods match but are not Ready.

Only Ready Pods are added to a Service. That is the entire point of a readiness probe, and it means a misconfigured probe silently empties the Service while the Pods look fine in kubectl get pods until you read the READY column.
0/1 with status Running is the signature.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=payments-api

sections.title: Testing without exposing anything
paragraphs: port-forward is the right way to reach an internal Service from a laptop. Switching a Service to NodePort or LoadBalancer just to test it is a common and unnecessary way to expose something internal.

codeBlock.code:
# Forward a local port to the Service
kubectl port-forward service/payments-api 8080:80

# Or call it from inside the cluster
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -s http://payments-api.payments/healthz

sections.title: Headless Services
paragraphs: Setting clusterIP: None allocates no virtual IP. DNS then returns every ready Pod IP rather than a single Service address:

This is what StatefulSets use, because database clients doing their own topology discovery need the real member addresses. It is also the foundation of client-side load balancing, which is the standard fix for gRPC traffic pinning to one Pod.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: cassandra

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A developer reports a ClusterIP Service is broken because ping 10.96.41.203 times out, though curl to the same address on port 80 works. What is happening?
kubectl get pods shows a Pod as Running with READY 0/1, and the Service returns connection refused. What is the cause?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a ClusterIP Service?

It is the default Service type, giving a stable virtual IP and DNS name reachable only from inside the cluster, with load balancing across the Pods matching its selector. It is what you should use for anything internal, databases, caches, service-to-service APIs, because it provides a fixed address in front of Pods whose own IPs change constantly, without exposing anything externally.
Why can't I ping a ClusterIP?

Because nothing is listening on it. kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS rules that rewrite the destination of packets sent to the Service IP and port, and ICMP has no port for those rules to match, so ping never works regardless of whether the Service is healthy. Test with curl against the actual port instead, or kubectl port-forward service/<name> 8080:80 from a laptop.
Why does my Service have no endpoints?

Either the selector matches no Pods, or the matching Pods are not Ready. Compare them directly with kubectl get svc <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}' and kubectl get pods --show-labels; Kubernetes never validates that a selector matches anything, so a small typo creates a perfectly healthy Service that goes nowhere. If the labels do match, check the READY column, only Ready Pods become endpoints, so a failing readiness probe empties the Service silently.
How do I access a ClusterIP Service from my laptop?

kubectl port-forward service/<name> 8080:80 tunnels a local port through the API server to the Service. This is the right approach for debugging and for reaching internal tools, and it needs no change to the Service itself. Switching a Service to NodePort or LoadBalancer in order to test it exposes an internal service unnecessarily and is easy to forget to undo.
What is a headless Service and when do I need one?

Setting clusterIP: None allocates no virtual IP, and DNS returns every ready Pod IP instead of one address. StatefulSets use this so each replica is individually addressable, which database clients and quorum-based systems need in order to discover cluster topology. It is also how you do client-side load balancing, which is the usual fix for gRPC connections that would otherwise pin all traffic to a single Pod.
Can a ClusterIP Service be reached from outside the cluster?

Not directly, that is the point of the type. To expose something externally you use a NodePort Service, a LoadBalancer Service, or, most commonly for HTTP, an Ingress that routes to your ClusterIP Service by hostname and path. kubectl port-forward provides temporary access for debugging without changing anything, which is usually what you actually want.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how a Kubernetes NodePort Service works: the three ports, the 30000-32767 range, externalTrafficPolicy, why it is weak for production and debugging.
A NodePort Service opens the same port on every node in the cluster and forwards anything arriving there to the Service's Pods, including nodes running none of those Pods.
It is the simplest way to reach a Service from outside a cluster, and it is rarely the right way in production.

sections.title: It builds on ClusterIP
paragraphs: NodePort does not replace ClusterIP; it adds to it. Creating a NodePort Service gives you all three of:
80:30080/TCP reads as "ClusterIP port 80, node port 30080".
Omit nodePort and Kubernetes assigns a free one. Prefer that unless you need a fixed value. Hardcoding invites collisions, since a node port is cluster-wide and two Services cannot share one.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: payments-api
  ports:
    - port: 80           # the ClusterIP port
      targetPort: 8080   # the Pod's port
      nodePort: 30080    # the port on every node (optional)

sections.title: The three ports, again
paragraphs: This is where people lose track, because there are now three numbers:
So curl http://<node-ip>:30080 from outside and curl http://payments-api:80 from inside reach the same Pods on port 8080.
On minikube there is a shortcut:

codeBlock.code:
# Find a node IP to test against
kubectl get nodes -o wide
curl http://192.168.1.24:30080/healthz

sections.title: Why the port range is what it is
paragraphs: 30000 to 32767 avoids colliding with well-known ports and with anything the node's own OS is likely to use. You cannot expose a NodePort on 80 or 443 without changing an API server flag, which is not something to do casually.
That restriction is one of the main reasons NodePort is a poor production front door. Nobody wants to publish http://api.example.com:31847.

sections.title: externalTrafficPolicy: the setting that matters
paragraphs: By default (Cluster), traffic arriving at any node is forwarded to a Pod on any node. That gives even distribution and means every node is a valid entry point, but the extra hop source-NATs the packet, so your application sees the node's IP rather than the client's.

With Local, a node only forwards to Pods running on itself. The client IP is preserved and the extra hop disappears, at the cost of two things: nodes with no matching Pod drop the traffic, and load becomes uneven if Pods are unevenly distributed.

If you need real client IPs, for rate limiting, geolocation, allowlisting, or audit logs, use Local and make sure something in front only sends traffic to nodes that have Pods. Cloud load balancers do this automatically via health checks, which is exactly why Local is common on LoadBalancer Services.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local

sections.title: Why it is a poor production choice
paragraphs: Every node opens the port, including nodes running none of the Service's Pods. On a 50-node cluster that is 50 open ports for one application.
You still need something in front. Nodes come and go, so clients cannot target a node IP directly. You need a load balancer, which is what a LoadBalancer Service creates for you automatically.
The port range is unusable for a public URL.
No TLS, no host or path routing. That is what an Ingress provides.
Where NodePort genuinely fits:
For anything public and HTTP, use an Ingress. For non-HTTP traffic on a cloud provider, use LoadBalancer.

sections.title: Debugging
paragraphs: Work outward from the Pods.

If it works internally but not from outside, the Service is fine and the problem is network access to the node. On a cloud provider, the node's security group or firewall rule almost certainly does not allow inbound traffic on the 30000 to 32767 range, that is the single most common cause. Check too whether you are using a private node IP from outside the VPC.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Does the Service have endpoints at all?
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=payments-api

# 2. Does it work internally?
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- curl -s payments-api/healthz

# 3. What is the assigned node port?
kubectl get svc payments-api -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}'

# 4. Can you reach the node at all?
kubectl get nodes -o wide

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An application behind a NodePort Service logs the same handful of source IPs for all traffic, matching the cluster nodes. Rate limiting by client IP is therefore useless. Why?
A NodePort Service works when curled from inside the cluster but times out from a laptop using a node's public IP and the node port. What should you check first?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a NodePort Service and how does it work?

It exposes a Service on a static port, between 30000 and 32767, on every node in the cluster. Traffic arriving at any node's IP on that port is forwarded to the Service's Pods, even if that particular node runs none of them. A NodePort Service also includes a ClusterIP, so internal callers are unaffected. NodePort adds an external path rather than replacing the internal one.
Why is the NodePort range limited to 30000-32767?

The range is chosen to avoid colliding with well-known service ports and with ports the node's own operating system may use. Exposing a Service on 80 or 443 directly would require changing the --service-node-port-range flag on the API server, which is not something to do casually. This restriction is a large part of why NodePort is unsuitable as a public entry point. Nobody wants to publish a URL with port 31847 in it.
What is the difference between NodePort and LoadBalancer?

LoadBalancer builds on NodePort. It does everything NodePort does and additionally asks the cloud provider to create a real external load balancer that distributes traffic across the nodes and gives you a stable public address. NodePort leaves you to solve that yourself, which is fine on bare metal where you already run a load balancer and awkward on a cloud provider where LoadBalancer does it in one line.
Should I use NodePort in production?

Usually not. Every node opens the port regardless of whether it runs the workload, the port range is unusable for a public URL, and you still need something in front to spread traffic across nodes and handle nodes coming and going. For public HTTP traffic use an Ingress, which gives you hostname and path routing plus TLS through a single load balancer. NodePort is genuinely useful for local development with minikube or kind, and on bare metal behind a load balancer you manage yourself.
Why does my application see the node's IP instead of the client's?

Because externalTrafficPolicy defaults to Cluster, which allows a node to forward traffic to a Pod on another node, and that second hop requires source NAT, replacing the client address. Setting externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps traffic on the receiving node and preserves the original source IP. The trade-off is that nodes with no matching Pod drop traffic rather than forwarding it, so whatever sits in front must health-check and only send traffic to nodes that have Pods.
My NodePort Service works inside the cluster but not from outside. What is wrong?

If it works internally, the Service, its selector and its endpoints are all correct, so the problem is network reachability to the node. On a cloud provider the node's security group or firewall almost certainly does not allow inbound traffic on 30000 to 32767, which is the most frequent cause. Also confirm you are using an IP that is actually reachable from where you are testing. A private node IP will not work from outside the VPC.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Use a Kubernetes LoadBalancer Service, configure cloud annotations, restrict access, set externalTrafficPolicy, and fix an EXTERNAL-IP stuck on pending.
A LoadBalancer Service asks your cloud provider to create a real load balancer pointing at your cluster, and reports its address back in the Service object.
It is the simplest path to a public endpoint, and its cost model is the thing to understand before you use it widely.

sections.title: It layers on NodePort, which layers on ClusterIP
paragraphs: Creating a LoadBalancer Service gives you all three:
Provisioning takes a minute or two. The 31847 is the node port underneath. You can ignore it, but it explains what the load balancer is actually targeting.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: payments-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

sections.title: The cost problem
paragraphs: This is one cloud load balancer per Service. Each has its own hourly charge, its own IP, and its own certificate and DNS record to manage. Ten public services means ten load balancers and ten sets of everything.
That is the entire argument for Ingress: one load balancer, routing to many Services by hostname and path, with TLS terminated centrally.

Use LoadBalancer for non-HTTP traffic, a database, a game server, a gRPC endpoint needing its own address, and for the single load balancer that fronts your Ingress controller. Use Ingress for everything HTTP.

sections.title: Annotations do the real configuration
paragraphs: The Service spec is deliberately minimal, so provider-specific behaviour is configured through annotations:
These are not portable. An AWS annotation on a GKE cluster is ignored silently, which is worth remembering when copying manifests between environments.
The internal scheme is the one people most often forget. Without it, a Service intended for private traffic gets a public address, and an internal API is suddenly on the internet.

codeBlock.code:
metadata:
  annotations:
    # AWS: NLB instead of the legacy classic load balancer
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "nlb"
    # Internal only, no public IP
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internal"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"

sections.title: Restricting who can connect
paragraphs: This programs the cloud firewall to accept only those sources. Support varies by provider, but where available it is far better than relying on application-level checks.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 203.0.113.0/24
    - 198.51.100.14/32

sections.title: externalTrafficPolicy
paragraphs: The same trade-off as NodePort, and here it usually matters more because you are handling real external clients.

Cluster, the default, source-NATs traffic so your application sees a node IP instead of the client's. Local preserves the client IP and removes a hop, and the cloud load balancer's health checks naturally stop sending traffic to nodes with no matching Pod, which is why Local is much safer on a LoadBalancer Service than on a bare NodePort.
If you need genuine client IPs for rate limiting, allowlisting or audit logs, set Local. Spread your Pods across nodes with a topology spread constraint so the distribution stays even.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local

sections.title: EXTERNAL-IP stuck at pending
paragraphs: Nothing is fulfilling the request. The causes, in order of likelihood:

No cloud provider. On kind, minikube or bare metal there is no controller to create a load balancer, so it stays pending forever. Install MetalLB, or use kubectl port-forward locally. On minikube, minikube tunnel fakes it.

Subnet tagging on AWS. The controller discovers where to place a load balancer from subnet tags. Public subnets need kubernetes.io/role/elb=1 and private ones kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1. Without them it cannot decide and gives up.
Missing permissions. The cloud controller manager's IAM role cannot create load balancers.
Quota exhausted. Cloud accounts cap load balancers per region, and busy clusters hit it.

codeBlock.code:
NAME           TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)        AGE
payments-api   LoadBalancer   10.96.41.203   <pending>     80:31847/TCP   12m

sections.title: Keeping the address stable
paragraphs: A load balancer's address changes if the Service is deleted and recreated, which breaks any DNS record pointing at it.
Two mitigations. Request a static IP where the provider supports it:

Or run ExternalDNS, which watches Services and Ingresses and updates Route 53, Cloud DNS or Cloudflare automatically. That is the more robust answer, since it survives recreation rather than trying to prevent it.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  loadBalancerIP: 203.0.113.42     # must be pre-allocated

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A LoadBalancer Service on a kind cluster has shown EXTERNAL-IP as pending for twenty minutes. What is happening?
A team exposes twelve HTTP microservices, each with its own LoadBalancer Service, and the cloud bill shows twelve load balancers. What is the appropriate fix?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a LoadBalancer Service?

It is a Service type that asks the cloud provider to create an external load balancer routing traffic into your cluster, then reports its address in the Service's EXTERNAL-IP field. It includes everything NodePort and ClusterIP provide, so internal access continues to work unchanged. It is the simplest way to get a stable public endpoint for a Service, and it provisions real chargeable cloud infrastructure each time you create one.
Why is my LoadBalancer Service stuck at pending?

Nothing is fulfilling the request. On kind, minikube or bare metal there is no cloud controller at all, so it will never resolve. Install MetalLB, run minikube tunnel, or use kubectl port-forward for local access. On a cloud cluster, check the Service events with kubectl describe svc and the cloud controller manager logs; the usual causes are missing subnet role tags on AWS, insufficient IAM permissions, or having hit the account's load balancer quota for that region.
What is the difference between LoadBalancer and Ingress?

A LoadBalancer Service creates one cloud load balancer per Service and routes on port alone. An Ingress uses a single load balancer, fronting an Ingress controller that routes HTTP traffic to many Services by hostname and path and terminates TLS centrally. For more than one or two public HTTP services, Ingress is substantially cheaper and easier to manage. LoadBalancer remains the right choice for non-HTTP protocols and for exposing the Ingress controller itself.
How do I make a LoadBalancer internal rather than public?

Through a provider-specific annotation: service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internal" on AWS, networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal" on GCP, and service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-load-balancer-internal: "true" on Azure. Omitting it gives you a public address, which is a genuinely common way to expose an internal API to the internet by accident. These annotations are not portable and are ignored without warning on a different provider.
Why does my application see node IPs instead of client IPs?

externalTrafficPolicy defaults to Cluster, which lets any node forward traffic to a Pod on another node and source-NATs the packet in the process. Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local to keep traffic on the receiving node and preserve the client address. On a LoadBalancer Service this is relatively safe, because the cloud load balancer health-checks each node and stops sending traffic to those without a matching Pod. The same setting on a bare NodePort has no such protection.
Can I keep the same IP address if the Service is recreated?

Some providers allow requesting a pre-allocated static address via spec.loadBalancerIP, though support and syntax vary and several clouds have moved to annotations instead. The more durable approach is ExternalDNS, which watches Services and Ingresses and updates your DNS provider automatically whenever an address changes. That way recreation is handled rather than avoided, which also covers cluster rebuilds and failovers.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how a Kubernetes Ingress works with an ingress controller, write a working manifest with pathType and TLS, and debug routing problems step by step.
An Ingress is a set of HTTP routing rules: send api.example.com here, send /admin there, terminate TLS for these hostnames. One entry point, many backend Services.
It exists because the alternative is a cloud load balancer per Service, which gets expensive and unmanageable at anything past a handful of applications.

sections.title: An Ingress on its own does nothing
paragraphs: This is the single most important thing to understand, and the cause of most "my Ingress isn't working" confusion.

An Ingress object is just configuration. It has no behaviour. Something has to read it and act on it, and that something is an Ingress controller. A separate component you install yourself. Kubernetes does not ship one.
If kubectl get ingressclass returns nothing, no controller is installed, and your Ingress will sit there with an empty ADDRESS field forever.

Common choices: ingress-nginx (the usual default), Traefik, and cloud-native controllers such as the AWS Load Balancer Controller, which provisions a real ALB rather than running a proxy in the cluster.

codeBlock.code:
# Is a controller installed?
kubectl get pods -A | grep -i ingress

# What classes are available?
kubectl get ingressclass

sections.title: A working Ingress
paragraphs: An empty ADDRESS after a few minutes means the controller has not picked it up, usually a missing or wrong ingressClassName.
The backend Service must be in the same namespace as the Ingress. There is no cross-namespace backend reference; an Ingress per namespace is the normal pattern.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: acme-public
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /payments
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: payments-api
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /users
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: users-api
                port:
                  number: 80

sections.title: pathType matters more than it looks
paragraphs: Prefix is what you want almost always. Exact on /api means /api/users gets no match and falls through to a 404, which is a surprisingly common self-inflicted outage.
Rules are evaluated longest-path-first, so a specific /api/admin rule wins over a general /api one regardless of the order you write them.

sections.title: TLS
paragraphs: Ingress terminates TLS using a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls:
The Secret must live in the same namespace as the Ingress, which catches people running one shared certificate across namespaces. It has to be copied, or issued per namespace.
In practice, don't manage certificates by hand. cert-manager issues and renews them from Let's Encrypt automatically:

cert-manager sees the annotation, solves the ACME challenge, writes the Secret, and renews before expiry. A certificate stuck in False usually means the HTTP-01 challenge cannot reach the cluster. Check that DNS points at the Ingress address and that the challenge path is not being intercepted by another rule.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.example.com
      secretName: api-example-com-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      # ...

sections.title: Annotations are controller-specific
paragraphs: This is where portability breaks down. The Ingress spec covers hosts, paths and TLS. Everything else, rewrites, timeouts, body size limits, rate limiting, auth, is done through annotations that each controller defines itself.

Those are ingress-nginx annotations. On Traefik or the AWS Load Balancer Controller they do nothing at all. Silently, with no warning. Copying a snippet from a blog post written for a different controller is a very common way to lose an afternoon.
Two defaults worth knowing on ingress-nginx: the request body limit is 1 MB, which breaks file uploads with a 413, and the read timeout is 60 seconds, which cuts off long-running requests.

codeBlock.code:
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "50m"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "120"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"

sections.title: Debugging
paragraphs: Work from the outside in.
The failures you will actually meet:

404 from the default backend: no rule matched. Either the Host header does not match your host: value (testing by IP instead of hostname does this), the path does not match given its pathType, or the Ingress is in a different namespace from the Service.

502 Bad Gateway: a rule matched but the backend is unreachable. Nearly always the Service has no endpoints, or the port in the Ingress does not match the Service's port. Note it must match the Service port, not the pod's targetPort.
503 Service Unavailable: the controller has no healthy endpoint to send to.
Empty ADDRESS: wrong or missing ingressClassName, or no controller installed.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Does the Ingress have an address?
kubectl get ingress

# 2. Did the controller accept it? Events name the problem.
kubectl describe ingress acme-public

# 3. Does the backend Service actually have endpoints?
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=payments-api

# 4. What is the controller saying?
kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller --tail=50

sections.title: Ingress and the Gateway API
paragraphs: The Gateway API is the successor to Ingress. It splits responsibilities properly. Cluster operators define Gateway resources, application teams define HTTPRoute resources, and moves the things that currently require annotations into the actual specification, including header matching, traffic splitting and cross-namespace routing.
It is worth knowing about and worth choosing for a greenfield platform. Ingress is not going away, still has far broader ecosystem support, and remains the right choice for most existing clusters.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An Ingress has been applied successfully but kubectl get ingress shows an empty ADDRESS column after 15 minutes. What is the most likely cause?
An Ingress rule uses path /api with pathType: Exact. Requests to /api succeed but /api/users returns the default backend 404. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between an Ingress and a Service?

A Service provides stable networking to a set of pods and routes on port alone. It has no understanding of HTTP. An Ingress sits in front of Services and routes HTTP traffic based on hostname and URL path, terminates TLS, and lets many applications share one entry point. They work together: the Ingress decides which Service should receive a request, and the Service decides which pod. You still need a Service for every backend an Ingress references.
Why is my Ingress returning 404?

No rule matched the request. Check three things in order. First, the Host header, if you are testing against the Ingress IP directly, no hostname is sent and a rule with host: api.example.com cannot match; use curl -H "Host: api.example.com". Second, the path and its pathType, Exact on /api will not match /api/users. Third, the namespace, because the backend Service must be in the same namespace as the Ingress. kubectl describe ingress and the controller logs usually name the problem outright.
Do I need an Ingress controller, and which should I choose?

Yes. An Ingress resource is inert configuration and Kubernetes ships no controller. ingress-nginx is the most widely used and the safest default, with the largest body of documentation and examples. Traefik is popular where dynamic configuration and a built-in dashboard matter. On AWS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller is often the better fit because it provisions a real ALB instead of running a proxy inside the cluster, which moves TLS termination and scaling to managed infrastructure.
How do I add HTTPS to an Ingress?

Reference a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls in the spec.tls block, in the same namespace as the Ingress. Rather than creating and rotating that Secret yourself, install cert-manager and add a cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer annotation; it will obtain a certificate from Let's Encrypt, write the Secret, and renew it automatically before expiry. If a certificate never becomes ready, the HTTP-01 challenge usually cannot reach the cluster. Verify DNS points at the Ingress address and no rule is intercepting the challenge path.
Why do the annotations from a tutorial have no effect?

They were almost certainly written for a different Ingress controller. Only hosts, paths and TLS are part of the Ingress specification itself; rewrites, timeouts, body size limits, rate limiting and authentication are all controller-specific annotations. An nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/* annotation is ignored entirely by Traefik or the AWS Load Balancer Controller, with no error to tell you. Check which controller you are running with kubectl get ingressclass and use its own documentation.
Should I use the Gateway API instead of Ingress?

For a new platform, it is worth serious consideration. The Gateway API separates the cluster operator's concerns from the application team's, and brings header-based matching, traffic splitting and cross-namespace routing into the specification rather than leaving them to vendor annotations. For existing clusters, Ingress remains well supported, has far more ecosystem tooling and examples, and is not being removed. Migrating is a project rather than a quick win, so most teams adopt the Gateway API for new workloads first.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn when to use a Kubernetes ConfigMap vs a Secret, how to consume them as env vars or files, why base64 is not encryption, and where real secrets belong.

The same container image should run in dev, staging and production. What changes between them is configuration, database hosts, feature flags, credentials, and Kubernetes provides two objects to supply it at runtime: ConfigMaps for ordinary values, Secrets for sensitive ones.
Getting this split right is what makes an image promotable rather than environment-specific.

sections.title: Why configuration does not belong in the image
paragraphs: An image with DATABASE_URL baked in is a staging image or a production image, never both. Promoting a build then means rebuilding it, which means the artifact you tested is not the artifact you shipped, and rotating a credential means a rebuild and redeploy of everything that uses it.
Externalising configuration is the third factor of the twelve-factor methodology, and it is the difference between promoting a tested artifact and rebuilding a hopefully-identical one.

sections.title: ConfigMap or Secret?
paragraphs: The honest summary: a Secret is a ConfigMap with different defaults and its own RBAC surface. Base64 is encoding, not encryption, and anyone who can get secrets in a namespace can read every one of them.
What a Secret genuinely gives you is worth listing, because it is not nothing:
What it does not give you is meaningful protection against someone with read access to the namespace. That is what external secret managers are for.

sections.title: Two ways to consume them, and one important difference
paragraphs: Both objects can be injected as environment variables or mounted as files. The choice is not cosmetic.
As environment variables:
The difference that matters operationally:
Mounted volumes update live. Environment variables never do.

Change a ConfigMap consumed as a volume and the kubelet refreshes the file inside the running container within a minute or so. Change one consumed as an environment variable and the running pod keeps the old value until it is replaced, because environment variables are fixed at process start.
This catches people constantly: they update a ConfigMap, see no change, and conclude Kubernetes is broken. To pick up a changed environment variable you must restart the pods:

There is one exception to the live-update rule. A volume mounted with subPath does not update. It is mounted once and stays frozen. subPath is how you place a single config file into a directory that already has other contents, so this trips up exactly the people trying to be tidy.

codeBlock.code:
env:
  - name: LOG_LEVEL
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: LOG_LEVEL
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: app-secret
        key: DB_PASSWORD

sections.title: Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets
paragraphs: Setting immutable: true prevents any further change to the data:

Two benefits. It removes a whole class of accident, nobody edits production config in place, and it measurably reduces API server load, because the kubelet stops watching immutable objects for changes.

The pattern is to version the name (app-config-v3) and update the Deployment to reference the new one, which also makes config changes visible in your rollout history and rollback-able like any other change.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config-v3
immutable: true
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info

sections.title: Where real secret management lives
paragraphs: For production, most teams keep the source of truth outside the cluster and sync it in:
The common thread is that no plaintext secret is ever committed to a repository, and rotation happens in one place rather than across every manifest.
One thing to do regardless: never commit a Secret manifest with real base64 data to Git. Base64 is not obfuscation, and Git never forgets.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: You update a ConfigMap consumed by pods as environment variables via envFrom. Minutes later the running pods still report the old value. What is happening?
A team moves database passwords from a ConfigMap into a Secret. What security improvement have they actually gained?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret?

Functionally they are near-identical key-value objects, both capped at 1 MiB and both consumable as environment variables or mounted files. The differences are that Secrets are a separate RBAC resource so access can be granted independently, their values are base64-encoded and omitted from kubectl describe, they can be encrypted at rest in etcd if the cluster is configured for it, and mounted Secret volumes are backed by tmpfs rather than node disk. Use ConfigMaps for ordinary settings and Secrets for anything sensitive, but do not mistake a Secret for encryption.
Why doesn't my pod pick up an updated ConfigMap?

Because it consumes the value as an environment variable. A process gets its environment once at start-up and it cannot be changed afterwards, so the pod keeps the old value until it is replaced. ConfigMaps mounted as volumes do update in place, typically within a minute. To apply an environment variable change, run kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>, which triggers a normal rolling update with no downtime. Note that volumes mounted with subPath also never update, which is a separate and easily missed cause of the same symptom.
Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted?

Not by default in the sense people usually mean. Values are base64-encoded in the API, which is trivially reversible. Kubernetes can encrypt Secrets at rest in etcd, but that must be configured explicitly, on managed clusters it generally means enabling envelope encryption with a cloud KMS key. Even then, anyone with get secrets permission in the namespace reads the plaintext through the API. RBAC is the real control, and for high-value credentials an external manager such as Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, synced in via the External Secrets Operator, is the right answer.
How do I store secrets in Git safely?

Never commit a Secret manifest containing real base64 data. It is not obfuscated and Git history is permanent. The two established approaches are Sealed Secrets, which encrypts a Secret with a cluster-held key so the encrypted file is safe to commit and only the in-cluster controller can decrypt it, and the External Secrets Operator, where Git holds only a reference to a secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager, Parameter Store or Vault. Both keep plaintext out of the repository while staying compatible with GitOps.
Is there a size limit on ConfigMaps?

Yes, 1 MiB, imposed by etcd. It is more than enough for configuration and too little for data. If you are approaching it, the content probably belongs somewhere else: a file fetched at start-up from object storage, a volume, or an init container that materialises it. Very large ConfigMaps also put real pressure on the API server, since every kubelet consuming one watches it for changes unless it is marked immutable.
Should I use environment variables or mounted files?

Mounted files when the value may change while the pod runs, when the application expects a config file on disk, or when the value is large or structured. Environment variables when the value is small, static for the pod's lifetime, and the application reads its configuration from the environment. A practical default is environment variables for simple scalars and volumes for anything file-shaped, while remembering that only volumes refresh without a restart.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create a Kubernetes ConfigMap with kubectl or YAML, use it as env vars with envFrom or as mounted files, and find out why a ConfigMap change did not apply.
A ConfigMap holds non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs so your application reads settings at runtime rather than having them compiled into the image. One image, many environments.
It is a plain data object with no behaviour of its own. Everything interesting happens in how a pod consumes it.

sections.title: Creating a ConfigMap
paragraphs: Good for a handful of scalars. Beyond that it becomes unreadable and unreviewable.

The key becomes the filename (nginx.conf) and the value is the entire file contents. Point it at a directory and every file in it becomes a key, which is the tidiest way to ship a set of config files.
Override the key name when the filename is not what you want inside the container:
This is the form you should keep in version control, because it is reviewable and reproducible:

Two notes on data. Values must be strings, LOG_LEVEL: 8080 or DEBUG: true is rejected by the API server, so quote them: "8080", "true". And the | block scalar is how you embed an entire file, preserving newlines.
For binary content there is a separate binaryData field taking base64 values.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl create configmap app-config \
  --from-literal=APP_ENV=dev \
  --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info

sections.title: Consuming as environment variables
paragraphs: Convenient, but it imports every key, including any that are not valid environment variable names, which are skipped silently. It also makes it hard to tell from the pod spec which variables the application actually depends on.
Mark it optional if the pod should still start without the ConfigMap:
Without optional: true, a missing ConfigMap leaves the pod stuck in CreateContainerConfigError, which kubectl describe pod will tell you plainly.
More verbose, and usually the better choice: the pod spec documents exactly what the application needs, and you can rename a key on the way in.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: env-config-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ['sh', '-c', 'env | grep APP_ && sleep 3600']
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config

sections.title: Consuming as mounted files
paragraphs: Every key becomes a file under /config, with the value as its contents.
Mounting a volume at a path replaces whatever was in that directory in the image. To place a single file into an existing directory, project just the keys you want:
The other approach is subPath, which mounts one file without hiding the directory, but it comes with a significant catch covered below.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: file-config-demo
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: config-volume
      configMap:
        name: app-config
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ['sh', '-c', 'ls /config && sleep 3600']
      volumeMounts:
        - name: config-volume
          mountPath: /config

sections.title: Why your ConfigMap change did not take effect
paragraphs: This is the most common ConfigMap question, and there are three distinct causes.
1. It is consumed as an environment variable. A process receives its environment once, at start. Nothing updates it afterwards. Restart the pods:

2. It is mounted with subPath. A subPath mount is resolved once at container start and never refreshes, unlike a normal volume mount which the kubelet keeps in sync. If you need live updates, mount the volume normally and use items to control filenames.

3. It is a normal volume mount and you are impatient. These do update, but not instantly. The kubelet refreshes on its sync period, typically up to about a minute, plus cache propagation. The file changes; your application still has to notice, which means either watching the file or being sent a signal.

A useful pattern that sidesteps all of this: version the ConfigMap name (app-config-v4), mark it immutable: true, and reference the new name from the Deployment. The config change then flows through a normal rolling update, appears in your rollout history, and rolls back with everything else.

codeBlock.code: kubectl rollout restart deployment/payments-api

sections.title: Inspecting
paragraphs: That last pair is worth reaching for early. Checking what the container sees, rather than what the manifest says, resolves most configuration arguments in seconds.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get configmaps
kubectl describe configmap app-config
kubectl get configmap app-config -o yaml

# One key's value, cleanly
kubectl get configmap app-config -o jsonpath='{.data.LOG_LEVEL}'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A ConfigMap is mounted with subPath to place one config file into /etc/nginx. Editing the ConfigMap updates it in the API, but the file in the running container never changes. Why?
Applying a ConfigMap with "MAX_CONNECTIONS: 100" in its data block fails with a type error. What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I create a ConfigMap from a file?

kubectl create configmap <name> --from-file=path/to/file creates one key named after the file, with the whole file as its value. Pointing --from-file at a directory makes a key per file in it. Use --from-file=wanted-name=path/to/file to control the key name, and --from-env-file=.env to turn a KEY=VALUE file into separate keys. For anything you intend to keep, generate the YAML with --dry-run=client -o yaml and commit that instead of running the imperative command against the cluster.
Why is my pod not seeing updated ConfigMap values?

There are three possibilities. If the value is injected as an environment variable, it can never update in a running process. Restart with kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>. If the volume uses subPath, it is mounted once and never refreshed; mount the volume normally and use items to set the filename. If it is a normal volume mount, updates do arrive but take up to roughly a minute, and your application still has to reread the file. Many need a signal or a restart to notice.
What is the difference between envFrom and valueFrom?

envFrom with configMapRef imports every key in the ConfigMap as an environment variable, which is concise but hides what the application actually depends on and silently skips keys that are not valid variable names. valueFrom with configMapKeyRef pulls one named key and lets you give it a different variable name. Prefer valueFrom for anything important, because the pod spec then documents the contract between the application and its configuration.
Can I store a whole configuration file in a ConfigMap?

Yes, and it is a common pattern. Use a YAML block scalar so newlines survive, then mount the ConfigMap as a volume so the key appears as a file. Be aware that mounting a volume at a directory replaces that directory's existing contents from the image. Use the items field to project only the keys you want, with the filenames you want. The 1 MiB ConfigMap limit applies, which is ample for configuration but not for data files.
Is there a size limit on a ConfigMap?

1 MiB, imposed by etcd, covering all keys and values together. Large ConfigMaps are also a real load on the API server, because every kubelet consuming one watches it for changes. If you are close to the limit the content probably is not configuration. Fetch it from object storage at start-up, bake it into the image, or use a volume. Marking large ConfigMaps immutable: true removes the watch overhead entirely.
Should I use immutable: true?

Usually yes, paired with a versioned name such as app-config-v4. It makes accidental in-place edits of production configuration impossible, and it lets the kubelet stop watching the object, which noticeably reduces API server load in large clusters. The trade-off is that a change means creating a new ConfigMap and updating the Deployment to reference it, which is arguably the point, since the config change then appears in your rollout history and rolls back like any other change.
