sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create Kubernetes Secrets, mount them as env vars or files, use imagePullSecrets and TLS secrets, and learn why base64 is not encryption.

A Secret holds sensitive data, passwords, API tokens, TLS keys, registry credentials, as a distinct object type with its own RBAC surface, kept out of describe output and optionally encrypted at rest in etcd.
Start with what it is not, because the misunderstanding here causes real incidents.

sections.title: Base64 is not encryption
paragraphs: Secret values are base64-encoded in the API. That is an encoding, chosen so binary data survives JSON, and it is reversible by anyone in one command:
So a Secret gives you no protection at all against a principal who can read Secrets in that namespace. What it genuinely provides:
RBAC is the control that matters. A role granting get on secrets in a namespace grants every secret in it, so audit those grants carefully:

Encryption at rest must be turned on explicitly via an EncryptionConfiguration on the API server. On managed clusters this usually means enabling envelope encryption with a cloud KMS key, on EKS, for example, it is a cluster setting, not a default.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get secret app-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d

sections.title: Creating Secrets
paragraphs: Note this puts the value in your shell history. --from-file avoids that:
In YAML, use stringData rather than data so you write plaintext and let Kubernetes encode it:
stringData is write-only. Read the object back and you will see data with base64 values.
Do not commit this file to Git with a real password in it. Base64 is not obfuscation and Git history is permanent. See the production section below.
Reference it from the pod:
A pod in ImagePullBackOff against a private registry is usually a missing imagePullSecrets, or a Secret in a different namespace, Secrets are namespaced and are not shared across namespaces.
To avoid repeating it in every pod spec, attach it to the namespace's ServiceAccount instead:
This creates a kubernetes.io/tls Secret with the fixed keys tls.crt and tls.key, which is the form Ingress expects. In practice let cert-manager create and renew these rather than doing it by hand.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl create secret generic app-secret \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=supersecret \
  --from-literal=API_TOKEN=abc123

sections.title: Consuming Secrets
paragraphs: Simple, and the most common approach, but environment variables leak more readily than files. They appear in /proc/<pid>/environ, are often captured by crash reporters and APM agents, and are inherited by every child process. For genuinely high-value credentials, prefer a file.
They also never update: changing the Secret does nothing to a running pod until it is replaced.

Each key becomes a file under /secrets. These volumes are backed by tmpfs, so the value stays in memory and never lands on node disk, and they do refresh when the Secret changes, within about a minute, and not at all if mounted with subPath.
defaultMode: 0400 is worth setting. Some tools refuse to use a key file that is group- or world-readable; SSH is the classic example.

codeBlock.code:
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: app-secret
        key: DB_PASSWORD

sections.title: Production: keep the source of truth outside the cluster
paragraphs: Writing Secret manifests by hand does not scale and cannot be safely committed. The established options:
A ExternalSecret looks like this, no secret material in the repository at all:
Rotation then happens in one place, and the operator propagates it.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: app-secret
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: app-secret
  data:
    - secretKey: DB_PASSWORD
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/payments/db
        property: password

spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A cluster has encryption at rest enabled for Secrets. A developer with get secrets permission in the namespace runs kubectl get secret -o yaml. What do they see?
A pod in the payments namespace cannot pull a private image. A regcred Secret exists and the pod spec references it in imagePullSecrets. What should you check?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted?

Not by default in the way the name implies. Values are base64-encoded in the API, which is trivially reversible with base64 -d. Kubernetes can encrypt Secrets at rest in etcd through an EncryptionConfiguration, and managed clusters generally expose this as envelope encryption with a cloud KMS key, but it must be enabled, and it protects the datastore on disk rather than API reads. An authorised caller always sees plaintext. RBAC is the control that actually restricts access.
How do I decode a Kubernetes Secret?

kubectl get secret <name> -o jsonpath='{.data.<key>}' | base64 -d. The fact that this is a one-liner is the point: base64 is an encoding for safe transport of binary data in JSON, not a security measure. kubectl describe secret deliberately shows key names and byte counts without values, which is safer when sharing terminal output.
What is the difference between data and stringData?

data expects base64-encoded values, so you must encode them yourself. stringData accepts plaintext and Kubernetes encodes it on write, which makes manifests far more readable and removes a whole class of "I forgot to encode it" errors. stringData is write-only. Reading the object back always shows data with base64 values. If both specify the same key, stringData wins.
Why does my pod fail with ImagePullBackOff on a private registry?

Most often the imagePullSecrets reference is missing from the pod spec, or the Secret exists in a different namespace. Secrets are namespaced and are never shared across them. Confirm the Secret is in the pod's namespace and was created with kubectl create secret docker-registry, which produces the required kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson type. kubectl describe pod quotes the registry's own error, which distinguishes an authentication failure from a genuinely missing tag. To avoid repeating the reference everywhere, attach the Secret to the namespace's ServiceAccount instead.
Should I use environment variables or files for secrets?

Files, for anything high-value. Environment variables are visible in /proc/<pid>/environ, are frequently captured by crash reporters and APM agents, are inherited by child processes, and never refresh when the Secret changes. Mounted Secret volumes are backed by tmpfs so the value never reaches node disk, they update within about a minute when the Secret changes, and you can restrict permissions with defaultMode: 0400. Environment variables remain reasonable for low-sensitivity values where simplicity matters.
How should secrets be managed in production?

Keep the source of truth outside the cluster and sync it in. The External Secrets Operator reads from AWS Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Vault or Azure Key Vault and creates native Secrets, so Git holds only a reference. Sealed Secrets takes the other approach, encrypting a Secret with a cluster-held key so the encrypted file is safe to commit. The usual fit for GitOps. Either way, no plaintext credential is committed and rotation happens in one place instead of across every manifest.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Compare Kubernetes storage options from emptyDir to PersistentVolumes. Learn PVCs, ReadWriteOnce vs ReadWriteMany, reclaim policies and CSI drivers.
Pods are designed to be thrown away. Anything written to a container's own filesystem dies with it, which is exactly right for a stateless API and exactly wrong for a database.
Kubernetes storage is the set of abstractions that let data outlive the pod using it, while keeping application teams out of the business of provisioning disks.

sections.title: Everything a container writes is temporary by default
paragraphs: A container's writable layer lives for the life of that container. Restart it, not the pod, just the container after a crash, and the layer is recreated empty. Nothing you wrote survives.
That surprises people who see their pod still Running with a restart count of 1 and wonder where their files went.

sections.title: The storage options, in order of how long data lasts
paragraphs: Pod → PVC → PV → Storage backend
cluster-wide resource
Created empty when the pod is assigned to a node, deleted when the pod is removed. Its main use is sharing a directory between containers in the same pod:
It consumes node disk, and by default nothing bounds it. A runaway process filling an emptyDir can fill the node and get every pod on it evicted. Set a limit:

hostPath mounts a directory from the node itself. It survives pod deletion, but only on that node, so the moment the pod is rescheduled elsewhere the data is gone. It is also a serious security concern: a pod that can mount / or the container runtime socket effectively owns the node.
Legitimate uses are node-level agents. Log collectors reading /var/log, monitoring agents reading /proc. For application data, use a PersistentVolumeClaim.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: scratch
      emptyDir: {}
  containers:
    - name: app
      volumeMounts:
        - name: scratch
          mountPath: /var/cache/app
    - name: log-shipper
      volumeMounts:
        - name: scratch
          mountPath: /logs
          readOnly: true

sections.title: PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims
paragraphs: The abstraction has two halves, and the split exists to separate two audiences.

An application team writes a PVC. The platform provides the PV. Developers never name a disk ID or a NFS export, so the same manifest works on a laptop, in staging, and on a cloud cluster where the backing storage is completely different.
In practice you rarely write a PV by hand. A StorageClass provisions one dynamically when the PVC is created, that is what storageClassName: gp3 above is asking for.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: payments-data
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: gp3
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi

sections.title: Access modes
paragraphs: This is where expectations most often break.

The critical detail: RWO is per node, not per pod. Two pods on the same node can both mount an RWO volume. Two pods on different nodes cannot, which is why a Deployment with 3 replicas and one RWO PVC leaves two pods stuck in Pending. The volume is already attached elsewhere.
And most block storage is RWO only. AWS EBS, GCP Persistent Disk and Azure Disk cannot do RWX at all. Shared read-write access needs a file system: EFS, Azure Files, Filestore, or NFS.
If you need many replicas each with their own storage, that is a StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplate, not a Deployment sharing one PVC.

sections.title: Reclaim policy: what happens when the claim goes
paragraphs: Delete is the default on most cloud StorageClasses, which means deleting a namespace can permanently destroy a database volume. For anything you would be upset to lose, use a StorageClass with reclaimPolicy: Retain, and rely on volume snapshots rather than hoping.

sections.title: CSI: where the implementations come from
paragraphs: Kubernetes itself does not know how to talk to EBS or Ceph. The Container Storage Interface is the plugin standard, and drivers are installed separately. The EBS CSI driver on EKS, and so on. This matters when a PVC stays Pending and the events say no provisioner is available: the driver is not installed.
CSI drivers also supply volume snapshots and volume expansion, which is how you grow a PVC:
Expansion works only if the StorageClass sets allowVolumeExpansion: true, and shrinking is never supported.

codeBlock.code: kubectl patch pvc payments-data -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'

sections.title: Debugging a Pending PVC
paragraphs: That particular message is not an error. It is volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer working correctly, deferring provisioning until the scheduler picks a node so the disk is created in the right Availability Zone. It binds as soon as a pod uses it.
Real causes of a stuck PVC:

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get pvc
kubectl describe pvc payments-data

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Deployment with 3 replicas mounts a single PVC with ReadWriteOnce backed by an EBS volume. One pod runs; two stay Pending with a volume attachment error. Why?
A new PVC sits in Pending with the event "waiting for first consumer to be created before binding". No pod uses it yet. What should you do?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a PersistentVolume and a PersistentVolumeClaim?

A PersistentVolume is the actual storage resource in the cluster and is cluster-scoped. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a namespaced request for storage. This much capacity, these access modes, this StorageClass. The split separates the platform team who supply storage from the application team who consume it, so a manifest asking for "20Gi ReadWriteOnce" works unchanged whether the backing store is EBS, Ceph or a local disk. With dynamic provisioning you write only the PVC and the StorageClass creates the PV automatically.
Why is my PersistentVolumeClaim stuck in Pending?

Run kubectl describe pvc <name> and read the events. If it says "waiting for first consumer", nothing is wrong. The StorageClass uses WaitForFirstConsumer and binds once a pod schedules. Otherwise the usual causes are no default StorageClass (kubectl get storageclass should show one marked default), no CSI driver installed so nothing can provision, an access mode the backing storage cannot provide such as ReadWriteMany on block storage, or a zone mismatch between an existing volume and where the pod can be scheduled.
Can multiple pods share the same PersistentVolume?

It depends entirely on the access mode and the backing storage. ReadWriteOnce allows read-write mounting by one node at a time, so pods on that same node can share it but pods elsewhere cannot. ReadWriteMany allows many nodes simultaneously, but block storage, EBS, GCP Persistent Disk, Azure Disk, cannot provide it at all. For genuine shared read-write access you need a file-based system such as EFS, Azure Files, Filestore or NFS. If each replica needs its own storage rather than shared storage, use a StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplate.
What happens to my data when I delete a PVC?

That is set by the reclaim policy on the PersistentVolume. With Delete, which is the default for most cloud StorageClasses, the underlying disk is destroyed along with everything on it. With Retain, the PV and data survive and an administrator decides what to do next. Because Delete is the default, removing a namespace can permanently destroy a database volume. For anything valuable, use a StorageClass with reclaimPolicy: Retain and take volume snapshots.
Should I ever use hostPath?

Only for workloads that genuinely need access to the node's own filesystem. Log collectors reading /var/log, monitoring agents reading /proc, some CSI and networking components. For application data it is a poor choice: the data is bound to one node, so a rescheduled pod finds nothing, and it is a significant security risk since a pod able to mount host paths can often escalate to controlling the node. Use a PersistentVolumeClaim instead, or emptyDir if the data is genuinely temporary.
What is emptyDir and when should I use it?

emptyDir is a directory created when a pod is assigned to a node and deleted when the pod is removed. It survives container restarts but not pod replacement, which makes it right for scratch space, caches, and sharing files between containers in the same pod. An application writing logs that a sidecar ships, for instance. Set a sizeLimit, because by default it can consume all node disk and cause evictions across the node. Setting medium: Memory makes it a tmpfs, which is fast but counts against the pod's memory limit.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand Kubernetes PersistentVolumes and PVCs: static vs dynamic provisioning, access modes, reclaim policies, expansion, and why a PVC stays Pending.
A PersistentVolume (PV) is storage that exists in the cluster. A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a namespaced request for some of it. A pod mounts the claim, never the volume.
The indirection is the point: an application manifest asks for "20Gi, ReadWriteOnce, fast" and works unchanged whether that resolves to an EBS volume, a Ceph RBD image, or a directory on a laptop.

sections.title: Scope and ownership
paragraphs: Because a PV is cluster-scoped and a PVC is namespaced, a PVC in staging can never bind a PV already claimed by production. Bindings are exclusive and one-to-one.

sections.title: Static versus dynamic provisioning
paragraphs: Static means an administrator creates PVs ahead of time and claims bind to whichever one fits. You will see this in tutorials and on bare metal, and rarely anywhere else:
Dynamic means a StorageClass creates the PV on demand when a PVC appears. This is how essentially every real cluster works:

Omitting storageClassName entirely uses the cluster's default StorageClass. Setting it to "" explicitly disables dynamic provisioning and forces binding to a pre-created PV. A distinction that catches people out, because the two are not the same thing.
Pod → PVC → PV → Storage backend
cluster-wide resource

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: demo-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath:
    path: /data/demo-pv        # local clusters only, never production

sections.title: Binding states
paragraphs: Released is the state worth understanding. A released PV is not reusable as-is: it still carries a claimRef pointing at the deleted PVC, so no new claim can bind to it even though the data is intact. Recovering it means clearing that reference. See below.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get pv,pvc

sections.title: Access modes
paragraphs: Two things people get wrong here. RWO is a node constraint, so several pods on the same node can share an RWO volume, which makes the failure look intermittent, working until the scheduler spreads replicas. And block storage cannot do RWX at all: EBS, GCP Persistent Disk and Azure Disk are RWO only, so shared read-write requires EFS, Azure Files, Filestore or NFS.
ReadWriteOncePod is the strict one, useful when even two pods on the same node writing concurrently would corrupt data.

sections.title: Reclaim policies
paragraphs: Dynamic provisioning defaults to Delete on nearly every cloud StorageClass. That means deleting a namespace destroys its database volumes with it, permanently.
For anything valuable, use a StorageClass with reclaimPolicy: Retain. You can also flip an existing PV:
This is a five-second change that has saved a great many people.

codeBlock.code: kubectl patch pv pvc-a1b2 -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'

sections.title: Expanding a volume
paragraphs: Requirements and caveats:

codeBlock.code: kubectl patch pvc payments-data -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'

sections.title: Recovering data from a Released PV
paragraphs: The scenario: someone deleted a PVC, the policy was Retain, and the data is still on the volume. The PV is Released and will not bind to anything.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Confirm the data is still there
kubectl get pv pvc-a1b2 -o yaml

# 2. Remove the stale claim reference so it returns to Available
kubectl patch pv pvc-a1b2 -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}'

# 3. Create a PVC that targets it explicitly

sections.title: A PVC stuck in Terminating
paragraphs: Almost always a finalizer waiting on something still using the volume.
The kubernetes.io/pvc-protection finalizer holds the PVC while any pod still references it. Find and remove the consumer:
Force-removing the finalizer is possible and is a genuinely bad idea unless you are certain nothing is attached. You can end up with a volume attached to a node that Kubernetes no longer tracks.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get pvc payments-data -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'

sections.title: Storage for StatefulSets
paragraphs: A Deployment sharing one PVC does not scale past one replica on RWO storage. When each replica needs its own volume, that is a StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplate:
This creates data-postgres-0, data-postgres-1, data-postgres-2, each bound to its own volume and reattached to the same pod ordinal after rescheduling.

One thing to know: deleting a StatefulSet does not delete its PVCs. That is deliberate protection, and it also means scaling down then up reuses the old data, and that orphaned PVCs keep costing money until someone removes them.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  serviceName: postgres
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: postgres }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: postgres }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:17
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
        storageClassName: gp3
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 20Gi

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A PVC was deleted by mistake. The PV has reclaimPolicy Retain and shows status Released, and the data is intact. A new PVC with identical specs stays Pending. Why?
You delete a StatefulSet that ran three Postgres replicas with a volumeClaimTemplate. What happens to the three PVCs?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a PV and a PVC?

A PersistentVolume is the storage itself and is cluster-scoped; a PersistentVolumeClaim is a namespaced request for storage with a given size, access mode and class. Pods reference claims, never volumes directly. The separation lets application teams ask for storage in portable terms while the platform decides what actually backs it, so the same manifest works across clusters with entirely different storage. With dynamic provisioning you write only the PVC and a StorageClass creates the matching PV.
Why is my PVC stuck in Pending?

Check kubectl describe pvc <name> first. "Waiting for first consumer" is normal WaitForFirstConsumer behaviour and resolves once a pod uses the claim. Genuine causes are no default StorageClass, no CSI driver installed so nothing can provision, an access mode the backing storage does not support, most commonly ReadWriteMany on block storage, insufficient capacity in a statically provisioned pool, or a zone mismatch between an existing volume and where the pod can schedule.
How do I resize a PersistentVolumeClaim?

Patch the requested storage upward: kubectl patch pvc <name> -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'. This requires allowVolumeExpansion: true on the StorageClass. Shrinking is never supported by any provisioner. Some drivers complete the filesystem resize online while others set a FileSystemResizePending condition and finish when the pod restarts, so check the PVC's status conditions if the new size does not appear inside the container.
Can I recover data after accidentally deleting a PVC?

Only if the reclaim policy was Retain. In that case the PV moves to Released with the data intact but will not bind to anything, because it still references the deleted claim. Clear it with kubectl patch pv <pv> -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}', then create a PVC with volumeName set to that PV and storageClassName: "" so dynamic provisioning does not hand you a new empty volume instead. With Delete, the underlying storage was destroyed and only a snapshot or backup will help.
Why is my PVC stuck Terminating?

The kubernetes.io/pvc-protection finalizer is holding it because a pod still references the claim. Run kubectl describe pvc <name> and look at the "Used By" field, then delete or reschedule that pod. The finalizer clears automatically once nothing is using the volume. Removing the finalizer by hand does work but risks leaving a volume attached to a node that Kubernetes no longer knows about, so it should be a last resort after confirming nothing is mounted.
Do StatefulSet volumes get deleted when I delete the StatefulSet?

No. PVCs created from a volumeClaimTemplate deliberately outlive the StatefulSet so that deleting a workload cannot destroy a database. Recreating the StatefulSet with the same name reattaches the existing volumes, which is also how scaling down and back up preserves data. The flip side is that finished workloads leave PVCs behind that continue to cost money, so decommissioning something properly means deleting its claims explicitly.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how a Kubernetes StorageClass enables dynamic provisioning: key fields, volumeBindingMode, allowVolumeExpansion, the default class and debugging.
A StorageClass describes a kind of storage the cluster can create on demand. A PersistentVolumeClaim names one, and a provisioner creates a matching volume automatically.
Without StorageClasses an administrator has to pre-create every PersistentVolume by hand. With them, an application team writes a claim and gets a disk.

sections.title: What one looks like
paragraphs: Using it is a single line in the claim:

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "3000"
  throughput: "125"
  encrypted: "true"
reclaimPolicy: Delete
allowVolumeExpansion: true
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

sections.title: The fields that matter
paragraphs: Which CSI driver creates the volume, ebs.csi.aws.com, disk.csi.azure.com, pd.csi.storage.gke.io, efs.csi.aws.com, and so on.

The driver must actually be installed. A StorageClass naming a provisioner that is not present leaves claims Pending forever with an event saying no provisioner is available. This is the most common cause of a PVC that never binds on a self-managed cluster:
Provisioner-specific and completely unportable. AWS gp3 parameters mean nothing to the Azure driver. Check the driver's own documentation rather than copying between clouds.
encrypted: "true" is worth making the default. Encryption at rest costs nothing on most providers and cannot be turned on after the volume exists.
What happens to the underlying disk when the PVC is deleted.
Delete is the default, and it means deleting a namespace can permanently destroy a database volume. A practical pattern is to offer two classes and use the retaining one for anything stateful:
The trade-off is that retained volumes accumulate and keep costing money, so someone has to clean them up deliberately.
The field most worth understanding, because its default behaviour produces a confusing symptom.

With Immediate on a multi-zone cluster, the volume is created in some zone before anyone knows where the Pod will run. If the scheduler later picks a node in a different zone, the Pod cannot mount it and sits Pending with a volume node affinity conflict.
WaitForFirstConsumer defers provisioning until the scheduler has chosen a node, so the disk is created in the right zone. Use it for any zonal block storage.
The side effect is an event that looks like a problem and is not:
A PVC sitting Pending with that message is working correctly. It binds as soon as a Pod uses it.
Immediate remains appropriate for genuinely zone-independent storage such as EFS or NFS.
Must be true before a PVC can grow:
Shrinking is never supported by any provisioner. Enable expansion on every class you create. There is no downside, and turning it on later does not help volumes that already exist.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get csidrivers

sections.title: The default StorageClass
paragraphs: A PVC with no storageClassName uses whichever class is annotated as default:

Two things to watch. Exactly one class should be default, with several, behaviour is unpredictable. And storageClassName: "" is not the same as omitting the field: an empty string explicitly disables dynamic provisioning and forces binding to a pre-created PV.

Managed clusters ship a default, and it is rarely the best choice. On EKS it has historically been gp2, which is slower and more expensive than gp3 for most workloads. Checking and replacing it is a quick win.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl patch storageclass gp3 \
  -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'

sections.title: Snapshots
paragraphs: CSI drivers that support it provide volume snapshots, which is the real backup mechanism for Kubernetes storage:
A snapshot can then be restored into a new PVC via dataSource. reclaimPolicy: Retain is not a backup. It only helps if the PVC is deleted, and does nothing for corruption or accidental writes.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-snapshots
driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
deletionPolicy: Delete

kubectl describe pvc payments-data
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl get csidrivers
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=ebs-csi-controller -c csi-provisioner --tail=50

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A StorageClass uses volumeBindingMode: Immediate on a three-zone cluster. A PVC binds instantly, but the Pod using it stays Pending with "volume node affinity conflict". What happened?
A team deletes a staging namespace to clean up. The Postgres data volume is gone permanently. Which StorageClass setting caused this?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a StorageClass in Kubernetes?

It is a cluster-scoped object describing a type of storage that can be created on demand, which CSI driver provisions it, what parameters that driver should use, what happens to the disk when the claim goes away, and when provisioning should happen. A PersistentVolumeClaim names a StorageClass and the provisioner creates a matching PersistentVolume automatically, which removes the need for an administrator to pre-create volumes by hand.
What does volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer do?

It defers creating the volume until a Pod using the claim has been scheduled, so the disk is provisioned in the same Availability Zone as the node that will mount it. With Immediate, the volume is created straight away in some arbitrary zone, and if the scheduler later places the Pod elsewhere the Pod is stuck with a volume node affinity conflict. Use WaitForFirstConsumer for any zonal block storage, and do not mistake its "waiting for first consumer" event for an error. It is the mode working as intended.
Why is my PVC stuck in Pending with a StorageClass set?

Check kubectl describe pvc for the exact event. "Waiting for first consumer" is normal and resolves once a Pod uses the claim. "No volume plugin matched" or a missing provisioner means the CSI driver named by the StorageClass is not installed. Confirm with kubectl get csidrivers. Otherwise look at the provisioner's own logs, since quota limits, permissions and unsupported parameter combinations all surface there rather than on the claim.
How do I set or change the default StorageClass?

Add the annotation storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" to the class you want, and remove it from any other. Having two defaults makes the behaviour unpredictable. Claims that omit storageClassName then use it. Be aware that storageClassName: "" is not the same as leaving the field out: an empty string explicitly disables dynamic provisioning and forces binding to a pre-created PersistentVolume.
How do I stop deleting a namespace from destroying my data?

Create a second StorageClass with reclaimPolicy: Retain and use it for anything stateful. With Delete, which is the default on nearly every cloud StorageClass, removing a PVC destroys the underlying disk, and deleting a namespace removes every PVC in it. Retain keeps the volume and its data, leaving the PV in a Released state that an administrator can recover. Retained volumes do accumulate cost, so they need deliberate cleanup, and real volume snapshots remain the actual backup mechanism.
Can I change a StorageClass after volumes have been created?

Most fields on a StorageClass are immutable, and in any case changes do not apply retroactively to existing PersistentVolumes. They were provisioned with the settings in force at the time. To move a workload onto different storage you create a new StorageClass, create a new PVC using it, and migrate the data, typically from a volume snapshot. This is why enabling allowVolumeExpansion and encryption from the beginning matters: neither can be added to a volume that already exists.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how Kubernetes namespaces work, which resources are namespaced, cross-namespace DNS, how to split a cluster, and fix a namespace stuck Terminating.

A namespace is a name-scoping boundary inside a cluster. Two Deployments can both be called api as long as they live in different namespaces, and RBAC, quotas and network policy can all be applied per namespace.
What a namespace is not is a security boundary on its own. Pods in different namespaces can reach each other over the network by default, and they share the same nodes and kernel.

sections.title: What is namespaced and what is not
paragraphs: The PV/PVC split is the one that catches people: a PersistentVolumeClaim is namespaced but the PersistentVolume it binds is not. So a claim can only be used by Pods in its own namespace, while the underlying volume is a cluster resource.
Secrets being namespaced is the other frequent surprise. A registry credential created in default does nothing for a Pod in payments.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true | head
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false

sections.title: The built-in namespaces
paragraphs: Avoid default for anything real. It has no quota, no network policy and no meaningful RBAC, and things accumulate there until nobody knows what is safe to delete.

sections.title: Working with them
paragraphs: Set a default so you stop typing -n:
Forgetting the namespace is the most common reason kubectl get pods reports "No resources found" when something is definitely running.
Label your namespaces. They are the handle for network policy selectors, quota reporting and cost allocation, and adding them later means reconstructing who owns what.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl create namespace payments

# or declaratively, which is what you want in Git
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: payments
  labels:
    team: payments
    environment: production
EOF

sections.title: Cross-namespace DNS
paragraphs: A Service's short name only resolves within its own namespace. Across namespaces you need the namespace segment:
A call that works from one namespace and fails from another is nearly always this.
Where you genuinely want to alias a Service from elsewhere, an ExternalName Service does it without hardcoding the FQDN in application config:

codeBlock.code:
payments-api                                    # same namespace
payments-api.payments                           # from another namespace
payments-api.payments.svc.cluster.local         # fully qualified

sections.title: What namespaces are actually good for
paragraphs: RBAC. A Role and RoleBinding grant permissions within one namespace, which is how you give a team full control of its own space and nothing else:
Note the roleRef points at a ClusterRole while the binding itself is namespaced, that is the normal pattern for reusing the built-in view, edit and admin roles per namespace.
Resource quotas. Without one, any namespace can consume the whole cluster:
Pair it with a LimitRange, because once a quota constrains a resource every Pod must specify it or be rejected.
Network policy. This is what turns a namespace into an actual boundary. By default all Pods can reach all Pods; a default-deny policy plus explicit allows changes that:

Network policies require a CNI that implements them. Calico, Cilium, and similar. On a CNI that does not, the policy is accepted and silently does nothing, which is a dangerous way to believe you are protected.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: payments-team
  namespace: payments
subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: payments-engineers
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit           # built-in: read/write most things, no RBAC changes
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

paragraphs: Common patterns, with their trade-offs:
What does not work is one namespace for everything. You lose quotas, per-team RBAC and any meaningful network policy, and everything ends up in default.

sections.title: Deleting, and the Terminating trap
paragraphs: This deletes everything inside it. Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and PVCs. A PVC whose StorageClass has reclaimPolicy: Delete takes its data with it. Deleting a namespace is one of the most destructive single commands in Kubernetes.

Sometimes it hangs in Terminating indefinitely. The cause is virtually always a finalizer on a resource whose controller is gone, commonly a custom resource left behind after its operator was uninstalled:
The correct fix is to remove the blocking resources or reinstall the operator so its finalizers can run:

Force-removing the namespace's own finalizer through the API is the widely-circulated trick, and it does work, but it orphans any resources that had not been cleaned up, including cloud load balancers and volumes that will keep billing. Treat it as a last resort and check for leftovers afterwards.

codeBlock.code: kubectl delete namespace payments

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team puts an internal admin service in its own namespace, assuming other teams cannot reach it. Is that assumption correct on a default cluster?
A namespace has been Terminating for an hour. Its conditions report "Some resources are remaining: widgets.example.com has 2 resource instances". What is the correct first action?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a Kubernetes namespace used for?

It partitions a cluster into named scopes so resource names only need to be unique within one, and it gives RBAC, resource quotas, limit ranges and network policies something to attach to. That combination is what lets several teams share a cluster: each gets its own space, its own permissions, and a cap on how much it can consume. It is an organisational and policy boundary rather than a runtime one. Workloads still share the same nodes.
Are namespaces a security boundary?

Only partly, and assuming otherwise is a common mistake. Kubernetes networking is flat by default, so a Pod in any namespace can reach a Service in any other. Namespaces do provide an RBAC boundary, so you can stop people managing resources elsewhere, but they do not stop workloads talking to each other. Real isolation needs NetworkPolicy resources enforced by a capable CNI such as Calico or Cilium, plus Pod Security Standards. For strong isolation between untrusted tenants, separate clusters remain the safer answer.
How do I call a Service in another namespace?

Include the namespace in the DNS name: service-name.namespace, or the fully qualified service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. The bare short name only resolves within the caller's own namespace because the cluster DNS search path appends that namespace first. This is why a request that works between two services in the same namespace fails the moment one of them moves.
Which resources are not namespaced?

Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, CustomResourceDefinitions and namespaces themselves are all cluster-scoped. kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false lists them for your cluster. The distinction that surprises people most is that PersistentVolumeClaims are namespaced while the PersistentVolumes they bind are not, and that Secrets are namespaced, so a registry pull secret must exist in the same namespace as the Pod that needs it.
Why is my namespace stuck in Terminating?

Something inside it has a finalizer that is not completing, almost always a custom resource whose operator has been uninstalled so nothing is left to run the cleanup. Check with kubectl get namespace <name> -o json | jq '.status.conditions', which names the remaining resource types. Fix it by deleting those resources or reinstalling the operator. Force-removing the namespace's finalizer is widely suggested and does work, but it orphans whatever the finalizers were protecting, including cloud load balancers and disks that carry on costing money.
Should I use one namespace per environment or separate clusters?

Namespaces per environment are cheap and fine for development and staging, where sharing nodes and a control plane is acceptable. For production, separate clusters are safer: namespaces share nodes, a kernel and a control plane, so a resource-hungry workload or a cluster-wide upgrade affects everything at once. A common arrangement is one non-production cluster split by namespace and a dedicated production cluster, itself split by team or service.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how Kubernetes manages CPU and memory: requests vs limits, units, what happens at the limit, QoS classes, namespace controls and how to choose values.
Two numbers per container decide almost everything about how your workload behaves under pressure: requests, which drive scheduling, and limits, which cap consumption at runtime.
Get them wrong and you get nodes that look idle while Pods cannot schedule, containers killed at 2am, or latency that appears only under load and makes no sense from the application's own metrics.

sections.title: Requests and limits are two different mechanisms
paragraphs: The scheduler only ever looks at requests. It sums the requests of everything already on a node and places your Pod where the remaining capacity fits. It never looks at actual usage.

That is why a node can show 20% real CPU usage in monitoring and still refuse to schedule anything. Its requests are fully committed. kubectl describe node shows both, and the gap between them is usually the story:
Limits exceeding 100% is normal, that is deliberate overcommit, betting that not everything peaks simultaneously. Requests at 95% means this node is effectively full.

codeBlock.code: kubectl describe node ip-10-0-1-42 | grep -A8 "Allocated resources"

sections.title: Units
paragraphs: CPU is measured in cores, and m means millicores. Thousandths of a core.
CPU is compressible: exceed your limit and you are throttled, not killed.
Memory is measured in bytes with suffixes. The distinction between the two families catches people:
Use Mi and Gi. Memory is incompressible: exceed the limit and the kernel kills the process. There is no throttling option.

codeBlock.code:
1     = 1 core
500m  = half a core
100m  = a tenth of a core

sections.title: What actually happens at the limit
paragraphs: Exceeding a CPU limit throttles the container. The kernel simply stops scheduling it for the remainder of each 100ms period. Nothing crashes; requests just get slower. This is genuinely hard to diagnose from inside the application, because the process sees time passing with no work done.
A high nr_throttled relative to nr_periods means the limit is costing you latency.
Exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOMKilled immediately.
A Pod that restarts periodically with no error in its own logs is the signature. The application is killed without warning, so it never gets to log anything.

codeBlock.code: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat | grep throttled

sections.title: The CPU limit argument
paragraphs: Setting CPU requests is uncontroversial. Do it always.

Setting CPU limits is genuinely contested. The case against: throttling adds latency, and multi-threaded runtimes hit the limit sooner than intuition suggests because the quota is consumed across all threads. A service limited to 1000m running eight threads can exhaust its quota in 12ms of wall-clock time and then stall for 88ms.
The case for: without limits, one badly behaved workload starves its neighbours, and performance becomes unpredictable in a way that depends on what else happens to be scheduled nearby.

A defensible middle position: always set memory limits, an unbounded leak takes down the whole node, and set CPU requests but be cautious with CPU limits, particularly on latency-sensitive services. If you do set CPU limits, set them well above observed peak, not at it.

sections.title: QoS classes
paragraphs: Kubernetes assigns each Pod a class from its requests and limits, and that class decides eviction order when a node runs out of memory.

BestEffort Pods are evicted first and are also placed carelessly, since the scheduler thinks they need nothing. A production workload with no requests set is not merely unoptimised. It is first in line to be killed under pressure.
For anything critical, Guaranteed gives the strongest protection: set requests equal to limits.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'

sections.title: Namespace-level controls
paragraphs: LimitRange supplies defaults and bounds within a namespace, so a Pod submitted with nothing set does not become BestEffort:
ResourceQuota caps the namespace in aggregate, which is how you stop one team consuming a shared cluster:

One consequence worth knowing: once a ResourceQuota constrains a resource in a namespace, every Pod must specify it. A Pod with no memory request is rejected outright. Pair a ResourceQuota with a LimitRange so existing manifests keep working.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:              # applied as the limit if unset
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
      defaultRequest:       # applied as the request if unset
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "4"
        memory: 8Gi

sections.title: Choosing the numbers
paragraphs: Measure rather than guess:
A reasonable starting point:
kubectl top needs metrics-server installed; without it the command fails. For real sizing you want historical data from Prometheus, since a single snapshot misses daily peaks.
Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode is useful here: it observes actual usage and suggests values without changing anything.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl top pods --containers
kubectl top nodes

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Monitoring shows a node at 20% CPU utilisation, but new Pods will not schedule there and report Insufficient cpu. Why?
A node is under memory pressure. Three Pods are running: A with no resources set, B with requests below its limits, and C with requests equal to its limits. Which is evicted first?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between requests and limits?

A request is what the scheduler reserves for a container when deciding which node can host it; a limit is the hard ceiling the kubelet and the kernel enforce at runtime. The scheduler only ever reads requests and never looks at actual usage, so requests determine placement and limits determine behaviour under pressure. Exceeding a CPU limit throttles the container; exceeding a memory limit kills it.
What does OOMKilled mean and how do I fix it?

The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel terminated it. Confirm it with kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}'. The application gets no warning and so logs nothing, which is why a Pod that restarts periodically with clean logs is almost always this. Either the limit is genuinely too low, check real usage with kubectl top pods before raising it, or there is a leak that a higher limit only postpones. Runtimes with their own heap settings, the JVM especially, must be told about the container limit or they will size against the node's total memory.
Should I set CPU limits?

This is genuinely debated. CPU limits throttle rather than kill, and throttling adds latency that is difficult to diagnose because the application sees time passing with no work done. Multi-threaded runtimes hit the quota faster than expected, since it is consumed across all threads within each 100ms window. Without limits, though, one workload can starve its neighbours. A defensible position is to always set CPU requests, always set memory limits, and either omit CPU limits on latency-sensitive services or set them well above observed peak.
What are QoS classes and why do they matter?

Kubernetes derives a class from your requests and limits. Guaranteed means requests equal limits for every container and both resources; Burstable means requests are set but differ from limits; BestEffort means nothing is set. Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed. A production workload with no requests is therefore first to be killed, as well as being placed by a scheduler that believes it needs nothing.
Why won't my Pod schedule when the node looks idle?

The scheduler works from the sum of requests on each node, not measured usage. If existing Pods request 95% of a node's allocatable CPU, nothing more fits there even if real usage is 20%. Run kubectl describe node <name> and look at the "Allocated resources" section, which shows requests and limits as percentages of capacity. Over-large requests are the most common cause of clusters that cost far more than their actual workload justifies.
How do I choose the right values?

Measure first. kubectl top pods --containers gives a current snapshot, and Prometheus history is better because a single reading misses daily peaks. A reasonable starting point is a memory request at observed steady-state plus about 25%, a memory limit with genuine headroom above that, and a CPU request at observed average rather than peak. Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode watches real usage and suggests values without changing anything, which is a low-risk way to sanity-check your numbers.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Set Kubernetes CPU and memory requests and limits correctly. Learn the units, enforcement, QoS classes, OOMKilled, throttling, LimitRange and ResourceQuota.

Every container can declare two numbers for CPU and two for memory. They look symmetrical and they are not: requests are a scheduling input, limits are a runtime constraint, and they are enforced by entirely different parts of the system.

sections.title: The YAML
paragraphs: Note the deliberate asymmetry: a memory limit but no CPU limit. That is a defensible default, for reasons below.
Resources are per container, not per Pod. A Pod's effective request is the sum across its containers. Init containers count too, taking the maximum rather than the sum, since they run sequentially.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: payments-api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: payments-api }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.2
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 200m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi

sections.title: Units
paragraphs: CPU is in cores, where m is millicores:
Memory is in bytes, and the suffix matters:
Use Mi and Gi. The difference is about 5% at gigabyte scale, which is enough to turn a limit you calculated carefully into one that kills the process.

sections.title: How each is enforced
paragraphs: The scheduler sums the requests of everything on a node and places your Pod where the remainder fits. It never looks at actual usage.
Requests at 95% means the node is full for scheduling purposes, whatever kubectl top says. Limits above 100% is normal overcommit.
Exceed a CPU limit and the kernel stops scheduling the container for the rest of the current 100ms period. Nothing crashes; things get slower.

nr_throttled as a meaningful fraction of nr_periods means the limit is costing latency. This is worth checking whenever a service has unexplained tail latency, because it is invisible from inside the application. The process simply sees wall-clock time passing with no CPU.
Exceed a memory limit and the container is killed immediately, with no signal and no chance to log.
A Pod with a rising restart count and no errors in its own logs is almost always this.

codeBlock.code: kubectl describe node ip-10-0-1-42 | grep -A8 "Allocated resources"

sections.title: QoS classes
paragraphs: Kubernetes derives a class from what you set, and it determines eviction order under node memory pressure.

Guaranteed requires both CPU and memory to have requests equal to limits, for every container. Setting only memory equal leaves you Burstable. This is the trade-off behind omitting CPU limits: you give up Guaranteed in exchange for no throttling.
For a critical, latency-sensitive service the choice is genuinely between the two. Pick deliberately rather than by accident.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,QOS:.status.qosClass

sections.title: Namespace defaults with LimitRange
paragraphs: A Pod submitted with no resources is BestEffort: scheduled carelessly, evicted first. A LimitRange stops that happening by accident:
defaultRequest and default fill in missing values; max and min reject Pods outside the range at admission.

A subtlety worth knowing: if a LimitRange sets a default limit but no defaultRequest, Kubernetes sets the request equal to the limit. That can quietly make every Pod in the namespace request far more than it needs.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: payments
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest:        # used when request is unset
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      default:               # used when limit is unset
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
      max:
        cpu: "4"
        memory: 8Gi
      min:
        cpu: 10m
        memory: 16Mi

sections.title: ResourceQuota
paragraphs: Where LimitRange constrains individual containers, ResourceQuota caps the namespace as a whole:

Once a quota constrains a resource, specifying it becomes mandatory. A Pod without a memory request is rejected outright. Always pair a ResourceQuota with a LimitRange, or every existing manifest in the namespace stops deploying.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-quota
  namespace: payments
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 40Gi
    limits.cpu: "40"
    limits.memory: 80Gi
    pods: "50"

sections.title: Choosing values
paragraphs: A workable starting point:

kubectl top requires metrics-server and shows only a moment in time. For real sizing use Prometheus history, or run Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Off (recommendation) mode, which observes usage and suggests values without changing anything.

One language-specific trap: runtimes that manage their own heap, the JVM above all, but also Node and .NET, need to be told about the container limit. A JVM that sizes its heap against the node's 64GB while the container limit is 512Mi will be OOMKilled reliably. Modern JVMs handle this with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage; older ones need explicit -Xmx.

codeBlock.code: kubectl top pods --containers -n payments

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A container sets memory request and limit both to 512Mi, and a CPU request of 200m with no CPU limit. What QoS class does the Pod get?
A platform team adds a ResourceQuota with requests.memory to a namespace. Existing Deployments that previously worked now fail to create Pods. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between requests and limits in Kubernetes?

A request is what the scheduler reserves when deciding which node can host a container. It is pure accounting and the scheduler never consults actual usage. A limit is the ceiling enforced at runtime by the kernel through cgroups. The consequences differ by resource: exceeding a CPU limit throttles the container, while exceeding a memory limit terminates it. Requests also determine QoS class, which decides eviction order under node pressure.
Why does my container keep getting OOMKilled?

It exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it without warning, which is why the application's own logs show nothing. Confirm with kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}'. Measure real usage with kubectl top pods --containers before simply raising the limit, if usage grows without bound it is a leak that a larger limit only delays. For JVM, Node or .NET applications, check that the runtime knows about the container limit, since a heap sized against the node's total memory will exceed a small container limit every time.
Should I set CPU limits on my containers?

It is a genuine trade-off rather than a settled best practice. Limits prevent one workload starving its neighbours and are required for the Guaranteed QoS class, but they throttle rather than kill, and throttling adds latency that is very hard to see from inside the application. Multi-threaded runtimes reach the quota quickly because it is consumed across all threads within each 100ms window. A common position is to always set CPU requests and memory limits, and either omit CPU limits on latency-sensitive services or set them comfortably above observed peak.
What is the difference between Mi and M?

Mi is mebibytes, a multiple of 1024², and M is megabytes, a multiple of 1000². So 128Mi is 134,217,728 bytes while 128M is 128,000,000, about 5% apart, which grows to a meaningful gap at gigabyte scale. Kubernetes accepts both, but the binary suffixes Ki, Mi and Gi match how memory is actually reported by tools and by the kernel, so mixing them up can turn a carefully sized limit into one that triggers the OOM killer.
How do I know what values to use?

Measure before guessing. kubectl top pods --containers gives a current snapshot but misses daily peaks, so Prometheus history is better if you have it. Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode watches real usage over time and proposes values without modifying anything, which is a safe way to validate your numbers. As a starting point, set memory request to steady-state usage plus around 25%, memory limit with real headroom above that, and CPU request to the observed average rather than peak.
What happens if I set no requests or limits at all?

The Pod becomes BestEffort, which is the worst of both worlds. The scheduler believes it needs nothing and will place it on an already-loaded node, and under memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort Pods first. The container is also uncapped, so a memory leak can consume the node and take down everything else running on it. A LimitRange in the namespace with defaultRequest and default values prevents this happening by accident.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Set up the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: the scaling formula, required resource requests, autoscaling/v2 YAML, behavior and fixing unknown targets.

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds and removes replicas to keep an observed metric near a target. More Pods, not bigger ones, that is the horizontal part, and it is what makes it suitable for stateless services.
It is one of the more genuinely useful controllers in Kubernetes, and also one people wire up once and never verify.

sections.title: The formula
paragraphs: Everything the HPA does follows from one line:
Three replicas averaging 90% CPU against a 50% target gives ceil(3 × 1.8) = 6 replicas. The controller re-evaluates every 15 seconds by default.

Two consequences worth noticing. It is proportional, so a large overshoot produces a large jump rather than one replica at a time. And it depends on currentReplicas, which is why an HPA cannot scale up from zero. Anything times zero is zero. Scale-to-zero needs KEDA.

codeBlock.code: desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas × ( currentMetric / targetMetric ) )

sections.title: It requires resource requests
paragraphs: This is the single most common reason an HPA does nothing.
CPU and memory targets are expressed as a percentage of the request. A container with no CPU request has no denominator, so utilisation is undefined and the HPA reports <unknown> and refuses to act.
<unknown> means one of exactly two things: metrics-server is not installed, or the target Pods have no resource requests.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get hpa

sections.title: A working HPA
paragraphs: Use autoscaling/v2. The older v1 supports CPU only.

Remove replicas from the Deployment manifest once an HPA manages it. Otherwise every kubectl apply resets the replica count to whatever the file says, and the HPA scales it back up moments later. A loop that looks like flapping and is really two controllers disagreeing. If you use GitOps, exclude the field from diffing.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: payments-api
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60

sections.title: Controlling how it scales
paragraphs: By default the HPA scales up quickly and down slowly. A deliberate asymmetry, since being briefly over-provisioned is much cheaper than being under-provisioned. The behavior block makes it explicit:

stabilizationWindowSeconds on scale-down is the setting that matters most. It makes the HPA use the highest recommendation from the last N seconds, which prevents a brief dip in traffic from removing capacity that is needed again a minute later. The 300-second default is sensible; shortening it causes thrashing.

codeBlock.code:
spec:
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0      # react immediately
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 100                     # at most double
          periodSeconds: 15
        - type: Pods
          value: 4                       # or at most +4
          periodSeconds: 15
      selectPolicy: Max                  # whichever allows more
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300    # wait 5 minutes of calm
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 10
          periodSeconds: 60

sections.title: Beyond CPU
paragraphs: CPU is a poor proxy for load in plenty of services. An I/O-bound API may be saturated at 20% CPU. autoscaling/v2 supports better signals.
Memory, though be careful: many runtimes hold memory rather than returning it, so memory rarely falls after a spike and the HPA will not scale back down.
Custom metrics from your application, via Prometheus Adapter. Requests per second is usually far more meaningful than CPU:
External metrics such as queue depth, which is the correct signal for a worker pool:

With several metrics listed, the HPA computes a desired replica count for each and takes the highest. That is the safe behaviour. Any one signal indicating pressure is enough to scale up, and every signal must be calm to scale down.

codeBlock.code:
- type: Resource
      resource:
        name: memory
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70

sections.title: Nodes have to exist
paragraphs: An HPA that wants 20 replicas on a cluster with room for 12 leaves eight Pods Pending. Pod autoscaling and node autoscaling are separate concerns, and you generally need both:
Set maxReplicas to a number your cluster or your budget can actually absorb. It is a safety limit as much as a scaling parameter.

sections.title: Diagnosing
paragraphs: Those three conditions answer most questions directly:

codeBlock.code: kubectl describe hpa payments-api

sections.title: What it will not do
paragraphs: KEDA is worth knowing about: it extends the HPA with scale-to-zero and dozens of event sources. Kafka lag, SQS depth, RabbitMQ, cron. For queue-driven workers it is usually the better tool.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: kubectl get hpa shows TARGETS as <unknown>/50% and the replica count never changes. kubectl top pods works correctly. What is wrong?
An HPA scales a Deployment to 8 replicas. After every CI deploy the count drops to 3 and then climbs back. The Deployment manifest specifies replicas: 3. What is happening?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does my HPA show <unknown> for the target metric?

Two causes only. Either metrics-server is not installed, in which case kubectl top pods also fails, or the target Pods have no resource request for the metric being measured. A Utilization target is a percentage of the request, so without a request there is nothing to compute against. Check with kubectl get deployment <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}' and add requests if they are missing.
How does the HPA decide how many replicas to run?

It applies desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × (currentMetric / targetMetric)), recalculated every 15 seconds by default. Three replicas averaging 90% CPU against a 50% target gives six. Because the calculation is proportional it corrects large overshoots in one step rather than incrementing. It also explains why an HPA cannot scale up from zero: multiplying zero replicas by any ratio gives zero, which is why scale-to-zero requires KEDA.
Can the HPA scale on something other than CPU?

Yes, with autoscaling/v2. Memory works but is often a poor signal, since many runtimes retain memory rather than releasing it so the value never falls enough to scale back down. Custom metrics from your application, requests per second, for example, are available through Prometheus Adapter, and external metrics such as SQS queue depth suit worker pools. When several metrics are configured, the HPA computes a target for each and uses the largest, so any one signal under pressure triggers a scale up.
Why does my HPA keep scaling up and down repeatedly?

Usually the scale-down stabilization window is too short, so a brief dip removes capacity that is immediately needed again. The default of 300 seconds makes the HPA take the highest recommendation from the last five minutes, which damps exactly this. The other common cause is a conflict: if the Deployment manifest still specifies replicas and something reapplies it, the HPA and your deployment tooling will fight over the same field on every apply.
Do I need Cluster Autoscaler as well as the HPA?

Almost certainly. The HPA adds Pods; it does not add machines. If the cluster has no spare capacity the new Pods simply sit in Pending and no extra traffic is served. Cluster Autoscaler adjusts node group sizes in response, and Karpenter does the same job by provisioning right-sized instances directly and generally reacts faster. Set maxReplicas to something your cluster and budget can genuinely absorb, treating it as a safety limit rather than an aspiration.
Can I use HPA and Vertical Pod Autoscaler together?

Not on the same metric. VPA adjusts CPU and memory requests while the HPA scales replicas based on utilisation of those requests, so both react to each other and the result oscillates. The workable split is VPA managing memory and the HPA scaling on CPU or a custom metric, which keeps them out of each other's way. VPA in recommendation-only mode is always safe to run alongside an HPA, since it reports suggested values without changing anything.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what Helm is for Kubernetes: charts, releases and repositories, how helm upgrade works, where Helm falls short, and how it compares with Kustomize.
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. It bundles a set of manifests into a versioned, parameterised chart, installs it as a named release, and tracks enough history to upgrade and roll back.
Its two jobs are genuinely different, and it is worth being clear which one you need: consuming third-party software, and packaging your own.

sections.title: Three terms
paragraphs: The chart/release distinction matters: one chart can be installed many times in the same cluster under different names, each with its own values and its own history.

sections.title: The case for Helm
paragraphs: Installing other people's software. This is where Helm is uncontested. Prometheus, ingress-nginx, cert-manager, Grafana and almost everything else in the ecosystem ships as a chart. Installing Prometheus by hand means dozens of interdependent manifests with CRDs, RBAC and service discovery configuration:

Packaging your own applications. Here it is a real trade-off. You gain one chart serving every environment through values files; you pay in Go templating, which is genuinely hard to read once it grows conditionals and helper functions.

codeBlock.code:
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring --create-namespace

sections.title: Helm 3 removed the thing people disliked
paragraphs: Helm 2 ran a cluster-side component called Tiller that needed broad permissions and became a well-known security problem. Helm 3 is client-side only. It talks to the Kubernetes API with your own kubeconfig credentials, so it can do exactly what you can do, no more.
Release state is stored as Secrets in the release's namespace, which is why helm list is namespace-scoped and why helm list -A exists.

sections.title: The workflow
paragraphs: Two habits worth forming early:

helm show values <chart> > values.yaml before installing anything. Charts have dozens or hundreds of settings and the defaults are rarely what you want in production. Resource limits, replica counts and persistence settings especially.
--atomic on every upgrade. Without it a failed upgrade leaves the release half-applied. With it, Helm rolls back automatically. Pair it with --timeout so it does not wait forever.

codeBlock.code:
# Find and inspect
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo nginx
helm show values bitnami/nginx > values.yaml

# Install
helm install my-nginx bitnami/nginx -f values.yaml

# Observe
helm list
helm status my-nginx

# Change
helm upgrade my-nginx bitnami/nginx -f values.yaml --atomic

# Undo
helm rollback my-nginx 1

# Remove
helm uninstall my-nginx

sections.title: What Helm actually does at upgrade time
paragraphs: This surprises people. Helm does not diff against the live cluster by default. It computes a three-way merge between the old release manifest, the new one, and the current cluster state, then applies the result.
Two practical consequences:
Manual kubectl edit changes may be preserved or clobbered depending on the field, which is why mixing Helm with hand edits produces confusing results. Pick one.
Removing a resource from a chart does delete it on upgrade, because Helm tracks what it created. That is usually what you want, and occasionally alarming.
Preview before applying:
The helm-diff plugin is the single most useful thing you can add to Helm. Install it.

codeBlock.code:
helm diff upgrade my-nginx bitnami/nginx -f values.yaml   # requires helm-diff plugin
helm upgrade my-nginx bitnami/nginx -f values.yaml --dry-run

sections.title: Where Helm is weak
paragraphs: CRDs. Custom Resource Definitions in a chart's crds/ directory are installed once and never upgraded or deleted by Helm. Upgrading a chart that changed its CRDs requires applying them yourself. This causes real, confusing failures.
Templating readability. A chart with nested conditionals and _helpers.tpl indirection is hard to reason about. helm template to see the rendered output is often the only way to be sure.
Rollback is not a time machine. helm rollback reverts Kubernetes objects. It does not undo a database migration, and it will not restore data deleted by a PVC that the upgrade removed.

sections.title: Helm or Kustomize?
paragraphs: The pragmatic answer most teams land on: Helm for third-party software, Kustomize for your own manifests. You get the ecosystem without writing Go templates for your own services, and your manifests stay readable YAML. ArgoCD and Flux both support either, and both support Kustomize overlays on top of a rendered Helm chart, which is a genuinely good pattern.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: You upgrade an operator chart to a version whose custom resources have new fields. The controller starts, but applying a resource with the new fields fails validation. What is the most likely cause?
A helm upgrade fails partway through. The release shows status failed and some resources are on the new version while others are on the old. Which flag would have prevented this?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is Helm and do I actually need it?

Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes that bundles manifests into versioned, parameterised charts and tracks each installation as a release with upgrade and rollback history. You almost certainly need it for consuming third-party software, because Prometheus, ingress-nginx, cert-manager and most of the ecosystem ship as charts and installing them by hand means managing dozens of interdependent manifests. Whether you package your own applications with it is a genuine choice. Many teams use Helm for external software and Kustomize for their own services, keeping their manifests as readable YAML.
What is the difference between a chart and a release?

A chart is the package: templates, default values and metadata, versioned and distributable. A release is one installed instance of that chart in a cluster, with its own name, its own values and its own revision history. The same chart can be installed many times under different names, which is how you run several instances of the same application side by side. helm list shows releases, not charts.
What is the difference between Helm and Kustomize?

Helm uses Go templating with variables substituted at render time, and adds packaging, distribution and release tracking with rollback. Kustomize patches plain YAML through overlays, so base manifests remain valid Kubernetes YAML you can apply directly, and it is built into kubectl via apply -k. Helm is stronger for distributing software to other people and for managing installed releases; Kustomize is easier to read and reason about for your own manifests. Using both, Helm for third-party charts, Kustomize for internal services, is common and works well.
Why doesn't helm upgrade update my CRDs?

By design. CRDs placed in a chart's crds/ directory are installed once on first install and never upgraded or deleted afterwards, because an incorrect CRD change can invalidate or destroy every custom resource of that type in the cluster. Helm takes the view that this is too destructive to automate. When a chart upgrade includes CRD changes, apply them yourself with kubectl apply -f before running the upgrade. The chart's release notes normally say so, and skipping it produces validation errors that look unrelated.
How do I roll back a Helm release?

helm history <release> lists the revisions, then helm rollback <release> <revision> reverts to one. Helm stores each revision's manifest as a Secret in the release namespace, so rollback simply reapplies an earlier state. Two caveats: it only reverts Kubernetes objects, so a database migration run by the bad release still needs handling separately, and data lost through a deleted PersistentVolumeClaim is not coming back. Upgrading with --atomic avoids most rollbacks by reverting automatically on failure.
Is Helm safe to use in production? What happened to Tiller?

Helm 3 is safe in a way Helm 2 was not. Helm 2 ran a cluster-side component called Tiller that typically held broad cluster-admin permissions and was a well-documented privilege escalation risk. Helm 3 removed it entirely and runs client-side, authenticating with your own kubeconfig, so it can only do what you are already permitted to do. Release state lives in Secrets in the release's namespace rather than in a privileged service. Any guide that mentions helm init or Tiller is describing Helm 2 and is out of date.
