sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Install Helm, add a repository, read chart values, then run helm install, helm upgrade, helm list and helm uninstall to manage a release on Kubernetes.
Helm 3 is a single binary that runs on your machine. There is nothing to install into the cluster. It authenticates with your existing kubeconfig and talks to the Kubernetes API as you.
That means whatever Helm can do, you could already do with kubectl. If your kubeconfig cannot create Deployments in a namespace, neither can Helm.

sections.title: Install
paragraphs: On Debian or Ubuntu you can use the apt repository instead, which gets you upgrades through the package manager. Piping a script to a shell is convenient but worth reading first on a machine you care about.
winget install Helm.Helm and scoop install helm both work too.
Confirm it is v3.x. Any guide telling you to run helm init or mentioning Tiller is describing Helm 2, which is end-of-life. Helm 3 has no cluster-side component and no initialisation step.
Helm uses the same kubeconfig and current context as kubectl, so check where you are pointed before installing anything:

codeBlock.code: brew install helm

sections.title: Repositories
paragraphs: A repository is an index of charts served over HTTP. Add one, then refresh the local cache:

helm repo update is the step people forget. Without it you install whatever version was current when you added the repository, which can be months old. helm search repo only ever searches your local cache.
To search everything published publicly instead, use helm search hub.
Many projects now publish to OCI registries rather than classic repositories, in which case there is no repo add at all. You reference the chart directly:

codeBlock.code:
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

sections.title: Read the values before you install
paragraphs: Do this every time. Charts commonly expose a hundred or more settings, and the defaults are tuned for a demo, usually one replica, no resource limits, and persistence switched off. Installing straight from defaults is how you end up with an unlimited pod that gets evicted under memory pressure.
Also worth a look before installing something unfamiliar:

codeBlock.code: helm show values bitnami/nginx > nginx-values.yaml

sections.title: Install a chart
paragraphs: my-nginx is the release name. Your name for this installation, not the chart's name. It must be unique within the namespace.
Namespaces are worth being explicit about, because Helm does not create them for you by default:
For anything automated, prefer the idempotent form. It installs if the release is absent and upgrades if it exists, so the same command works on first run and every run after:

codeBlock.code: helm install my-nginx bitnami/nginx -f nginx-values.yaml

sections.title: Inspect what is installed
paragraphs: helm list is namespace-scoped. A release you cannot find is usually in another namespace:
helm get values my-nginx --all shows the merged result of your overrides and the chart defaults, which answers "why is this setting not what I expected" faster than anything else.

codeBlock.code: helm list

sections.title: Upgrade and roll back
paragraphs: --atomic makes the upgrade all-or-nothing, if the new resources do not become ready within the timeout, Helm reverts the release rather than leaving it half-applied. Use it every time.

codeBlock.code: helm upgrade my-nginx bitnami/nginx -f nginx-values.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m

sections.title: Uninstall
paragraphs: This removes the resources Helm created and the release history. Two things it does not remove:
Use --keep-history if you want the release history retained for reference after removal.

codeBlock.code: helm uninstall my-nginx

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A colleague installed a release yesterday, but helm list on your machine shows nothing. Both of you use the same cluster and the same kubeconfig. What is the most likely explanation?
You run helm uninstall on a database release. Weeks later the cloud bill still shows the volume. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I install Helm?

Use your platform's package manager: brew install helm on macOS, choco install kubernetes-helm or winget install Helm.Helm on Windows, and either the official install script or the apt repository on Linux. Confirm with helm version that you have v3.x. There is no cluster-side installation step. Helm 3 is a client that uses your existing kubeconfig, so if kubectl works, Helm works.
Do I still need to run helm init or install Tiller?

No. helm init and Tiller belong to Helm 2, which reached end of life. Tiller was a cluster-side service that usually held broad permissions and was a recognised security risk. Helm 3 removed it: the client talks directly to the Kubernetes API using your credentials, and release state is stored as Secrets in each release's namespace. Any tutorial mentioning helm init is out of date and should be treated with suspicion generally.
What is the difference between helm install and helm upgrade --install?

helm install fails if a release with that name already exists. helm upgrade --install installs it when absent and upgrades it when present, making the command idempotent. That is what you want in CI or any script that may run more than once, since it removes the need to check state first. Adding --atomic makes it safer still by rolling back automatically if the release does not become ready.
Why can't Helm find my release?

helm list only shows releases in the current namespace, because Helm 3 stores release state as Secrets in the namespace where the release lives. Run helm list -A to search every namespace, or helm list -n <namespace> to target one. If it is still missing, confirm you are on the expected cluster with kubectl config current-context. Pointing at the wrong context is the other common cause.
Does helm uninstall delete everything?

Not quite, and the exceptions are deliberate. PersistentVolumeClaims are usually left in place so that uninstalling an application does not destroy its data, which means the underlying cloud volumes keep incurring cost until you delete the claims yourself. CRDs installed from a chart's crds/ directory are also left alone, because deleting a CRD would delete every custom resource of that type across the cluster. After uninstalling anything stateful, check kubectl get pvc in that namespace.
How do I see what a chart will actually create before installing it?

helm template <release-name> <chart> -f values.yaml renders the chart locally and prints the full set of manifests without contacting the cluster. This is the best way to review a third-party chart before trusting it, and to debug your own templates. helm install --dry-run --debug does something similar but validates against the live API server, which additionally catches schema problems and missing CRDs. Pair either with helm show values so you know which settings are available to change.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how a Helm chart is built: directory structure, Chart.yaml, templates, built-in objects, _helpers.tpl, debugging with helm template and dependencies.
A chart is a directory with a specific layout. Helm reads it, renders the templates against a set of values, and applies the result to the cluster.
Everything below is either part of that layout or part of how the rendering works.

sections.title: Structure
paragraphs: That scaffolds a working chart with a Deployment, Service, ServiceAccount, Ingress and HPA. It is a reasonable starting point, though most of it should be deleted rather than carried around unused.

codeBlock.code:
mychart/
├── Chart.yaml          # metadata: name, version, dependencies
├── values.yaml         # default configuration
├── charts/             # vendored subcharts
├── crds/               # CRDs, installed once and never upgraded
├── templates/
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   ├── _helpers.tpl    # reusable snippets, not rendered itself
│   └── NOTES.txt       # printed after install
└── .helmignore

sections.title: Chart.yaml
paragraphs: version and appVersion are independently versioned and people mix them up constantly. version is the chart's own semantic version and must be bumped for every chart change, because repositories key on it. appVersion is the software being deployed and is usually the default image tag.
condition lets a user switch a dependency off entirely. Here, setting postgresql.enabled: false to point at a managed database instead.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: v2
name: payments-api
description: The payments service
type: application
version: 1.4.0          # the CHART version
appVersion: "2.7.1"     # the APPLICATION version
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "15.5.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled

sections.title: Built-in objects
paragraphs: .Capabilities is how a chart supports several Kubernetes versions at once:

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
    app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion | quote }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"

sections.title: Template syntax you will actually use
paragraphs: Whitespace control. {{- trims whitespace before, -}} after. Without it, conditionals leave blank lines that break YAML indentation. The most common source of "invalid YAML" from a chart that looks fine.
default and required. Give a fallback, or fail loudly with a useful message:
required is underused. Failing at render time with a clear sentence beats deploying something that comes up misconfigured.
quote and toYaml. Quote anything that might be read as a number or boolean, and use toYaml with nindent for nested blocks:
nindent adds a newline and indents; indent does not add the newline. Mixing them up is a reliable way to produce broken YAML.
Inside with and range, . is rebound to the current item. To reach the root from inside one, use $: $.Release.Name.

sections.title: Helpers
paragraphs: _helpers.tpl holds named templates so naming logic lives in one place:

Two details. Use include, not template, include returns a string you can pipe into nindent or quote, while template cannot be piped. And that trunc 63 matters: Kubernetes names are capped at 63 characters, and a long release name plus a long chart name silently exceeds it.

sections.title: Debugging
paragraphs: helm template is the command to reach for whenever output is not what you expect. Chart bugs are almost always visible in the rendered YAML, and reading it takes seconds compared to deploying and inspecting live objects.
helm lint catches missing required fields and malformed Chart.yaml, but it does not validate against the Kubernetes schema, --dry-run against a real cluster does.

codeBlock.code:
# Render locally, no cluster needed
helm template my-release ./mychart

# Render with your values, only the file you care about
helm template my-release ./mychart -f prod-values.yaml -s templates/deployment.yaml

# Catch structural problems
helm lint ./mychart

# Render against the live API server. Validates schema and CRDs
helm install my-release ./mychart --dry-run --debug

sections.title: Dependencies
paragraphs: Commit Chart.lock so builds are reproducible. Whether you commit charts/ is a judgement call: vendoring makes installs work offline and pins exact content, at the cost of a larger repository.
Parent values reach a subchart by nesting under its name:
global is the escape hatch for values every subchart should see, such as a shared image registry.

codeBlock.code:
helm dependency update ./mychart   # fetch into charts/ and write Chart.lock
helm dependency list ./mychart

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A template uses {{ template "app.labels" . | nindent 4 }} and Helm fails with a parse error. What is wrong?
You fix a bug in a chart template and push it to your repository, bumping appVersion but leaving version unchanged. Users running helm repo update still get the old template. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between version and appVersion in Chart.yaml?

version is the chart's own semantic version and identifies the package in a repository index; appVersion describes the software the chart deploys and is usually the default image tag. They move independently. Fixing a template bug bumps version while appVersion stays put, and deploying a new application release bumps appVersion and also requires a version bump because the chart changed. Forgetting to bump version is why a published fix never reaches users.
Why does my Helm template produce invalid YAML?

Almost always whitespace. Go template actions leave blank lines and stray indentation unless you trim them with {{- and -}}, and a conditional that emits nothing still leaves the line it occupied. The second frequent cause is confusing indent with nindent: nindent prepends a newline before indenting, indent does not, so using the wrong one shifts a whole block. Run helm template and read the rendered output. The broken indentation is visible immediately.
How do I debug a Helm chart without installing it?

helm template <release-name> ./chart -f values.yaml renders everything locally with no cluster contact, and -s templates/deployment.yaml narrows it to one file. Add helm lint for structural problems in Chart.yaml and missing required fields. When you need schema validation against real API versions and CRDs, helm install --dry-run --debug renders against the live API server without persisting anything, which catches errors local rendering cannot.
What is _helpers.tpl for?

It holds named templates, reusable snippets defined with define and invoked with include, and the leading underscore tells Helm not to treat the file as a manifest to render. The standard use is generating consistent names and label sets in one place so every resource in the chart agrees. Note the trunc 63 you will see in generated helpers: Kubernetes object names are limited to 63 characters, and a long release name combined with a long chart name will otherwise exceed it.
How do chart dependencies work?

Declare them in Chart.yaml under dependencies with a name, version range and repository, then run helm dependency update to fetch them into charts/ and generate Chart.lock. Values reach a subchart by nesting under its name in the parent's values.yaml, and global values are visible to every subchart. Adding a condition such as postgresql.enabled lets users disable a dependency entirely. Useful when some will run the bundled database and others point at a managed one. Commit Chart.lock for reproducible builds.
Should I use helm create as a starting point?

It is a reasonable scaffold and worth running once to see the conventions, but the generated chart includes a ServiceAccount, Ingress, HorizontalPodAutoscaler and a large values.yaml that most services do not need. Carrying unused templates makes a chart harder to read and review. Generate it, delete what your application genuinely does not use, and keep _helpers.tpl. The naming and label helpers it produces follow the recommended Kubernetes label conventions and are worth preserving.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Override Helm values with values.yaml files and --set, understand precedence, upgrade safely with --atomic, use helm rollback and fix a stuck release.
Values are how one chart serves every environment. Upgrades are how you change a running release. Rollbacks are how you undo it.
These three are where most day-to-day Helm friction lives, and most of it comes from not knowing exactly which values ended up applied.

sections.title: Start by reading the defaults
paragraphs: Charts frequently expose more than a hundred settings, and the shipped defaults target a demo. One replica, no resource limits, persistence disabled. Skipping this step is how a production install ends up with an unbounded pod and no storage.

codeBlock.code: helm show values bitnami/nginx > values.yaml

sections.title: Overriding
paragraphs: A values file: the form to use for anything real, because it is reviewable and belongs in version control:
You can pass several, and later files win on a per-key basis:
This layering is the clean way to handle environments: a shared base plus a small per-environment overlay, rather than four near-identical files that drift apart.
--set for one-off values, typically an image tag from CI:
--set has sharp edges worth knowing:
--set-string exists because --set infers types. An image tag like 1.10 parsed as a float becomes 1.1, which fails to pull with a confusing error.
For values containing secrets, --set-file reads from a file so nothing lands in shell history or CI logs.

codeBlock.code: helm install myapp ./mychart -f production-values.yaml

sections.title: Precedence
paragraphs: From lowest to highest:
Merging is per key, deep for maps. A values file that sets only replicaCount leaves everything else at the chart defaults.
Arrays are replaced entirely, not merged. Overriding one element of a list means supplying the whole list. This catches people with ingress.hosts and extraEnv constantly.
When the result is not what you expect, stop guessing:
That second command answers nearly every "why is this setting wrong" question in one step.

codeBlock.code:
# Exactly what you supplied
helm get values myapp

# The full merged result, defaults included
helm get values myapp --all

sections.title: Upgrading
paragraphs: Four things in that command, each earning its place:

--atomic is the single most valuable flag in Helm. Without it, a failed upgrade leaves the release partly applied, some resources new, some old, status failed, and you have to reason about a half-state during an incident. With it, Helm reverts and you are back where you started.

A genuine trap. By default, helm upgrade discards previously supplied values that are not passed again, so an upgrade that only passes --set image.tag=x silently loses every other override you made at install time.

The reliable way to avoid thinking about this at all: always pass the complete values file on every upgrade, and keep that file in Git. Then the command is deterministic and --reuse-values never comes up.
The helm-diff plugin shows a real diff against the live release and is worth installing before you need it.

codeBlock.code: helm upgrade --install myapp ./mychart -f production.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m

sections.title: Rolling back
paragraphs: A rollback creates a new revision rather than deleting history. Rolling back from 3 to 2 produces revision 4 with revision 2's content. History stays complete and auditable.
Three limits worth stating plainly:

codeBlock.code: helm history myapp

sections.title: When a release is stuck
paragraphs: An upgrade interrupted partway can leave a release in pending-upgrade, and Helm will refuse to do anything else with it:
If rollback itself refuses, the release Secret holding the pending state can be removed so Helm reverts to the last completed revision:
Do that only when you are certain no upgrade is still running, and check the actual cluster objects afterwards.

codeBlock.code: helm status myapp

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A release was installed with -f production.yaml. A later upgrade ran with only --set image.tag=1.5.0. Afterwards, replica count and resource limits are back at chart defaults. Why?
A chart default sets ingress.hosts to three hostnames. Your values file specifies one. After install, only your single host is configured. Is this expected?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the order of precedence for Helm values?

From lowest to highest: subchart values.yaml, then the parent chart's values.yaml, then each -f file in the order given with later files winning, then --set and --set-string. Merging is deep for maps, so a file setting only one key leaves the rest of the defaults intact. Arrays are the exception. A higher-precedence list replaces the lower one entirely rather than merging. helm get values <release> --all shows the final merged result.
Why did my helm upgrade lose the values I set at install time?

Because helm upgrade computes values from the chart defaults plus what you pass on that specific command; anything supplied previously and not repeated is dropped. Passing only --set image.tag=x therefore reverts every other override. --reuse-values carries the previous set forward, but the robust habit is to keep a values file in Git and pass it in full on every upgrade, so the command is deterministic and does not depend on release state.
What does --atomic do and should I always use it?

--atomic makes an upgrade all-or-nothing: Helm waits for the resources to become ready and, if they do not, automatically rolls the release back to the previous revision. Without it a failed upgrade leaves the release partially applied with some resources new and some old, which is a bad state to reason about during an incident. Use it on every upgrade, and pair it with --timeout because --atomic implies --wait and will otherwise wait a long time on a stuck rollout.
Why does my image tag break when I use --set?

--set infers types from the value, so 1.10 is parsed as a float and becomes 1.1, and 01 becomes 1. The resulting image reference does not exist and the pull fails with an error that gives no hint about the cause. Use --set-string image.tag=1.10 to force string handling. The same inference affects values like true, false and anything that looks numeric, so --set-string is the safer choice for any value that must stay textual.
How do I roll back a Helm release, and what are the limits?

helm history <release> lists revisions and helm rollback <release> <revision> reverts to one, creating a new revision rather than erasing history. The limits are important: it reverts Kubernetes objects only, so a database migration applied by the bad release remains applied, and data removed with a PersistentVolumeClaim is not restored by recreating the claim. History is also capped by --history-max, which defaults to 10, so very old revisions are not available indefinitely.
How should I structure values files for multiple environments?

Keep a shared base file with everything common, then a small per-environment overlay holding only what differs, and pass both: -f base.yaml -f production.yaml. Later files override earlier ones per key, so the overlay stays short and the shared settings have exactly one definition. This avoids the usual failure mode of three or four near-identical full values files that quietly drift apart. Keep secrets out of these files entirely. Use --set-file, or an external secret manager synced into the cluster.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Monitor Kubernetes with metrics-server, kubectl top, Prometheus and kube-state-metrics. Learn what to watch, which alerts matter, and how logs fit in.
Kubernetes ships almost no monitoring. kubectl top does not work on a fresh cluster, there is no metric history, and container logs vanish when a Pod is deleted.
Everything below has to be installed deliberately.

sections.title: metrics-server is not a monitoring system
paragraphs: metrics-server collects current CPU and memory usage from each kubelet and serves it through the Metrics API. It is what kubectl top and the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler read.
It stores nothing. There is no history, no querying, no alerting, just the last reading. If kubectl top fails or your HPA shows <unknown>, metrics-server is the first thing to check:
Install it, but do not mistake it for observability.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods --containers

sections.title: Prometheus is the actual answer
paragraphs: The near-universal choice, and the practical way to install it is the kube-prometheus-stack chart, which bundles Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, node-exporter and kube-state-metrics with dashboards and alert rules already wired together:
Assembling those components individually is a genuine time sink for no benefit.
Three sources feed it, and knowing which produces what saves a lot of confusion:

kube-state-metrics is the one people miss. It does not measure resource usage; it exposes what the API server knows. That is where kube_deployment_status_replicas_unavailable, kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total and kube_pod_status_phase come from, and those are the metrics most of your alerts should be built on.

codeBlock.code:
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring --create-namespace

sections.title: Scraping your own applications
paragraphs: Expose Prometheus metrics from your service, then tell Prometheus to collect them with a ServiceMonitor:

Two things break this more often than anything else. The port must be the name of a port on the Service, so the Service must declare named ports. And the ServiceMonitor's own labels must match what the Prometheus resource selects, with kube-prometheus-stack that is usually release: <helm release name>.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: payments
  labels:
    release: monitoring        # must match the Prometheus instance's selector
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api
  endpoints:
    - port: metrics            # the NAME of a Service port, not a number
      interval: 30s

sections.title: What to actually watch
paragraphs: For applications, the RED signals: Rate, Errors, Duration. For resources, the USE signals: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors.
Cluster-level things worth a dashboard:
A useful query. Pods restarting repeatedly in the last hour:
And CPU throttling, which almost nobody watches and which explains a lot of unexplained latency:

codeBlock.code: increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[1h]) > 3

sections.title: Alerts worth having
paragraphs: Alert on symptoms users feel, not on every deviation. An alert nobody acts on trains people to ignore the channel.
The for clause matters as much as the expression. Without it, every transient blip pages someone.

A short, honest starting set: crash-looping Pods, a Deployment with unavailable replicas, nodes not ready, disk above 85%, certificates expiring within two weeks, and your own error rate and latency SLOs.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: payments
  labels:
    release: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
    - name: payments-api
      rules:
        - alert: PodCrashLooping
          expr: increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{namespace="payments"}[15m]) > 3
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "{{ $labels.pod }} is crash-looping"

        - alert: DeploymentUnavailable
          expr: kube_deployment_status_replicas_unavailable{namespace="payments"} > 0
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "{{ $labels.deployment }} has unavailable replicas"

sections.title: Logs
paragraphs: Container logs live on the node and are deleted with the Pod. kubectl logs reads them directly, which is fine for debugging and useless afterwards:

For anything you need to keep, run a log shipper as a DaemonSet. Loki with Promtail or Alloy is the common pairing with Prometheus and Grafana and is far cheaper to operate than Elasticsearch; the ELK or OpenSearch stack remains the choice where full-text search over large volumes matters.
Log to stdout in JSON. Writing to files inside the container means the collector cannot see them, and structured logs make fields queryable instead of regex-matched.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl logs <pod>
kubectl logs <pod> --previous        # the run that crashed
kubectl logs -l app=payments-api --tail=100 --prefix
kubectl logs <pod> --since=1h

sections.title: Events expire
paragraphs: Events are how Kubernetes explains itself, and they are only retained for one hour by default:

That hour is routinely shorter than the time between an incident and someone investigating it. Ship events into your logging system, kube-prometheus-stack does not do this by itself, and the gap is easy to miss until you need an event that has already expired.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=payments-api-7d4f-x8k2

sections.title: Tracing
paragraphs: Metrics say something is slow; traces say where. OpenTelemetry is the standard instrumentation layer, with Tempo, Jaeger or a commercial backend behind it.
Worth adding once you have several services calling each other. Before that, metrics and logs cover most of what you need.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team installs metrics-server and asks why they cannot graph last week's memory usage. What is the explanation?
A ServiceMonitor is applied, the application exposes /metrics correctly, but no target appears in Prometheus. What are the two things to check first?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does kubectl top not work on my cluster?

metrics-server is not installed, or is not healthy. It is a separate component that collects current CPU and memory from each kubelet and serves the Metrics API that kubectl top reads, and most distributions do not ship it by default. Check with kubectl get deployment metrics-server -n kube-system. The same component backs the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, so an HPA showing <unknown> targets usually has the same root cause. The other possibility there being Pods with no resource requests.
What is the difference between metrics-server and Prometheus?

metrics-server serves only current CPU and memory readings, keeps no history, and exists to support kubectl top and autoscaling. Prometheus is a time-series database that scrapes many sources on an interval, stores the results, and supports querying, dashboards and alerting. They are complementary rather than alternatives: you generally run metrics-server for the HPA and Prometheus for everything a human looks at.
What is kube-state-metrics and do I need it?

It exposes the state of Kubernetes objects as Prometheus metrics. How many replicas a Deployment wants versus has available, which phase each Pod is in, container restart counts, job completions. It measures the API server's view rather than actual resource consumption, which is why it complements the kubelet's cAdvisor metrics rather than duplicating them. Most genuinely useful alerts are built on it, so yes. It is included in kube-prometheus-stack.
How do I keep logs after a Pod is deleted?

You cannot with kubectl logs. Container logs live on the node and are removed with the Pod, and --previous only reaches back one container generation. Run a log shipper as a DaemonSet on every node: Promtail or Grafana Alloy feeding Loki is the usual pairing alongside Prometheus, while Fluent Bit into OpenSearch or a commercial backend suits environments needing heavier full-text search. Have applications log to stdout in JSON, since files written inside the container are invisible to the collector.
Why do my Kubernetes events disappear?

Events have a one-hour retention by default, controlled by the API server's --event-ttl. That is often shorter than the gap between an incident and someone investigating it, so the scheduling failure or probe error that explains everything has already expired. Ship events into your logging system with a tool such as the Kubernetes Event Exporter. This is not included in kube-prometheus-stack and is easy to overlook until the moment you need an event that is gone.
What should I alert on?

Symptoms that users experience, not every metric that moves. A short, honest starting set: Pods crash-looping, Deployments with unavailable replicas, nodes not Ready, disk above 85%, certificates expiring within two weeks, and your own error rate and latency against an agreed SLO. Always include a for clause so transient blips do not page anyone. Alerts nobody acts on are worse than no alerts, because they teach people to ignore the channel that also carries the real ones.
